2.title: Lower Than the Angels: The Glory of the Humiliated Son
2.overview:
If chapter 1 is a summit, chapter 2 is a deliberate descent, and just as glorious. The obvious objection is: if Jesus is this exalted Son, why did he suffer and die? The answer comes through Psalm 8. Man was made to rule creation, but we do not yet see it. What we see is Jesus, made lower than the angels, tasting death for everyone, and crowned with glory. The humiliation was the road by which the founder of salvation brings many sons to glory. He shared our flesh to destroy the devil’s power and free us from the fear of death.

The chapter also contains the first of five warning passages (vv. 1–4): if the law given through angels carried penalties, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first of the letter’s warnings follows. Because of who the Son is, the readers must hold on all the more carefully to the message they heard, or they will drift away from it like a boat slipping its mooring. If the law delivered through angels was binding, and every breach of it was justly punished, there will be no escape for those who shrug off a salvation this great. It was first announced by the Lord himself, confirmed to us by those who heard him, and backed by God with signs, wonders, miracles and gifts of the Spirit given as he chose.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Danger Is Drift

The peril is not dramatic renunciation but neglect — slipping past the harbour without ever deciding to leave. The remedy is attention to what has been heard.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If the law given through angels carried penalties, neglecting the salvation declared by the Lord is more serious still.

Now: The question is not whether you have renounced Christ but whether you are still paying attention.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it. For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it. For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,

Meaning first. Hebrews 2 has two movements. First, the first of the letter’s five warnings (vv. 1–4): since the Son is so much greater than angels, his message is so much more serious than the law given through angels. If disobeying that law brought just punishment, there is no escape for those who neglect the great salvation announced by the Lord, confirmed by eyewitnesses, and attested by God with miracles and gifts of the Spirit. Second, why the Son became lower than the angels (vv. 5–18). Psalm 8 says God made humanity lower than the angels and crowned it with glory, putting everything under its feet. We do not yet see everything subject to humanity; but we do see Jesus, made lower than angels for a little while, now crowned with glory because he suffered death for others (vv. 5–9). It was fitting for God to make the pioneer of salvation perfect through suffering, so that he could bring many sons to glory; Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers (vv. 10–13). He shared our flesh and blood so that by his death he could destroy the devil, who held the power of death, and free those enslaved by fear of death (vv. 14–15). He helps the descendants of Abraham, not angels, and so he had to become like his brothers in every way, to be a merciful and faithful high priest who makes propitiation for the people’s sins and helps them when they are tempted, having been tempted himself (vv. 16–18).

How Hebrews is built. “Therefore” (dia touto, because of this), and the first of the letter’s five great warnings arrives hard on the heels of the argument that produced it. This is the architecture of the whole sermon: a stretch of doctrine, then an application with teeth in it, then more doctrine. The writer never lets a truth stand without asking what it requires. The Son is the radiance of God’s glory, the Creator, the enthroned King; therefore you cannot treat his word casually.

Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard. “Pay much closer attention” (perissoterōs prosechein) means give exceedingly greater heed. And note the pronoun. Not you must, but we must. The preacher puts himself inside the warning, and he will do it again and again through this letter. Whatever else these passages are, they are not a man lecturing people he considers less safe than himself. “What we have heard” is the gospel, the message about the Son that chapter 1 has just set in its glory.

Lest we drift away from it. Then the danger, and it is not the one we expect. The word (pararyōmen) is nautical. It is used of a ship that slips its moorings, or of a boat carried past the harbour mouth by a current the crew never noticed; it was also used of a ring slipping off a finger. The point is that nobody decides to drift. Drifting is what happens when nothing is decided at all. The danger is not dramatic rebellion but slow, careless drift. Neglect is enough to be lost. Nobody has to do anything to drift; they just have to stop paying attention.

The commoner peril. That is the peril this letter addresses, and it should be said plainly, because it is far commoner than open apostasy. These readers were not planning to renounce Christ. They were tired, socially battered and quietly attending less; the old ways were warm and familiar, and there was no particular moment at which they chose to leave. Drift requires no decision, no argument and no crisis. It requires only that you stop rowing. And the remedy is stated in the same breath: pay much closer attention. Not try harder to feel, but attend to what you have heard, because what is being lost is not grip but contact.

For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable. Verse 2 begins the argument, and it is an argument from the lesser to the greater. The message declared by angels is the law at Sinai, which Jewish tradition held was mediated through angels (Acts 7:38, 53; Galatians 3:19; Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek translation). It proved reliable (bebaios, firm, valid, legally binding). It held; it was not a word you could ignore without consequence.

And every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution. Two words for two failures. “Transgression” (parabasis) is stepping over the line, active sin. “Disobedience” (parakoē) is literally mis-hearing, refusing to listen, passive neglect. Both were punished. And the penalty is called just (endikon misthapodosian, fair payment, a deserved penalty): the writer is not describing arbitrary severity but a system that worked as advertised (Numbers 15:30–31; Deuteronomy 17:2–7). Notice that refusing to listen sits beside stepping over the line. In God’s reckoning, not hearing is not neutral.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law was less from God because angels were involved. It came from God through angelic mediation. The point is the argument from lesser to greater: if the lesser message was binding, how much more the greater.

How do I know if I am drifting? Drift is hard to see from inside, because it feels like nothing. Look for small signs rather than dramatic ones. Prayer has shrunk to emergencies. The Bible is opened less, and with less expectation. Missing church no longer bothers you. Sin that once grieved you now merely irritates you. Christian friends have quietly been replaced by others. Your thoughts about God are mostly about what he has not done. None of these proves you are lost; each is a current. The remedy is not panic but attention: return to the word, to prayer, to the gathered church, and to the Son who is greater than everything that has been pulling you away.

In a sentence. That is why we must pay much more careful attention to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. For if the message delivered through angels was binding, and every wrongdoing and disobedience was justly punished,

On a Tuesday. Are you drifting? Drift happens through neglect, so the answer is a deliberate stroke of the oar. Take one step today: read a chapter slowly, pray for ten minutes without your phone, text a Christian friend, decide now that you will be at worship on Sunday. Moorings are tied with small knots, and they are tied again every day.

For worship. The God who spoke at Sinai with fire and trumpet, through the ministry of angels, has spoken again, and this time in his own Son. He did not have to warn us. A God who wanted to be rid of careless people would have let them drift without a word. Instead he raises his voice in love, like a man on the shore shouting to a boat moving toward the rocks. Every warning in this letter is the Father calling his children back to the harbour, and the harbour is his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that the law was given through angels.

verseByVerse.quote: how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.

How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? The argument completes itself, and the logic is uncomfortable precisely because it is so simple. If the word that came through angels carried consequences, what happens to those who ignore the word that came through the Son? The greater the messenger, the greater the weight of the message. “Escape” (ekpheuxometha) is to flee out of, get away from, and the thing escaped is the judgement of God.

Neglect. Note the verb. Not reject, not deny, not blaspheme. The word (amelēsantes) means to be careless of, to pay no regard to, not to care for. It is the word Jesus used in his parable of those invited to the wedding who paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business (Matthew 22:5). It is the same idea as the drifting of verse 1. Nobody in this congregation was tearing up the gospel. They were letting it slide, and the writer says that is enough to be in danger. That should be allowed to land. A great deal of Christian anxiety attaches to dramatic sins, and Hebrews keeps pointing at something quieter. The question in this letter is never only, have you renounced Christ? It is, are you still paying attention?

Such a great salvation. This is the counterweight (tēlikautēs sōtērias, so vast a salvation). The warning is heavy because the thing being neglected is enormous, and the writer has spent a chapter establishing how enormous: a salvation won by the Creator of the ages, who made purification for sins and sat down. Neglect is dangerous in proportion to the worth of what is being neglected. The greater the gift, the greater the guilt of neglecting it. A man who loses a letter is careless; a man who loses a pardon from the king on the morning of his execution is something else.

Can a true Christian drift away and be lost? No, and the warning is still real. The escape in view is escape from final judgement, and the writer includes himself: how shall we escape. But he will also show that those who truly share in Christ hold fast to the end (3:14), and that warnings like this are among the means God uses to keep his people from drifting (compare 6:4–12). God does not keep his children in spite of the warnings; he keeps them through the warnings. The Christian who hears this and pays closer attention is doing exactly what the warning is for. The person who hears it and shrugs should be very afraid, not because a true child of God can be lost, but because the shrug may show he never was one.

It was declared at first by the Lord. Then three lines of transmission, and they repay tracing. The first is the source. The gospel was first spoken (laleisthai) by the Lord Jesus himself: the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel (Mark 1:14–15). Not by angels, but by the Son. The salvation you are tempted to neglect was preached by its own author.

And it was attested to us by those who heard. “Attested” (ebebaiōthē) means confirmed, guaranteed, made firm, from the same root as reliable in verse 2. Eyewitnesses, the apostles, confirmed it. And the phrase quietly tells us something about the writer. He places himself in the second generation, among those who received the message from the men who heard it. Whoever wrote Hebrews, he was not an apostle and did not claim to be, which is one reason most think Paul did not write the letter, since Paul insisted he received the gospel directly from Christ (Galatians 1:11–12).

While God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles. The third line is God’s own. “Bore witness” (synepimartyrountos) means testified together with, added his own testimony. The three words describe the miracles of Jesus and the apostles (Acts 2:22, 43; 2 Corinthians 12:12). “Signs” (sēmeiois) are miracles pointing to a meaning. “Wonders” (terasin) are miracles that astonish. “Miracles” (dynamesin) are works of power. The testimony is not merely human. God himself confirmed the message with supernatural evidence, so that the gospel arrived with three witnesses: the Lord, his apostles, and the Father’s own hand.

And by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will. “Gifts” (merismois) means distributions, apportionings. And the last clause guards them from being anybody’s possession: according to his will. God decides who receives what (1 Corinthians 12:11), which rules out treating any gift as an achievement or a right. Notice too that the signs are described in the past tense, as confirming the message to us in the apostolic generation.

Where Christians differ: do miraculous sign gifts continue today? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe the miraculous gifts, such as healing, tongues and prophecy, continue in the same way throughout the church age. Verdict: this verse describes the signs, wonders and miracles as God’s confirmation of the gospel through those who heard the Lord, that is, the apostolic generation (2 Corinthians 12:12). Their purpose was to authenticate the foundational revelation. With that revelation complete, the sign gifts have ceased in that form. God still works powerfully, answers prayer, heals as he wills, and gives every believer gifts for service (Romans 12:6–8; 1 Peter 4:10–11). This cessationist view is held charitably toward brothers who differ.

The order of the witnesses. Notice the order the verse itself gives. The Lord spoke; those who heard passed it on; and God bore witness with them, the first generation, by signs. The writer, who heard the gospel second-hand, speaks of the signs as part of how the message was first confirmed, and Paul calls such things the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). The message no longer needs confirming in that way. It has been confirmed, and it is written, and the same Spirit who once attested it with wonders now opens blind eyes to it through the word.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God can no longer do miracles. He is sovereign and may act extraordinarily at any time. It means the apostolic sign gifts, given to confirm new revelation, are not a normal ongoing feature of the church.

Should I pray for healing, then? Yes, with confidence and without embarrassment. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped healing; it is the belief that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gift of healing at will. James tells the sick to call the elders, who pray over them and anoint them in the name of the Lord (James 5:14–15), and that instruction is for the whole church age. So pray for the sick, specifically and persistently, and ask the elders to pray. Then leave the answer to God, who sometimes heals at once, sometimes through doctors and time, and sometimes by giving grace to bear what he does not remove (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

In a sentence. how can we possibly escape if we disregard so great a salvation? It was first announced by the Lord himself, and it was confirmed to us by those who heard him, while God added his own testimony through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit given out as he chose.

On a Tuesday. Have you grown careless about the gospel? Spend ten minutes today thinking only about how great your salvation is. Write down what you were saved from, what it cost, who accomplished it, and what you have been given. If the list leaves you unmoved, ask God to restore the wonder. Then tell one person, before the week is out, one sentence about what Christ has done for you. Neglect is cured by attention, and attention grows by speaking.

For worship. So great a salvation. It was planned before the foundation of the world, promised through a thousand years of prophets, preached by the Son with his own lips, sealed by his blood, confirmed by eyewitnesses who would not stop speaking even under the whip, and attested by the hand of God in signs and wonders. It was announced to people who did not ask for it and could not earn it. Of all the things in the world that could be neglected, this is the one that is too great to be ignored, and the God who gave it still pleads with us to receive it.
verseByVerse.note: The writer did not hear Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Founder Made Perfect Through Suffering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Psalm 8 says God crowned man with glory and put everything under him, but we do not yet see that. We see Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while, crowned because he suffered death for everyone. It was fitting that God should make the founder of salvation perfect through suffering, bringing many sons to glory. He is not ashamed to call them brothers. He shared flesh and blood to destroy the devil and free those enslaved by the fear of death. He was made like us in every way, to be a merciful and faithful high priest, and because he suffered when tempted, he can help those who are tempted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear of Death as Lifelong Slavery

We do not yet see everything subject to man, but we see Jesus — lowered, crowned, tasting death for everyone. He shared flesh and blood to break the devil's hold through the fear of death, and to make propitiation as a merciful and faithful high priest.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation that had lost property wondered why following a crowned Lord meant shame. The pattern he walked runs down first.

Now: Because he suffered when tempted, he is able to help those being tempted — today.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking. It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking. It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.

For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come. The writer returns to angels and to his real subject, which is man. “Subjected” (hypetaxen) means placed under authority. “The world to come” (tēn oikoumenēn tēn mellousan, the coming inhabited world) is the new creation, the age inaugurated by Christ and consummated at his return. Some Jewish thought held that angels governed the nations in this age (Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Greek; Daniel 10:13, 20). But the coming world will be ruled not by angels but by Christ and his people. And the argument now takes an unexpected turn, because the answer is not simply the Son. It is humanity, in the Son.

It has been testified somewhere. “Somewhere” (pou) is a curious way to introduce Scripture, and it recurs in this letter (4:4). It is not vagueness; the writer knows exactly what he is quoting. It reflects a way of citing in which the speaker that matters is God rather than the human author, so the message matters more than the reference.

What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? The quotation is Psalm 8:4–6, following the Greek translation, and it is a psalm about the dignity of human beings. David is lying under the night sky, overwhelmed by his own smallness under the moon and the stars God set in place. And the answer the psalm gives is not that man is nothing. It is that God remembers him, cares for him, and has crowned him. “Son of man” in the psalm means a human being. But the phrase also became Jesus’ favourite title for himself (Daniel 7:13), and the writer sees the psalm fulfilled in Jesus as the true representative man.

You made him for a little while lower than the angels. The phrase (brachy ti) can mean a little lower in rank, or lower for a little while in time, and the writer builds on the second, because it lets the psalm describe a temporary humiliation followed by a crowning. In the Hebrew psalm humanity is made a little lower than God, or than the heavenly beings; the Greek translation has angels. Humanity occupies a place in creation below the angels in power, yet crowned with dignity.

You have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet. That is the creation mandate of Genesis 1: dominion, given to humanity as God’s image-bearers, over the works of God’s hands (Genesis 1:26–28). That was the original design. Man was made a king, a gardener-king under the great King, to rule the earth for God.

Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. The psalm’s everything means everything: no exceptions. Not the beasts only, but the whole created order was to be under human feet, under God.

At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. Then the writer stops and says the honest thing. He has quoted a magnificent text about human dominion, and he immediately concedes that it is visibly untrue. “Not yet” (oupō). We do not rule. We are ruled: by decay, by circumstance, by disease, by disasters, by the devil and by death. The fall disrupted God’s design (Romans 8:20–22). The congregation he is writing to had been ruled by a mob that confiscated their property (10:34). That admission is one of the most honest sentences in Scripture, and everything in the next verse depends on it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the psalm was wrong or has failed. It awaits fulfilment, and that fulfilment has begun in Jesus. Nor does it deny that angels serve God in governing the world now; it means the age to come belongs to Christ and his redeemed people.

If human beings were made to rule, why do I feel so small and powerless? Because you are living in the not yet, and the Bible does not pretend otherwise. The smallness you feel is real: one diagnosis, one redundancy, one bereavement can show how little we control. But it is not the end of the story. You were made for dignity, and the dignity is not cancelled by the fall, only delayed and damaged. In Christ it is being restored, and in the world to come the redeemed will reign with him (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 5:10). So feel your weakness honestly, and do not despise it. It is the place where Psalm 8 is waiting to be fulfilled in you.

Does this psalm say anything about how I treat other people? A great deal. If God is mindful of every human being and crowned humanity with glory and honour, then no person is beneath your notice: not the unborn child, the elderly woman with dementia, the man sleeping in a doorway, the colleague you find tiresome. Each bears God’s image and was made for a crown. Contempt for any human being is contempt for something God has honoured. Treat people as the psalm sees them, and you will find yourself treating them as Christ did.

In a sentence. For God did not place the coming world, which we are talking about, under the authority of angels. Someone has testified somewhere: What is a human being, that you remember him, a mortal, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour and put everything under his feet. In putting everything under him, God left nothing that is not under him. Yet at present we do not see everything under human control.

On a Tuesday. Tonight, if the sky is clear, go outside for five minutes and look up, as David did. Let the size of it make you small. Then say Psalm 8 slowly, and thank God that the Maker of all that is mindful of you. Tomorrow, choose one person the world overlooks and treat them as a creature crowned with glory and honour: learn their name, listen to them, help them.

For worship. The God who flung out the galaxies stooped to remember a creature made of dust, and crowned him. Then that creature threw the crown away, and the world he was meant to rule turned against him. But God did not withdraw the psalm. He kept it, and sent his own Son to fulfil it from the bottom up. What humanity lost in a garden, the true Man is winning back, and one day every promise in Psalm 8 will be true of those who are his.

verseByVerse.quote: But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.

But we see him. Four words, and they are the answer to the crisis the last verse created. We do not see everything in subjection to man, but we see one man, and in him the psalm has come true. What is not visible in general is visible in a particular person. “See” (blepomen) is to look at, to perceive, and here it is the sight of faith. The readers had never laid eyes on Jesus, but they could see him in the gospel more clearly than they could see their own circumstances.

Who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus. Note where the name falls. The writer has been talking about the Son who is the radiance of God’s glory, and now, at the point of humiliation, he uses the human name for the first time in the letter. It is held back to the end of the phrase for emphasis. Jesus. The carpenter’s son from Nazareth. In becoming man he took the place of humanity, lower than the angels (Philippians 2:7–8). He is the true man, the last Adam, in whom Psalm 8 is fulfilled (1 Corinthians 15:27, 45).

Crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death. “Crowned” (estephanōmenon) is perfect tense: crowned, and still crowned. The psalm’s words have come true in Jesus. And the order is everything. Psalm 8 has humiliation and then crowning; Jesus has taken exactly that route, and the crowning is because of the suffering, not in spite of it (Philippians 2:8–9). The cross is not an obstacle he overcame on the way to glory. It is the ground of the glory. Through death to glory. That is the answer to a congregation asking why following a crowned Lord has landed them in poverty and shame. The pattern they are living is the pattern he lived, and it runs in one direction: down first, then up.

So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. “By the grace of God” (chariti theou) names the cause. His death was the gift of God’s grace; there was no necessity laid on God from outside. It puts the whole transaction where Hebrews always puts it, in the initiative of God rather than the achievement of man. And “taste death” (geusētai thanatou) does not mean sip. In Hebrew idiom to taste death is to experience it fully (Mark 9:1). He drank it to the bottom. “For everyone” (hyper pantos) is on behalf of each. In the context, the everyone are the many sons being brought to glory (v. 10), his brothers (v. 11), the children God has given him (v. 13), the offspring of Abraham (v. 16), the people (v. 17).

Textual note. A few manuscripts and some early church writers read “apart from God” (chōris theou) instead of “by the grace of God” (chariti theou). The two look similar in Greek. “Apart from God” might refer to Jesus’ cry of abandonment on the cross, or to his dying for all apart from God himself. But the great majority of manuscripts read “by the grace of God,” and that is almost certainly original.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every individual equally? Many read “for everyone” as proof that Christ’s death was equally for every human being, making salvation possible for all. Verdict: the surrounding verses define the everyone as the many sons brought to glory, the brothers he sanctifies, the children given to him by the Father (vv. 10–13). His death actually achieves their salvation: it brings them to glory, destroys the devil’s power over them, frees them, and makes propitiation for their sins (vv. 10, 14–17). This is definite atonement: Christ tasted death for each one of those he came to save, and none of them will be lost. Jesus lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:15). Yet his death is of infinite value, sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to every person.

What it does not mean. “For everyone” does not mean all will be saved. Hebrews warns repeatedly that those who reject Christ face judgement (2:3; 10:26–31).

Can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for him? You can tell him, truly and urgently, that Christ died for sinners, that his death is enough for anyone, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37). That is how the apostles preached: they did not begin by explaining whom God had chosen; they called everyone to repent and believe. Definite atonement does not narrow the offer; it guarantees that the offer is backed by a death that actually saves. You can say to anyone with full sincerity: come to Christ, and you will find that he died for you.

In a sentence. What we do see is Jesus, who for a short time was made lower than the angels and who is now crowned with glory and honour because he suffered death, so that by God’s grace he might experience death on behalf of each one of his people.

On a Tuesday. When your circumstances say that God’s promises have failed, do what the writer does: stop looking at everything, and look at him. Write at the top of a page what you cannot see working out. Under it write: but we see Jesus. Then list what is already true of him: crowned, seated, victorious, interceding. The not yet in your life is answered by the already in his.

For worship. He tasted death, all of it, the bitterness of it, the God-forsakenness of it, for each of his own. He did not sip and set the cup down. He drank it until there was nothing left, so that those for whom he died would never taste it as judgement. And now he wears a crown that was won on a cross. Every believer who closes his eyes in death will find that the cup has already been emptied, and that the one who emptied it is waiting with the crown he won.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.

For it was fitting that he. The word is startling. “Fitting” (eprepen) means appropriate, suitable, worthy of. The writer says that the cross was appropriate: that when you know who God is, this is what you would expect him to do. That cuts against every instinct. A God who saves by becoming a man and being executed looks to most religious sensibilities like a scandal to be explained away; Paul says as much, a stumbling block and folly (1 Corinthians 1:23). Hebrews says it suited him. Given his character, his holiness and his love together, no other method would have been in keeping. The cross was not an embarrassing necessity but entirely fitting with God’s character and wisdom.

For whom and by whom all things exist. The Father is named as the goal and the origin of everything. “For whom” (di’ hon): God is the goal of all things. “By whom” (di’ hou): God is the cause of all things (Romans 11:36). The one with no obligations to anybody, the Creator and goal of everything, chose this way of salvation, and it was worthy of him.

In bringing many sons to glory. Here is the aim, and pause on it. “Bringing” (agagonta) is leading. “Many sons” (pollous huious) are the redeemed, adopted as God’s children (Romans 8:14–17, 29). “Glory” is final salvation, sharing in Christ’s glory (Romans 8:18, 30), the same glory the psalm spoke of, the dominion humanity lost. The purpose is not merely to forgive people or to secure their safety. It is to lead a great family home to glory. God is not merely repairing the damage; he is completing the original design. And it is many: not a handful of survivors, but a great multitude that no one can number.

Should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering. “Founder” (archēgos) is a rich word: a pioneer who goes first and opens a way, a trailblazer cutting a path through the forest, the founder of a city, a chief at the head of a column, a champion who fights on behalf of his people (12:2; Acts 3:15; 5:31). It is not the word for an inventor of a scheme. It is the word for a man at the front, and the point is that he goes where the others will follow. Then the hard phrase: perfect through suffering. “Perfect” (teleiōsai) means to complete, to bring to the goal, to make fully fit for a purpose. It is a keyword of Hebrews, and in the Greek Old Testament it is used of consecrating a priest to his office. It does not mean Jesus was morally imperfect and needed improving; he was always sinless (4:15; 7:26). What the suffering completed was not his character but his qualification. He was made fully qualified as Saviour and High Priest by going through suffering, testing and death (5:8–9). He could not have been a high priest able to sympathise without having been through it.

Out in front. So the sentence holds two things a suffering congregation needed together. Their pioneer was made fit for his office by suffering, and he is out in front, on a road he has already walked. They were not lost in a wilderness. They were following tracks.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus was ever sinful or deficient in character. Nor does it mean God enjoyed his Son’s suffering. It means the path to glory for the Saviour, and for his people, passes through suffering, and that this was wise and right.

Does this mean my suffering is part of the path too? Yes. Not that suffering earns glory, which Christ alone earned, but that God leads his sons to glory by the same road their pioneer took. Your suffering is not a sign that you have taken a wrong turning, or that God has forgotten you. It is the country the founder of your salvation has already crossed. He is not shouting directions from the far side; he walked it, and he is leading you through it. And it has an end: the road goes to glory. Paul could call the heaviest affliction light and momentary beside the eternal weight of glory it is preparing (2 Corinthians 4:17).

In a sentence. It was right for God, for whom and through whom everything exists, in bringing many children to glory, to make the pioneer of their salvation fully qualified through suffering.

On a Tuesday. If you are suffering, say it to him plainly: Lord, you have been here. Name the thing, the pain, the loneliness, the injustice, and ask him how he walked through it. Read one account of his own suffering, Gethsemane or the trial or the cross, and notice how he trusted his Father. Then take one step on today’s part of the road, trusting that the pioneer is ahead of you.

For worship. The Lord of all things, for whom and through whom everything exists, set out to bring a great family home to glory, and he chose the road that was most worthy of himself: the road of the cross. His Son went first, through the thorns and the dark, through betrayal and agony and death, and came out the other side crowned. The way to glory is open now, and the one who opened it walks at the head of the column, leading many sons home.

verseByVerse.quote: For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.” And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.” And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”

For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified. “Sanctifies” (hagiazōn) means makes holy, sets apart for God. Jesus is the one who makes his people holy, by his blood (10:10, 14; 13:12). Those who are sanctified are believers, set apart for God. One makes holy; the others are made holy. The distinction is never blurred, and yet the next phrase binds them together.

All have one source. The Greek is literally are all of one (ex henos pantes), and the writer leaves it open: one Father, one stock, one family. “One” may be God, the one Father of both Jesus and believers; or Adam, shared human nature; or simply one family. Most likely God the Father: Jesus and his people share one Father and one family, and Jesus shares their humanity. What the writer is establishing is a shared origin. The sanctifier and the sanctified belong to the same household.

That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers. The phrasing concedes what it denies. To say a man is not ashamed of something is to admit there was every reason he might have been, and the writer means it. These are the people he has just described as drifting, and will describe as enslaved by lifelong fear, whose record is what it is. The exalted Son of God, the radiance of the Father’s glory, is not embarrassed to be publicly associated with them (Matthew 12:49–50). On the morning of his resurrection, the first message he sent was to the men who had run away: go to my brothers (John 20:17).

I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise. Then three quotations, and each does a distinct job. The first is Psalm 22:22. Psalm 22 is the psalm of the crucifixion; it opens with the cry Jesus made from the cross, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Psalm 22:1). And the writer takes the verse where the psalm turns from anguish to triumph. So the brotherhood is announced by a man coming out the far side of dereliction, and the first thing he does is sing among his brothers. “Congregation” is ekklēsia, church. The risen Christ leads his church in worship. When the people of God sing, the loudest voice in the room is his.

I will put my trust in him. The second is from Isaiah 8:17 (compare 2 Samuel 22:3; Isaiah 12:2). It is a short line and it carries a great deal. Here is the Son, in his humanity, doing the thing that most obviously marks a creature rather than the Creator: trusting God. He is like his brothers in that too. As a true man he lived by faith in his Father, as his brothers must, and he is the supreme example of trust (12:2). Whatever faith is asked of us, he exercised it first, in the dark, on a cross.

Behold, I and the children God has given me. The third comes from the next verse of the same passage (Isaiah 8:18). In Isaiah the prophet stands with his sons as living signs to an unbelieving nation. Here it is Christ presenting his own, and note the word given. They are not recruits he gathered. They were handed to him by the Father, which is the note of John 17:6 and of the promise that all the Father gives him will come to him, and he will lose none of them (John 6:37, 39; 10:29). Between them the three texts make the family complete: a brother who sings with them, who trusts alongside them, and who presents them to God as his own.

What it does not mean. “One source” does not mean believers are divine as Jesus is. He is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. He is the Sanctifier; we are the sanctified.

How can he not be ashamed of me, when I am ashamed of myself? Because his acceptance of you does not rest on what you are in yourself but on what he has done for you and the Father has given him. He calls you brother not because he overlooks your sin, but because he has dealt with it: he is the one who sanctifies. Shame says you must hide; the gospel says you have been claimed. When shame rises, do not argue with it on its own terms by listing your good points. Answer it with his words: here am I, and the children God has given me. He is not ashamed to stand beside you before the Father, and he has already done so.

What does it mean that Jesus sings in the church? It means that when the congregation gathers to praise God, Christ himself is present, leading the praise. Our worship is not a performance we offer to win God over; it is joining the song of the risen Son, who declares the Father’s name to his brothers. That should change how you come on Sunday. You are not dragging your weary voice into a void. You are standing next to the Son, and your weak praise is carried in his.

In a sentence. The one who makes people holy and those who are made holy belong to the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters. He says, I will declare your name to my brothers and sisters; in the assembly I will sing your praises. And again, I will put my trust in him. And again, Here I am, and the children God has given me.

On a Tuesday. Think of the believer you are most inclined to be embarrassed by: the awkward one, the one with the past, the one who says the wrong thing. Jesus calls him brother. This week, do something that publicly owns him as family: sit with him, invite him home, speak well of him. And when you are ashamed of yourself, say aloud: he is not ashamed to call me brother. Then go and sing on Sunday as if he were standing beside you, because he is.

For worship. The Son of God has brothers, and he is proud of them. He walked out of the tomb and sent word to the deserters that they were still family. He stands in the assembly of forgiven sinners and leads their song. He trusted his Father in the dark so that they could learn to trust. And on the last day he will present them all, not one missing, before the throne, and say: behold, I and the children you gave me.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.

Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood. Two different verbs, and the difference is the incarnation. The children share in flesh and blood (kekoinōnēken, perfect tense): an ongoing common possession, a settled condition; it is simply what they are. Flesh and blood (haimatos kai sarkos) is human nature, with all its weakness and mortality.

He himself likewise partook of the same things. “Partook” (meteschen) is a single decisive act, something he took up that was not natively his. He entered a condition the rest of us are merely born into. The eternal Son took on a real human body and soul. He did not merely appear human; he became fully human (John 1:14; Philippians 2:7; 1 John 4:2). He had to share our nature to save us.

That through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil. The purpose is stated with brutal directness. Read the mechanism. He became mortal in order to die. That is the whole reason for the flesh and blood: not primarily so that he could teach or set an example, but so that he would have something to lay down. God cannot die; a man can. “Destroy” (katargēsē) does not mean annihilate. It means to render powerless, to nullify, to put out of action, the same word Paul uses when he says Christ abolished death (2 Timothy 1:10). The devil has not ceased to exist. His weapon has been taken away.

How the devil held the power of death. The devil held the power of death (to kratos tou thanatou, the dominion of death) in that he brought sin into the world, and sin brings death (Genesis 3; Romans 5:12; John 8:44). He accuses sinners and holds them under death’s penalty. By dying for sin, Christ removed the ground of the devil’s accusation and broke his grip (Colossians 2:14–15; Revelation 12:10–11). The irony is magnificent: the devil’s weapon, death, became the means of his defeat. He drove the Son of God to the cross and found that he had broken his own weapon on him.

And deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery. This is one of the most penetrating verses in the New Testament. “Deliver” (apallaxē) is set free, release. The diagnosis is that the fear of death (phobō thanatou) is a form of slavery, and that it lasts a whole life: they were liable to bondage all their lives. Not an occasional dread at a graveside, but a permanent condition working underneath everything. It is what makes a man grasp, hoard, protect himself, refuse risks and cling to comfort. Much of what is called self-interest is fear of death wearing ordinary clothes.

Leverage taken away. And note how the devil’s power actually operates in this sentence. He holds people not chiefly by direct violence but through fear. Take the fear away and the leverage is gone, which is exactly what the resurrection does, and why the early Christians were so difficult for the empire to manage. You cannot finally threaten a man who has stopped being afraid of the worst thing you can do to him. For the believer, death is no longer a punishment but a passage to Christ (Philippians 1:21–23; 1 Corinthians 15:55–57).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the devil now has no activity at all; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8). It means his decisive power has been broken, and his final destruction is certain (Revelation 20:10). Nor does it mean believers never feel any fear of dying; it means that fear no longer rules them.

I am a Christian, but I am still afraid of dying. Is something wrong with my faith? Not necessarily. The verse frees you from slavery to the fear, not from every feeling of it. Death is still an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26); Jesus himself wept at a grave and sweated in the garden. What changes is that fear no longer has the last word or rules your choices. You can feel the dread and still trust the one who has gone through death and come out. Bring the fear to him honestly. Ask him to show you what death is now for you: not the jaws of judgement, but a door into his presence. Often it is the process of dying more than death itself we fear, and he has promised to be with you in the valley too (Psalm 23:4).

In a sentence. Since the children have flesh and blood, Jesus too shared in their humanity, so that by his death he might break the power of the one who holds the power of death, the devil, and set free all who have been held in slavery all their lives by their fear of death.

On a Tuesday. Ask what fear of death is quietly steering in your life: the need for control, the hoarding of money, the refusal of risk for Christ, the dread of growing old. Name one decision you have avoided because of it. Then make it in faith this week: give, speak, go, or rest. And if someone you love is facing death, sit with them and read them these two verses.

For worship. The Son of God took flesh so that he could die. He put on mortality like armour that was meant to be pierced, and walked into the stronghold of the enemy, and let death take him. And death could not hold him. The devil’s great weapon broke in his hand, and the prisoners walked out. The tyrant who ruled by fear has been disarmed by a crucified man, and the fear that enslaved the whole human race has met its master in the one who rose.

verseByVerse.quote: For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.

For surely it is not angels that he helps. The verb is vivid and rare: epilambanetai, to take hold of, to lay hands on and grip. It is the word used of Jesus reaching out and catching Peter as he sank (Matthew 14:31), and of God taking Israel by the hand to lead them out of Egypt (Jeremiah 31:32, quoted at 8:9). Not assistance offered from a distance, but a hand closing on someone who is going down. Christ did not take hold of angels to save them. Fallen angels have no redeemer (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). He did not become an angel; he became a man.

Specific mercy. The point of the comparison is not that angels are neglected. It is that the incarnation was specific. He did not take hold of angelic nature; he took hold of ours. If you are looking for the reason the Son became a man rather than something more glorious, this is it: he came for the ones he came for.

But he helps the offspring of Abraham. For a congregation of Jewish Christians wondering whether following Jesus had cost them their inheritance, this is a pointed way to put it (spermatos Abraam, seed of Abraham). Far from severing them from Abraham, the incarnation is the fulfilment of what was promised to him (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). And the phrase reaches further than ancestry. Abraham’s true children are all who share his faith, Jew and Gentile (Galatians 3:7, 29; Romans 4:16). The writer chooses a description that is true of his readers by blood and true of every believer by promise.

Why did God not save the fallen angels? Scripture does not tell us, and speculation is unprofitable. What this verse says is not that angels were refused but that the Son took hold of Abraham’s offspring, and it says it as an act of sheer, specific mercy toward people who had no more claim on him than anyone else. The right response is not to work out why we were chosen and they were not, but to wonder that he took hold of us at all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ saves only ethnic Jews. Abraham’s offspring, in the New Testament sense, are all who believe (Romans 4:11–12). Nor does it mean Christ is indifferent to angels; the holy angels serve him gladly. But redemption is for human beings.

In a sentence. For it is clearly not angels that he takes hold of to help, but the descendants of Abraham.

On a Tuesday. Picture Peter sinking in the waves and the hand that caught him. Then think of the place in your life where you are going under: a sin, a sorrow, a fear. Cry out as Peter did: Lord, save me. The hand that took hold of human nature in Bethlehem takes hold of human beings still. And this week, reach out your own hand to someone sinking, because those he has gripped are meant to grip others.

For worship. He passed by the angels, mighty and glorious, and stooped to the descendants of a nomad from Ur. He did not take hold of the stars or the seraphim. He took hold of flesh, and of frightened people sinking in the sea, and of you. He has taken hold of you, and he will not let go. The grip of the Son of God on the offspring of Abraham is the safest place in the universe.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.

Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect. Not in most respects. In every respect (kata panta, in all things): body, soul, emotions, temptations, weakness, suffering and death. Everything human, except sin, and the letter will supply that one exception later: yet without sin (4:15). Hunger, exhaustion, grief, the fear in the garden were genuinely his. He did not take a human body without a human mind, as some ancient heretics taught; he took full human nature. “Had to” (ōpheilen) means was obligated, needed. Given what he came to do, there was no shortcut available. A high priest must be taken from among the people he represents (5:1), and a representative who had not shared the condition could not have represented anybody.

So that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest. Now the letter’s great theme is named for the first time: Jesus as high priest. Everything from chapter 5 to chapter 10 will unpack it. The high priest (archiereus) was the chief priest of Israel, who entered the Most Holy Place once a year to make atonement (Leviticus 16). Jesus is the true High Priest to whom Aaron pointed. And the two adjectives face two directions. Merciful (eleēmōn, compassionate) toward us, because he knows from inside what it is like. Faithful (pistos, trustworthy, reliable) toward God, carrying out his task perfectly. A priest needs both, and most human priests manage one: severe men who are reliable, or kind men who are lax. This one is both, without remainder.

In the service of God. Literally in the things pertaining to God (ta pros ton theon). The priest represents people before God. He stands on the human side of the gap and reaches across it.

To make propitiation for the sins of the people. The word is hilaskesthai, the technical term for what happened on the Day of Atonement; the related noun names the mercy seat itself, the lid of the ark where the blood was sprinkled (9:5). It must be defined carefully, because it has been fought over. Propitiation means satisfying God’s just wrath against sin by an offering, so that he is favourable toward sinners. It includes expiation, the removal of sin itself. Christ is the propitiation for our sins (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2; 4:10). He bore the wrath we deserved: this is penal substitution. “The people” (tou laou) are God’s people, the brothers of verses 11 to 17.

Not a bribe. Some object that propitiation sounds pagan, like bribing an angry deity. The objection is worth taking seriously, and it does not carry. God’s wrath is not a temper to be bought off but his settled, holy opposition to evil. And the decisive difference from the pagan picture is who provides the sacrifice. In paganism a man appeases a god. Here God, in mercy, supplies the offering himself and, in the person of his Son, bears it himself. That is not bribery; it is the costliest possible love.

Where Christians differ: did Christ’s death turn away God’s wrath? Some modern theologians reject propitiation, arguing that God’s love does not need appeasing, and translate the word only as expiation (removal of sin). Verdict: Scripture teaches that God’s holy wrath is real (Romans 1:18; John 3:36), and that Christ’s death turned it away from his people by bearing it in their place (Isaiah 53:5–6, 10; Galatians 3:13). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son against his will; the Father in love sent the Son to be the propitiation (1 John 4:10). Propitiation and expiation go together: Christ removed our sin and satisfied God’s justice. This is penal substitutionary atonement, the heart of the gospel.

What it does not mean. “Made like his brothers in every respect” does not mean Jesus had a sinful nature or ever sinned. He was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (4:15). True humanity is not defined by sin; sin is a corruption of it.

If God is love, why does he need propitiation at all? Because his love is holy love. A God who shrugged at evil would not be loving; he would be indifferent to the victims of evil and to the ruin it brings. His wrath is the response of perfect goodness to what destroys his world and his creatures. The wonder of the gospel is that the same God whose justice must judge sin is the God whose love provides the sacrifice. The cross is not love overcoming justice, or justice overcoming love. It is both satisfied in one act, in one Person. That is why you can be completely sure of forgiveness: not because God has stopped caring about sin, but because he has dealt with it fully.

In a sentence. That is why he had to be made like his brothers and sisters in every way, so that he could become a merciful and faithful high priest serving God, and make the atoning sacrifice that turns God’s wrath away from the sins of his people.

On a Tuesday. When you sin this week, notice which priest you go to in your mind. Some of us go to a severe one and expect a rebuke; some go to a lax one and expect a shrug. Go to the real one, merciful and faithful. Confess the specific thing, and then thank him that the wrath it deserved has already been borne. Then, because he is faithful to God, ask him to help you turn from it.

For worship. The Son of God was made like us in every respect, so that he could stand where we stand and face what we deserved. He went into the holy place not with the blood of goats but with his own, and the wrath that should have fallen on his people fell on him. He is merciful, because he has felt our weakness; he is faithful, because he never failed his Father once. There is no condemnation left for those who are his, because there is no wrath left in the cup.

verseByVerse.quote: For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.

For because he himself has suffered when tempted. The chapter has climbed from the Son who upholds the universe down to this, and this is where it lands. Not a doctrine but a capability: he is able. “Suffered” (peponthen) is perfect tense: he suffered, and still bears the experience. “Tempted” (peirastheis) covers both temptation and testing, and both are in view. Jesus was truly tempted: in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42–44), and throughout his life (Luke 22:28).

Suffering in temptation. That word repays a moment. We tend to imagine that resisting temptation was easy for him because he was sinless. Hebrews says the opposite. Resisting temptation to the end is painful. Only the person who refuses all the way to the end knows the full force of the thing, because the one who gives in has stopped the pressure early. He felt the whole weight precisely because he never yielded.

Could Jesus have sinned? Some Christians say he must have been able to, or his temptations would not have been real. The historic answer of the church is that he could not, because he is the eternal Son, and his human will was never set against the will of God. That is the more likely answer. But it does not make the temptation unreal. A bridge that cannot fall still bears the full weight of the train; a fortress that cannot be taken still feels the whole force of the siege. Because Jesus never yielded, he felt temptation’s pressure to the very end (compare 4:15).

He is able to help those who are being tempted. “Able” (dynatai) is has the power. “Help” (boēthēsai) is a compound meaning to run to the cry of someone, to come quickly at a shout. It was used of answering a call for aid. It is not the picture of a sympathetic figure at a distance who understands what you are going through. It is somebody arriving. Because he has been through it, he knows exactly what we face, and he has the power to help (4:15–16; 1 Corinthians 10:13). And notice the tense: those who are being tempted, present, ongoing, happening now. The help is not a general provision made once. It is for the person in the middle of it this afternoon.

Competence and sympathy in one person. Put the chapter’s two halves together and the pastoral point is complete. He is the radiance of God’s glory who carries the universe along, and he has been hungry, frightened and pressed to the limit, so that when you call he does not need it explained. The competence and the sympathy are in the same person, which is a combination nobody had ever been offered before. This is the note the letter will return to at its hinge: let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (4:16). The whole argument about priesthood exists so that frightened people will ask.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus could have sinned in the sense that his divine person could have been overcome. But his temptations were real, and his human nature felt their pull. Nor does it mean that he understands only in theory; he knows from experience.

What does his help look like when I am tempted? Usually not a feeling that sweeps the temptation away, though sometimes the pull simply loosens when you pray. More often it is a way of escape God provides (1 Corinthians 10:13): a thought of Scripture brought to mind, a door you can walk out of, a friend who calls, a strength to say no that you did not have a moment before. So when temptation comes, call to him at once, in a sentence, before you argue with it. Then take the way out he gives, physically if you must. And if you fall, run to him just as quickly. The one who helps the tempted also cleanses the fallen.

Does Jesus understand temptations he never faced in exactly my form? Yes. He was not tempted by every modern form of sin, but he was tempted in every way that matters: to doubt his Father’s goodness, to grasp for comfort, to take a shortcut to glory, to hate his enemies, to give up under pain and loneliness (Matthew 4:1–11). Every temptation you face is some version of these. He knows the pull from inside, without the corruption that makes our resistance weaker. You will never be able to say to him, you do not understand.

In a sentence. Because he himself suffered when he was tested, he is able to come to the rescue of those who are being tested.

On a Tuesday. When you face temptation this week, cry out to Jesus in the moment, not afterwards: Lord, help me now. Learn the pattern of your own temptations, the time of day, the mood, the place, and plan ahead which way of escape you will take. Tell a trusted Christian friend where you are weak. He has been there, and he will run to help you, often through the people and the means he has already put around you.

For worship. He knows. The Lord who upholds the universe by the word of his power has been hungry in a desert, exhausted on a hillside, betrayed by a friend and pressed to the edge of his strength in a garden at night. He felt every ounce of temptation, because he never gave way. And now, enthroned, he has not forgotten what it was like. When you cry out, he does not stand at a distance and assess you. He runs. The merciful and faithful High Priest is the swiftest helper in heaven.

It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard,<sup>4</sup>while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.<sup>5</sup>For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking.<sup>6</sup>It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him?<sup>7</sup>You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor,<sup>8</sup>putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control.
