What Jesus faced was the wrath of God against sin, poured out on the one who would bear it for others (Isaiah 53:10; Mark 14:36). His holy human soul recoiled from it as no sinful soul ever could, because he knew the Father’s love perfectly and was about to be forsaken. The loud cries are the measure of what our salvation cost.

To him who was able to save him from death. Note the precision. God was able. The prayer was not addressed into a void or to a power that could not manage it. The Father could have rescued him from dying. The Greek can also be read as save him out of death (ek thanatou): bring him through death and out the other side, in resurrection.

And he was heard because of his reverence. Here is the difficulty every reader feels: he was heard, and he died. What does it mean that the prayer was answered? The answer lies in the shape of the prayer itself, which was conditional: if it be possible, let this cup pass; nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). A prayer that ends in that way is answered when the Father’s will is done, and it was. He was strengthened in the garden (Luke 22:43), carried through death, and raised out of it on the third day. He was heard, not by escaping death, but by triumphing over it. And the word for reverence (eulabeia) means godly fear, a holy caution: the disposition of a son who wants above everything not to displease his Father. He was heard because of that, not because of the volume of the crying.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus lacked faith or tried to escape his mission. His prayer expressed true human dread of the cup of God’s wrath, combined with perfect submission. Nor does it mean his tears were weakness; they were the measure of what he bore for us.

Why would the Son of God need to pray at all? Because he was truly man as well as truly God, and a true man depends on God and speaks to him. Jesus prayed through the night before choosing the twelve, rose early to pray, prayed at his baptism and on the mountain. He did not pray as an act for the disciples’ benefit. In his human nature he lived by faith in his Father, as we must, and in the garden that dependence was tested to the uttermost. His prayers are part of the obedience by which he saved us.

Is it wrong for me to cry out to God in anguish, or to ask him to take something away? No. The sinless Son did both. Loud cries and tears are not a failure of faith; they are faith speaking honestly to the only one who can help. The Psalms are full of them. What made Jesus’ prayer holy was not calm, but submission: he asked plainly for what he wanted, and then he put the Father’s will above his own. You may ask God to heal, to rescue, to spare, with all your heart. Then learn to add his words: nevertheless, not my will, but yours.

In a sentence. During his life on earth, Jesus offered prayers and pleas, with loud crying and tears, to the one who could rescue him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.

On a Tuesday. Consider what this verse gives to a praying person. The Son of God prayed with shouting and tears, did not get what he asked for in the form he asked for it, and was heard. So unanswered prayer, in the sense most people mean by the phrase, is not evidence of being unheard. If you are carrying a request God has not granted, bring it again, honestly, with tears if they come, and leave the form of the answer with him. A no that ends in resurrection is a better answer than a yes that ends anywhere else.

For worship. In the days of his flesh the eternal Son knelt in the dark and wept. He who upholds the universe by the word of his power (1:3) pleaded like a man holding out an olive branch for his life, and he did it for us. He drank the cup so that it would never be pressed to our lips. The Father heard him, and the answer was an empty tomb. Now he who once cried out in the garden lives to intercede for us, and there is no anguish we can bring to God that our high priest has not already prayed through, and prayed through to victory.
verseByVerse.note: Most likely a reference to Jesus’ agony in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

Although he was a son. The phrase concedes the objection before it is raised. Being the Son (huios) of God, one might think he would be exempt from suffering. It did not exempt him; if anything it was the reason for it. Sonship in this letter is not a shelter from the road of suffering but the path along which the Son leads many sons to glory (2:10).

He learned obedience through what he suffered. The Greek is a piece of wordplay: emathen, he learned, and epathen, he suffered. Learning and suffering rhyme, and the proverb was familiar in Greek: suffering teaches. “He learned obedience” needs care, because it cannot mean he moved from disobedience to obedience. He was never disobedient; he was always perfectly willing. What he learned was obedience by experience: the difference between a man who has always intended to be loyal and the same man after loyalty has cost him everything. He knew what obedience was; in the garden and on the cross he came to know what it weighs. His obedience was tested, proved and completed as he became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). Knowledge gained by experience is different from knowledge in principle.

And being made perfect. The same word as 2:10 (teleiōtheis): brought to completion, made fully fit for an office. Not moral improvement, since he had no moral flaw to improve. Qualification. Through suffering and obedience he was fully equipped as Saviour and High Priest, the finished article, everything a sinner needs in a priest.

He became the source of eternal salvation. The word for source (aitios) is the word for cause. He is not a means to salvation or a condition of it but its origin, its author. And note eternal (aiōnios), which in this letter is always set against the temporary. An annually repeated sacrifice produced an annually repeated forgiveness; the salvation Christ causes lasts forever (9:12). It cannot be outgrown, undone or used up.

To all who obey him. It is a striking way to describe Christians: not those who believe, which is what we might expect, but those who obey (hypakouousin, literally those who listen and respond). The two are not alternatives in this letter. The wilderness generation’s failure was called disobedience in one verse and unbelief in the next (3:18–19; 4:6). Paul speaks the same way of the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5; 16:26), and John sets believing in the Son against not obeying the Son (John 3:36). Faith that does not eventually move the feet was never the thing Hebrews means by faith.

The symmetry. There is a pattern here that the writer has arranged deliberately. He learned obedience through suffering; he became the source of salvation to those who obey. The road the Son walked is the road his people walk. He went first, and he went further than any of us will ever have to go.

Being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek. The name returns, closing the paragraph. “Designated” (prosagoreutheis) means addressed, hailed, formally named: God publicly proclaimed him high priest, in the words of Psalm 110:4. The writer is now ready to explain it, except that he has looked at his congregation and decided they cannot yet take it in.

What it does not mean. “All who obey him” does not mean salvation is earned by obedience. The obedience in view is trusting, submitting to and following Christ, which is the fruit and expression of faith. Those who truly believe will obey; those who refuse to obey show they do not believe (John 3:36, where disbelief and disobedience are paralleled). Nor does “learned obedience” imply Jesus was ever disobedient.

Am I among those who obey him, when my obedience is so patchy? The verse describes the direction of a life, not a flawless record. Those who obey him are those who have bowed to him as Lord, who listen to his word and want to do it, who fight sin and confess it when they fall, and who keep coming back to him. Your obedience will be imperfect all your life (1 John 1:8–9). What marks a believer is not that he never fails but that he does not make peace with failing, and that he runs to Christ, not away from him. If you grieve over your disobedience and long to please him, that grief and that longing are themselves the work of his Spirit in you. And remember whose obedience saves you. It is his, offered perfectly in your place.

Does suffering make me holier automatically? No. Suffering is a tool in a Father’s hand (12:5–11), but it does not work by itself; the same trial that softens one man hardens another. It trains those who receive it from God and keep trusting him in it. Jesus learned obedience through suffering because he kept obeying while he suffered. That is the opening for us: in pain, keep doing the next right thing, keep praying, keep trusting, and the suffering will not be wasted.

In a sentence. Son though he was, he learned what obedience means through his suffering. And once he had been made fully qualified, he became the cause of eternal salvation for everyone who obeys him, and God named him high priest in the order of Melchizedek.

On a Tuesday. Is there an area where obedience to Christ will cost you this week: an apology you would rather not make, a temptation you would rather keep, a truth you would rather not say, a person you would rather not forgive? Follow him through it, as he learned obedience through suffering for you. Obedience that costs nothing teaches nothing. The cost is where the learning happens.

For worship. He was the Son, and he suffered. He never needed to learn obedience for his own sake, and he learned it for ours, step by step, all the way to a cross. He was made perfect, not by becoming better, but by finishing everything our salvation required, and now he is its source and cause: not a helper in our saving, but the author of it. The salvation he gives is eternal, because the one who gives it lives forever. God himself has hailed him as high priest, and every one of his people may answer, amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer wants to say more about Melchizedek, but it is hard to explain because his readers have grown sluggish in listening. By this time they ought to be teaching others, yet they need someone to teach them the first principles all over again. Like infants, they need milk rather than solid food. Someone still on milk is not practised in the teaching about righteousness, whereas solid food is for the mature, whose powers of discernment have been trained by constant use to tell good from evil.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Maturity Actually Is

Maturity is not a store of information but a trained faculty — discernment exercised by constant practice until it can tell good from evil.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers had become dull of hearing; they had not always been so.

Now: When Scripture seems dry, ask whether the dullness is in the passage or in the hearer.

verseByVerse.quote: About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.

About this we have much to say. The sentence changes the temperature of the letter entirely. The writer has just named Melchizedek twice and is standing at the door of his central argument, and he stops, turns to his congregation, and tells them why he is not going on yet. “About this” means about Melchizedek and Christ’s priesthood after his order. There is a great deal more, and he intends to say it (7:1–28). But first he must deal with the ears that will hear it.

And it is hard to explain. Read the phrase carefully, because the fault is not located where we would expect. The word dysermēneutos means hard to interpret, hard to put into words, and the reason given is not that the subject is obscure. It is since you have become dull of hearing. The difficulty is in the audience. That is a bold thing for any preacher to say, and he says it without malice. He has called these people holy brothers (3:1) and will call them beloved (6:9). He is not writing them off; he is telling them the truth about why the sermon is stalling.

Since you have become dull of hearing. “Dull” is nōthroi: sluggish, slow, torpid. The word could be used of a numb limb or a lazy animal, and it comes back at 6:12, translated sluggish. It is the opposite of the alertness the letter has been urging since 2:1. And the decisive word is “become” (gegonate, a perfect tense: you have become, and you are now). They were not always like this. There was a time when these people were sharp, when they took the word in eagerly, when they stood their ground publicly and lost property for it; the writer will remind them of exactly that at 10:32–34. They have become dull, which means the condition was acquired, gradually, and probably without their noticing.

How it happens. That is the drift of 2:1 showing up in the ears. Nobody decides to stop hearing. Attention is not lost in a moment; it seeps away while a person is busy with other things, and the first symptom is that teaching which once thrilled them now seems difficult and rather abstract. It is a moral and spiritual problem, not an intellectual one. They had stopped listening attentively, perhaps because the truth was beginning to demand change, or suffering, and the easiest way to avoid a demand is not to hear it clearly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean deep truths are only for the intellectually gifted. The problem is not ability but attentiveness and spiritual appetite.

The diagnostic question. Ask the question this verse puts. If a passage of Scripture seems dry, the instinctive conclusion is that the passage is dry. Hebrews raises another possibility, and it is a possibility a person can only test by asking whether he was always this bored. Were there days when the same truths moved you? What has changed: the truth, or you?

How can I tell whether I have become dull of hearing? Look for the signs. Sermons wash over you and by Sunday lunch you cannot say what the text was. You know the answers but they no longer surprise or humble you. You read the Bible, if at all, to tick it off. You find yourself drawn to teaching that entertains or confirms what you already think, and impatient with anything that requires effort or change. And you have not acted on the last thing God clearly showed you. That last sign is usually the root: the ear grows dull when the will has stopped obeying. The remedy begins not with more information but with doing the last thing you heard, and then asking God, honestly, to open your ears again (Psalm 119:18).

In a sentence. We have a great deal to say on this subject, and it is difficult to explain, because you have become slow to listen.

On a Tuesday. Have you become sluggish in hearing God’s word? Before Sunday, read the passage that will be preached, and pray over it for five minutes. During the sermon, listen for one thing to do, and write it down. On Monday, do it. Ask God to sharpen your spiritual hearing, and come to church this Sunday ready to listen. Dull ears are healed less by sermons than by obedience to the sermons we have already heard.

For worship. How patient our God is with slow hearers. The writer could have abandoned these people; instead he paused his greatest argument to win them back to it, and in that pause we see the heart of the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine. Christ has much to say to us, more than we have ever taken in, glories of his priesthood that the angels long to look into. He does not withhold them because he is stingy. He waits, and he trains our ears, because he means us to hear every word.

verseByVerse.quote: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food, for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food, for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.

For though by this time you ought to be teachers. The rebuke is not that they know little. It is that they have not moved. “By this time” (literally because of the time) implies a clock: these were not new converts. Enough years had passed that they should have been instructing others, and instead they need the alphabet again.

The normal expectation. Note the assumption buried in it, which is quietly demanding. The normal expectation of a Christian is that he will eventually be able to teach somebody something. Not that everyone should hold office, since James warns against a rush to that (James 3:1), but that the ordinary path of a believer runs from being taught to being able to explain. A parent explaining the gospel to a child, a friend opening a passage over coffee, an older woman training a younger (Titus 2:3–5): that is what “teachers” means here. A person who has been a Christian for twenty years and cannot open the gospel to someone else has, on this letter’s reckoning, stalled.

You need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. “Again” (palin): they had gone backwards. “Basic principles” is ta stoicheia tēs archēs, the elements of the beginning, the ABC, the first letters in a sequence. And the “oracles of God” (ta logia tou theou) are God’s own utterances, his revealed word. Chapter 6 will list the first things: repentance, faith, washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment (6:1–2).

You need milk, not solid food. Paul uses the same image with the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 3:1–2), and Peter tells new believers to long for pure spiritual milk (1 Peter 2:2). In every place the point is not that milk is bad. Milk is exactly right, for an infant. It becomes a problem only when a person is still on it years later. Solid food (sterea trophē, firm nourishment) is deeper teaching, such as the Melchizedek priesthood of Christ the writer is longing to give them.

For everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child. Verse 13 explains what the diet produces. “Unskilled” (apeiros) is literally without experience: untried, not having handled the thing. The problem with the perpetual beginner is not that he lacks information but that he has never used any. The “word of righteousness” may mean the teaching about righteousness, the gospel of how God makes sinners righteous, or right teaching in general, or the skill of using God’s word to tell right from wrong. Probably the last, given verse 14: they lack experience in applying God’s word to life. And “child” (nēpios) is an infant. Spiritual infancy is natural at the start; it is a problem when it lasts too long.

What it does not mean. It does not mean milk is bad or unnecessary. The basics are always foundational (6:1). The problem is staying at that level. Nor does it mean only a few can reach maturity; all believers should grow.

Knowledge that is never used. This reframes the whole rebuke. The writer is not complaining that his readers have not read enough. He is saying that knowledge which is never exercised does not mature anybody. A man can sit under good teaching for decades and remain an infant, because hearing without doing produces nothing (James 1:22–25). The next verse will say how maturity actually comes.

Does this verse condemn me if I am not a natural teacher? It is not asking you to become a preacher, or to be good at public speaking. It asks whether you have grown enough to help someone else understand and follow Christ. Can you explain, simply, who Jesus is and why he died? Can you point a struggling friend to a promise, or show your child where a truth is found? If not yet, that is not a reason for shame but a direction for growth. Start where you are: learn one passage well enough to explain it, and then explain it to one person. Teaching in this sense is mostly the overflow of a believer who has been feeding well.

In a sentence. By now you ought to be teaching others, but you need someone to teach you the elementary truths of God’s word all over again. You need milk instead of solid food! Anyone who lives on milk is still a baby and has no experience in handling the message about what is right.

On a Tuesday. What is one step you can take this month to move from milk to solid food? Read a whole Bible book slowly, with a good commentary beside it. Work through a catechism or a confession, a question a week. Take one doctrine you have always accepted, such as the priesthood of Christ, and learn why it is true and where Scripture teaches it. Then, the harder half, find one person to pass it on to. Growth needs both the food and the exercise.

For worship. God has not given us a thin word. The oracles of God are inexhaustible, and the basics themselves open into depths that no one reaches the bottom of. Christ is milk to the newborn and solid food to the grown, and in every stage he is the nourishment. The God who rebukes his children for staying small does it because he has prepared a banquet for them, and he will not be content until they sit down to it.

verseByVerse.quote: But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.

But solid food is for the mature. The writer now defines maturity, and it is the most practically useful sentence in the chapter. “Mature” (teleioi) is complete, grown-up, adult, and it is related to the word for Christ being made perfect in verse 9. Christian maturity is the goal of the whole Christian life (6:1; Ephesians 4:13; Colossians 1:28). Take the terms in order, because every one of them is doing work.

For those who have their powers of discernment trained. “Powers of discernment” (aisthētēria) is literally the faculties or organs of perception, the same word used of the physical senses. The writer is describing moral and spiritual judgment as a sense: something that perceives directly, the way a tongue tastes, like a trained palate that knows good food from bad without consulting a chart. “Trained” is gegymnasmena, the gymnasium word, from which we get gymnastics. It means exercised, put through a training regime, as an athlete trains a body, and the perfect tense means trained and now in condition.

By constant practice. One word, hexis, meaning habit, settled usage, a state produced by repetition. Not by intensive study, not by a crisis, not by a conference. By habit. Maturity does not come by merely hearing more information. It comes through repeatedly applying God’s word in real life, making real choices, until discernment becomes second nature.

To distinguish good from evil. “Distinguish” (diakrisis) is discernment, judgment, telling apart. Not only moral good and evil, but true and false teaching. The readers, tempted back to Judaism, needed to discern that the old covenant, though good, had been surpassed, and that turning back would be turning away from Christ.

A definition of maturity. Put the terms together and you have a definition of Christian maturity that cuts against the common assumption. Maturity is not the accumulation of doctrine; the writer’s readers may well have known a great deal. It is a trained faculty: the capacity to tell right from wrong quickly and by feel, developed the way an athlete’s reflexes are developed, through repetition over a long time. And that explains why the writer will not proceed to Melchizedek yet. Solid food is not withheld from these people because they are unintelligent. It is withheld because the faculty that would digest it has not been exercised, and no amount of teaching substitutes for use.

What it does not mean. It does not mean mature believers no longer need basic truths. The mature are those who apply the basics more deeply and widely. Nor does maturity come automatically with age or years in church.

The comfort in it. There is a comfort here as well as a rebuke, and it should not be missed. If maturity came by intellect, most Christians would be excluded from it. It comes by practice, which is available to everybody. The ordinary believer who has spent thirty years making small decisions in the fear of God has a trained palate, whatever he can or cannot explain. The grandmother who has never read a theology book but can smell false teaching at fifty paces is mature in exactly this sense. And the writer’s next words, at the head of chapter 6, are let us go on. He does not leave them where they are.

How do I actually train my discernment? The same way an athlete trains: small, regular, real exercises. Read Scripture daily, and ask of each passage what it shows you about God and what it asks of you. When you face a decision, even a small one about words, money, time or entertainment, stop and ask what God’s word says, and then act on the answer. Notice afterwards whether it was right. Listen to teaching with an open Bible and test it (Acts 17:11). Spend time with mature believers and watch how they judge things. Confess quickly when you get it wrong. Over years, what began as slow deliberate thinking becomes instinct.

Is discernment the same as being critical? No. Some people mistake suspicion for discernment and spend their lives finding fault with sermons and other Christians. The discernment of this verse distinguishes good from evil, which means it recognises and delights in the good as quickly as it detects the evil. A mature palate does not only spit out what is bad; it relishes what is good. True discernment makes a person humbler, more thankful and more careful with his own heart, not sharper with everyone else’s.

In a sentence. But solid food is for grown-ups, whose senses have been trained by constant use to tell good from evil.

On a Tuesday. Train your discernment this week. Pick one recurring decision, what you watch in the evening, how you speak about a difficult colleague, what you do with an unexpected sum of money, and each time it comes up, stop and ask, what does God’s word say about this? Then act on it. A muscle is built by repetitions, not by reading about muscles. Thirty small obedient choices will do more for your discernment than a shelf of books you never use.

For worship. The God who made our bodies to grow by eating and exercise has made our souls to grow by his word and by obedience to it, and he has not left the mature life for a gifted few. He trains every one of his children. The Son who was made perfect through suffering is bringing many sons to that same maturity, and he is a patient trainer. He feeds us, exercises us, corrects us and keeps at it for a lifetime, until at last we see him and are like him, with every sense awake to his glory.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.<sup>2</sup>He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness.<sup>3</sup>Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.<sup>4</sup>And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.<sup>5</sup>So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”;<sup>6</sup>as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”<sup>7</sup>In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.<sup>8</sup>Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.<sup>9</sup>And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him,<sup>10</sup>being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.<sup>11</sup>About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.<sup>12</sup>For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food,<sup>13</sup>for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.<sup>14</sup>But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.

6.title: Press On to Maturity: The Anchor of the Soul
6.overview:
Chapter 6 holds both the most debated and the most encouraging passages in the letter. It begins with a call to maturity: build on the foundations, do not keep relaying them. Then comes the severest warning (vv. 4–8): those who have seen the full light of the gospel and then deliberately turn away cannot be restored to repentance. Its pastoral aim is to shock the drifting into seeing what is at stake.

At once the writer turns: “in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things” (v. 9). He grounds his confidence in God’s faithfulness, who will not forget their love. And the chapter ends with hope as an anchor for the soul, lodged behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner. Everything is secure because the Priest is already inside.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Hardest Warning, and the Confidence After It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So the writer urges them to leave the basic teaching about Christ behind and press on to maturity, without laying again the foundation they already have: turning from dead works and trusting God, teaching about ritual washings and the laying on of hands, the resurrection and eternal judgement. Then comes the letter’s sternest warning. Those who have been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift and the goodness of God’s word, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and who then fall away, cannot be brought back to repentance, because they are crucifying the Son of God again and holding him up to contempt. Like land that drinks the rain and produces only thorns, they face a curse. But the writer is confident of better things for his readers, things that belong to salvation. God will not forget their love and service to his people. He wants each of them to show the same eagerness to the end, not becoming lazy, but imitating those who inherit the promises through faith and patience.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Passage Set Out Honestly

Sincere Christians read verses 4–6 differently. The list describes what was received and seen, not what saves; and five verses later the writer calls his readers beloved and speaks of things that belong to salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Two fields drink the same rain; the crop shows the soil.

Now: The warning is not addressed to the anxious. God is not unjust so as to overlook love shown in serving the saints.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.

Meaning first. Hebrews 6 holds together the most solemn warning and the strongest assurance in the letter. It begins with a call to move on from the foundational teachings, which the readers already know, to maturity (vv. 1–3). Then comes the third and most sobering warning (vv. 4–8): it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who have experienced the blessings of the gospel community, been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Spirit’s work, and tasted God’s good word and the powers of the coming age, and then have fallen away, because they are crucifying the Son of God again and publicly disgracing him; they are like land that receives rain but produces only thorns, and is burned. But the author immediately says he is confident of better things in the readers’ case, things that accompany salvation, because God will not forget their love shown in serving the saints; he wants them to show the same diligence to the end, imitating those who inherit the promises through faith and patience (vv. 9–12). The chapter ends with assurance (vv. 13–20): God made a promise to Abraham and confirmed it with an oath, swearing by himself; by these two unchangeable things, in which God cannot lie, we who have fled to him have strong encouragement to hold onto our hope, which is a sure and steady anchor for the soul, fixed in the inner sanctuary where Jesus has gone ahead of us as our forerunner and eternal high priest. The chapter that frightens more Christians than almost any other ends with the most secure picture of a believer in the whole Bible: a soul tied to Jesus behind the curtain.

Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ. “Leave” (aphentes, let go of, move on from) sounds alarming until the metaphor is seen. The image is a building, and the next clause makes it explicit: not laying again a foundation. You do not abandon a foundation by building on it. You abandon it by digging it up every few years to check it is still there. That is what these readers were doing. Not denying the basics, but endlessly returning to them, and never getting a wall up. The “elementary doctrine of Christ” is literally the word of the beginning of Christ: the first lessons about him, the ABC of 5:12.

And go on to maturity. The verb (pherōmetha) is passive: let us be carried along, be borne forward. It is the word for a ship running before the wind, and the same word Peter uses of the prophets carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). Growth is something we press into and something God does to us at the same time. “Maturity” (teleiotēs) is completeness, adulthood, the grown-up faith of 5:14. And “let us” is worth noticing too. The preacher includes himself, as he does again and again in his warnings. He is not standing on the finished storey calling down.

Not laying again a foundation. Then six items, probably in three pairs, and they are the foundation (themelios) he means. The first pair is conversion: repentance from dead works and faith toward God, the two sides of one turning, away from and toward. Repentance (metanoia) is a change of mind and direction. Dead works are deeds that lead to death or come from spiritual death: sinful deeds, and perhaps also religious works done to earn God’s favour (9:14). Faith toward God is trusting him.

And of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands. The second pair is initiation. “Washings” (baptismōn) is plural, and it is the ordinary word for ceremonial cleansings rather than the usual term for Christian baptism (9:10; Mark 7:4). That suggests teaching Jewish converts how Christian baptism differed from the washings they had known all their lives, and from John’s baptism (Acts 19:1–5). The many washings of the old covenant gave way to the one Christian washing, given to those who have turned from dead works and come to faith. The laying on of hands was used in the New Testament to bless, to heal, to commission for service (Acts 6:6; 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14), and in the apostles’ ministry as the moment the Spirit was given (Acts 8:17; 19:6).

The resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. The third pair is the last things: the bodily resurrection of all people, the just and the unjust (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), and God’s final, everlasting judgment (9:27; Matthew 25:46). These were among the first things a convert was taught, not advanced topics for later.

Nothing peculiar to Christ. Here is the striking thing about the list: there is almost nothing in it that is distinctively Christian. Every item could have been taught in a synagogue. Repentance, faith in God, ceremonial washing, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment: a devout Pharisee would have affirmed the lot. That sharpens the writer’s complaint considerably. His readers were stalled precisely at the point where Judaism and Christianity overlap. They had never moved on to what is peculiar to Christ, his priesthood, his sacrifice, his finished work, and that is exactly why going back looked so easy. If you have not yet built anything above the shared foundation, stepping off it costs you nothing you can see.

And this we will do if God permits. A small qualifier with considerable weight (eanper epitrepē ho theos). Progress in understanding is not simply a matter of resolve; it is granted. The writer intends to press on, and knows that whether his readers actually advance is not finally in his gift. It also prepares for what follows, because the next verses describe a condition in which God does not permit progress.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the foundations are unimportant or can be forgotten. Every building rests on its foundation. It means believers should build on it, not keep relaying it.

Does “washings” here teach anything about how to baptise? Not directly; the verse is about instruction, not method. But it fits the wider teaching of the New Testament that baptism belongs at the beginning of the Christian life, alongside repentance and faith. The order of the first pair matters: those who have turned from dead works and trusted God are the ones who are washed. That is why this app, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds believer’s baptism, while gladly honouring paedobaptist brothers who read the covenant signs differently and who love the same Saviour. Whichever view a Christian holds, the point of the verse stands: baptism is foundation, not a place to camp.

Does the laying on of hands still give the Spirit today? The Spirit is given to every believer at conversion, through faith in Christ, not through anyone’s hands (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). In Acts the Spirit sometimes came at the laying on of apostolic hands, as the gospel crossed new boundaries and the church’s foundation was being laid (Acts 8:14–17; 19:6). That belonged to the apostolic foundation and is not repeated. What continues is the laying on of hands with prayer to set apart elders and missionaries for their work (Acts 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14), a sign of the church’s blessing and recognition, not a channel of power.

In a sentence. So let us move beyond the elementary teaching about Christ and be carried forward to maturity, without laying the foundation all over again: turning away from deeds that lead to death, faith in God, teaching about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgement. And God permitting, we will move on.

On a Tuesday. Can you explain these six foundations to someone else? If not, learn them; they are the first page of the catechism every Christian should know. If you can, build on them: go deeper into Christ, into what only the gospel says, his priesthood, his once-for-all sacrifice, his intercession for you now. And notice where you keep digging up the foundation instead: the assurance you re-examine every week without ever resting on it, the conversion you keep repeating. Stand on what God has laid, and build.

For worship. The foundation is God’s, and it holds. Repentance and faith were his gifts, the washing is his sign, the resurrection and the judgment are in his hands. And the building he is raising on it is his Son, the one thing Judaism at its best could only point to. He does not leave his people standing on the slab. He carries them forward, as the wind carries a ship, into the knowledge of Christ, which has no ceiling.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,

For it is impossible. The sentence that begins here is the most disputed in the letter and among the most disputed in Scripture. Go slowly, and it is worth saying at the outset that sincere Christians have read it differently. The word “impossible” (adynaton) stands at the head of the Greek sentence, in the emphatic position. It is strong: not difficult, but impossible. The same word is used of God’s inability to lie (v. 18), of the blood of bulls taking away sins (10:4), and of pleasing God without faith (11:6). And its object does not arrive until verse 6: impossible to restore them again to repentance. Everything between is description of the people in view. Five things are said about them, and they are not small.

In the case of those who have once been enlightened. “Once” (hapax) is the word for once for all. “Enlightened” (phōtisthentas) means given light, illuminated. Light has fallen on them; they have seen. They heard and understood the gospel, and the truth shone on them (10:32). Some early Christian writers used “enlightened” as a name for baptism.

Who have tasted the heavenly gift. Some have tried to soften “tasted” (geusamenous) into a sip rather than a meal, but the letter itself forbids it: at 2:9 Jesus tasted death for everyone, and he did not sample it. The word means real experience. The heavenly gift is the blessing of salvation that comes from heaven, perhaps Christ himself, or forgiveness, or the Spirit. These people had experienced those blessings within the life of the church.

And have shared in the Holy Spirit. The word (metochoi genēthentes, became partakers, partners) is the one used at 3:1 of sharing a heavenly calling and at 3:14 of sharing in Christ. They had participated in the Spirit’s work in the community: his convicting power, his gifts and his blessings, as Judas shared in the apostles’ ministry and was sent out to heal and cast out demons with the rest (Matthew 10:1–8).

And have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come. They have found Scripture good (kalon, beautiful, excellent): its comfort, its power, perhaps with joy, like the seed on rocky ground that springs up quickly and has no root (Matthew 13:20–21). And they have seen the future break into the present. The “powers” (dynameis) are the miracles and mighty works of 2:4, the foretaste of the age to come, which they had witnessed and perhaps experienced.

A formidable description. Any honest reader has to concede that this is a formidable description. It is not a list of things that could be said of a person who had merely attended once or twice. Whatever the passage finally means, it cannot be dismissed by saying these people were obviously never involved at all. They had been inside, near the fire, warmed by it.

What is absent. And yet the writer has chosen his words with care, and one thing is conspicuously missing from the list. Every term describes something received, experienced or seen. Not one of them says these people were justified, born again, forgiven, sanctified or loved by God. Compare what he says of the same congregation five verses later: beloved, and things that belong to salvation. He can use that language when he wants to, and here he does not.

Where Christians differ: are these true believers? This is one of the most debated passages in Scripture. Four main views: (1) these are genuine believers who lose their salvation (Arminian view); (2) these are genuine believers, but the warning is hypothetical, describing what would happen if they could fall away, which they cannot; (3) these are genuine believers who lose rewards, not salvation; (4) these are people who have experienced the blessings of the gospel community without being truly regenerated, and whose falling away shows they were never truly saved. The first view has a difficulty inside the letter itself, which says Christ is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (7:25); and by this reading the loss would be irreversible, which few who take the view actually teach. The second fits the theology but reads thinly against the urgency of the warning, and the third cannot do justice to burning (v. 8) or to 10:26–31. Verdict: The fourth view best fits the passage and the whole of Scripture. Every phrase in verses 4–5 describes real experiences that can be had without regeneration: being enlightened (understanding the gospel), tasting (experiencing without fully receiving), sharing in the Spirit’s work (as Judas and Balaam did), tasting the word with joy (like the rocky soil). Notably, the passage does not use words like justified, born again, saved or sanctified of these people. In verse 9 the author distinguishes them from those who have “things that belong to salvation.” And the land illustration (vv. 7–8) shows the difference: the same rain falls on two kinds of ground, but the fruit reveals the nature of the soil. Scripture elsewhere teaches that those whom God saves he keeps (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:29–30; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real: such people exist, and God uses this warning to stir true believers to persevere.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a believer who struggles, doubts or falls into sin is beyond hope. Peter denied Christ and was restored. The issue is a final, deliberate, public repudiation of Christ.

How can someone share in the Holy Spirit and not be saved? Because the Spirit works in more ways than regeneration. He convicts the world of sin (John 16:8), he gives gifts and power in the church, and he moves on people who hear the word, so that they are stirred, sobered and attracted. Balaam prophesied when the Spirit of God came upon him, and died among the enemies of God’s people (Numbers 24:2; 31:8). Saul had the Spirit come on him and ended consulting a medium (1 Samuel 10:10; 28:7). Judas preached and healed. Jesus warned of many who would say on the last day that they had prophesied and done mighty works in his name, to whom he would say, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Being near the Spirit’s work is not the same as being born of him.

Then how can I know I am not one of these? Not by the size of your experiences, since these people had large ones, but by what the Spirit produces over time. Do you trust Christ himself, not your experiences, for your acceptance with God? Do you love him and want to please him? Do you hate your sin and fight it, and confess it when you fall? Do you love other Christians and serve them (v. 10; 1 John 3:14)? Do you keep coming back to his word, even when it is hard? These are the things that belong to salvation, and they are usually clearer to others than to the anxious person himself. If you find even a weak longing for Christ in you, rest on his promise and not on your feelings: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. It is impossible for those who have once had the light shine on them, who have tasted the gift from heaven, who have taken part in the Holy Spirit’s work, who have tasted how good God’s word is and the powers of the coming age,

On a Tuesday. List the spiritual privileges you have known: a Christian upbringing, years of preaching, answered prayers, moments of real conviction, a church that loves you. Thank God for every one. Then ask the question this passage presses: have these led me to Christ himself, or have I been living on the experiences? Rain is a gift, but it is not a harvest. Go to Christ today, not to your memories of him.

For worship. How rich the goodness of God is, that he pours so much on the world: light on the darkened, tastes of heaven on the undeserving, his word and his Spirit at work among his people so that even those who finally reject him have tasted what they rejected. And how much richer his grace to his own, who are given not only the taste but the feast, not only the light but new eyes, not only the Spirit’s nearness but his indwelling for ever. We do not rest on our experiences. We rest on Christ, who never lets go of anyone the Father has given him.

verseByVerse.quote: and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.

And then have fallen away. The word (parapesontas) is a strong one: to fall aside, to defect, to apostatise. It is not stumbling into sin. It is the deliberate abandonment the letter has been warning about since 3:12, falling away from the living God. For these readers it would mean renouncing Christ and returning to the old covenant system to escape persecution, publicly and for good. Not a single sin, but a decisive turning away from Christ, the deliberate rejection of what they had experienced. Christians have read this warning in different ways; all agree it is a solemn call to persevere.

To restore them again to repentance. “Restore” (anakainizein) is to renew. “Again” implies they had shown repentance once, outwardly at least, and it is impossible to bring them back. Why? Because they have rejected the only means of repentance and forgiveness: Christ’s sacrifice. There is no other sacrifice (10:26). If you reject the only remedy, there is no remedy left. A drowning man who pushes away the one rope thrown to him has not merely missed a chance; he has refused the only rescue there is.

Since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm. The verb (anastaurountas) means to crucify again, or to crucify up, on a cross. By rejecting Christ, they side with those who crucified him and declare that he deserved it. And both participles are present and continuous: while they are doing this. That explains the impossibility. A person in the act of publicly repudiating Christ cannot simultaneously be repenting of it. And it is “to their own harm” (heautois, for themselves, to their loss): Christ cannot be crucified again in fact, but they crucify him for themselves, and the ruin is theirs.

And holding him up to contempt. The word (paradeigmatizontas) is a public word, used of exposing someone to open shame, making a public example of him. This is not a private lapse. These are people who have gone back and said, before witnesses, that the crucified man was rightly crucified. Publicly declaring that Christ is not worth following, they shame him before the world. The present tense explains the impossibility: as long as they continue in this attitude, repentance is impossible.

The pastoral force is the same. Whichever reading one holds, the pastoral force of these verses is identical, which is presumably why the writer left it as he did. The warning is not addressed to the anxious. A person terrified that this describes him is displaying precisely the softness of heart the passage says is absent. You cannot repent of having become unable to repent. The people in view are not agonising. They have walked out. John describes the same thing when he says, they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that anyone worried about having committed this sin has committed it. Those who fear they have fallen away and long to return to Christ show that their hearts are not hardened. The hardened do not care. Nor does it limit God’s power absolutely; it describes the condition of the hardened apostate, whom God has given over to his choice.

What about the Christian who has really wandered? This verse does not describe him. A believer may fall into serious sin and stay away for a season, cold, ashamed and defensive. Peter denied Christ three times with curses, and Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). David committed adultery and murder, and wrote Psalm 51. The warning is against final apostasy, not against backsliding. Whoever wants to come back to Christ may come, and the church is to restore him in a spirit of gentleness (Galatians 6:1). The door is not shut on anyone who knocks.

If true believers cannot finally fall away, why warn them? Because the warnings are one of the means God uses to keep them. God promises to preserve his people, and he does it not by switching off their wills but by speaking to them: by promises that draw and warnings that alarm. A sign at a cliff edge saying danger is not pointless because it works. The elect do persevere (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and they persevere partly because passages like this one make them flee to Christ. The warning is sincere, the danger it describes is real for those who are near the church but not in Christ, and for true believers it is a fence God has built on the path.

Is this the same as the unforgivable sin? They are closely related. Jesus spoke of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28–30): deliberately calling the Spirit’s plain work in Christ the work of the devil, against the light. Hebrews 6 and 10 describe the same settled, knowing, public rejection of Christ after seeing his truth. Neither is a sin someone commits by accident or in a moment of weakness, and neither is a sin committed by a person who wants forgiveness. Any sin that is repented of is forgiven, because the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7).

Should a church refuse to receive back someone who left the faith and now returns? No. The church cannot read hearts, and this verse is not a rule for church discipline. It describes from God’s side what happens to the hardened, not a policy for the elders. If someone who had walked away returns professing repentance, the church should receive him with joy, as the father received the prodigal (Luke 15:20–24), test the fruit patiently, and welcome him to the Lord’s Table when it is evident. That he has come back at all suggests he was not the person this verse describes.

In a sentence. and who then turn away, to be brought back to repentance, because they are nailing the Son of God to the cross all over again, to their own ruin, and holding him up to public scorn.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you have fallen away, that very fear is evidence of a tender heart. Come back to Christ now. He receives all who come (John 6:37). Do not wait to feel worthy, and do not try to settle first whether this verse describes you. Go to him in prayer today, name the sin, ask for mercy, and tell a mature Christian where you have been. And if you are strong and steady, let this verse make you serious about the drift that ends in falling away. No one falls away in a day. They stop listening first (5:11).

For worship. There is one sacrifice for sins, and it is enough. The Son of God was crucified once, outside the city, bearing the contempt of the world, and his blood does what no other offering could: it cleanses every sinner who comes to him, the denier, the adulterer, the persecutor, the backslider. To turn from it is ruin, because there is nothing beside it. To flee to it is life, because there is nothing it cannot cover. We worship a Saviour who was put to open shame once so that his people would never be put to shame, and who keeps every one of them from the fall this verse describes.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have read this warning in different ways; all agree it is a real warning against turning away from Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.

For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it. The writer illustrates, and the picture explains more than the argument does. One field. The rain is the same, the frequency is the same, the cultivation is the same. And the ground has genuinely absorbed it: “drunk” (piousa) is the word, which corresponds exactly to the tasting and sharing of verses 4 and 5. The rain that often falls is God’s repeated blessing, the gospel preached again and again, the Spirit’s work, the fellowship of believers.

And produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated. “Produces” (tiktousa) is literally gives birth to. “Useful” (euthetos) means fitting, suitable. Good land responds to the rain with fruit. Genuine believers bear fruit: by their fruits you will recognise them (Matthew 7:16–20; John 15:5, 8).

Receives a blessing from God. Fruitful land is blessed further. God gives to the fruitful field more rain and more harvest, as the vinedresser prunes the fruitful branch so that it bears more (John 15:2).

But if it bears thorns and thistles. Then two outcomes from identical treatment. “Thorns and thistles” (akanthas kai tribolous) is not a random pair. It is the exact phrase of the curse in Eden (Genesis 3:17–18). The unfruitful ground is doing what cursed ground does. Land that receives the same rain but produces only weeds shows its true nature.

It is worthless and near to being cursed. “Worthless” (adokimos) means failing the test, rejected. And note the writer’s carefulness, which is easily missed and matters enormously. He does not say the field is cursed. He says it is near to a curse (kataras engys). Near is not yet. As long as a field is only near, there is time for something else to come up, and the whole letter is written to make that happen.

And its end is to be burned. Farmers burned fields of weeds. It is a picture of final judgment (10:27; Matthew 3:10, 12; John 15:6). The fruit shows the soil; the soil determines the end.

What the picture settles. The image settles what the privileges of verses 4–5 actually prove, and that is the reason it is here. Rain falling on ground and being absorbed does not determine what comes up. Two fields under the same sky, drinking the same water, produce a harvest and a thornbush. What distinguishes them is not the rain but the nature of the soil, and the only way to tell them apart is to wait and see what grows.

What it does not mean. The illustration does not mean the same land changes from good to bad. It shows that the same blessings fall on different kinds of ground, and the fruit reveals the difference. This supports the view that the apostates of verses 4–6 were never good soil.

How do you tell the fields apart? The parable answers the pastoral question the previous verses raise. If both fields look identical while the rain is falling, how does anyone know? By the crop. Not by the intensity of the experience, not by how much was tasted, but by what is growing now, which is precisely what the writer turns to in the very next verse.

What fruit am I looking for, and what if mine looks small? The fruit Scripture means is mostly ordinary: trust in Christ that keeps returning to him, love for God’s people, hatred of sin and a fight against it, honesty, kindness, patience under trial, joy in God’s word, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). It grows slowly and is rarely spectacular. A small crop is still a crop; thorns are not small wheat. And remember who makes good soil. The new heart is God’s gift (Ezekiel 36:26), and the vinedresser does not neglect his vineyard. If you see little fruit, do not despair; ask him to work, stay under the rain of his word, and look again in a year.

In a sentence. Land that soaks up the rain that falls on it again and again and produces a crop useful to those who farm it receives God’s blessing. But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless and in danger of being cursed; in the end it will be burned.

On a Tuesday. What fruit is God’s rain producing in your life? Think of the sermons, the years of Scripture, the prayers of others for you, and ask what has come up. Thank him for any growth, however small, and name it. Then name one thorn, a habit, a resentment, a love of something that chokes your love for God, and ask him to pull it up. Bring it into the light with a friend this week. Thorns grow best in fields nobody walks through.

For worship. The rain is God’s, and it falls often. He sends his word and his Spirit again and again on fields that do not deserve a drop, and on his own people he does more: he breaks up the hard ground, takes out the stone, and makes the soil itself new. The thorns and thistles were the curse of Eden, and Christ wore them on his head so that the ground of his people’s hearts could be blessed. Every harvest in a believer’s life is the fruit of his cross and the work of his Spirit, and the Lord of the harvest will bring every good field to its full crop.

verseByVerse.quote: Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.

Though we speak in this way. The author recognises the severity of his warning. He has just written the hardest paragraph in the letter, and he knows how it will land on a congregation that loves him.

Yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things. “Beloved” (agapētoi) is the only time in the letter he uses that word, and he uses it here, immediately after the severest paragraph he has written. Whatever the warning was for, it was not to tell these people he had given up on them. “Feel sure” (pepeismetha) is a perfect tense: we have been persuaded, and we are convinced. He is not being polite. He has just described people who fall away, and he says: that is not you, and I am confident of it. And “better things” (ta kreissona) is the letter’s key word, the word that runs from 1:4 to 12:24: a better covenant, a better hope, better promises, a better sacrifice.

Things that belong to salvation. Note the language he now permits himself. “Belong to” (echomena) means hold on to, accompany, are connected with. There are things that accompany genuine salvation, which the apostates of verses 4–6 lacked and which the readers show. This is the very category conspicuously absent from the list in verses 4–5. He knows the difference and writes accordingly. This is the key to the passage: the experiences of verses 4–5 can happen without salvation; the fruit described in verse 10 accompanies it.

For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work. Then the ground of his confidence, and it is not what we might expect. The evidence is the crop. The parable asked how you tell one field from another, and the writer now points at what is growing in this one. “Unjust” (adikos): God is faithful to his promises, and he will not forget the fruit of faith. The phrasing repays care, because it could be misread as saying God owes them. It says the opposite of that and something better. It is not that their service has earned salvation; it is that a God who had produced such fruit and then discarded the field would be acting unjustly toward his own work. He will acknowledge it, down to a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42; 25:34–40).

And the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do. Work, love and service to other Christians, continuing. “For his name” (eis to onoma autou) means for God’s sake: they loved his people because they were his. And the verb comes twice, as a past and a present: having served (diakonēsantes) and still serving (diakonountes). They had cared for persecuted believers, visited prisoners and accepted the plundering of their property (10:32–34), and they were still doing it. They may be dull of hearing and stalled in understanding, and they are still looking after people. That is fruit, and he treats it as decisive. Love for fellow believers is a mark of genuine faith: we know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers (1 John 3:14).

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works save or that God owes us salvation for them. It means God will justly acknowledge the fruit of faith, which is itself his gift (Ephesians 2:10). Nor does the author’s confidence make the warning unnecessary; the warning is one of the means by which they will persevere.

If he is so sure of them, why did he warn them? Because confidence about a congregation and warnings to a congregation work together. He is sure of the body as a whole, from what he sees, and he knows that any one person in it might be quietly slipping (v. 11). He is also sure that true believers respond to warnings, and his warning is part of how God will keep them. A doctor can be confident that a patient will recover and still tell him firmly to finish the medicine. The confidence is not instead of the instruction; it rests on the expectation that the instruction will be taken.

The comfort of the double negative. And there is real pastoral comfort in this verse for anyone whose service has gone unnoticed. The meals taken to a sick house, the years of unremarkable faithfulness to awkward people, the hospital visit nobody thanked you for, the prayers for a church that never knew who was praying: God is not unjust so as to overlook it. He may be the only one who has not.

In a sentence. Even though we speak like this, dear friends, we are confident of better things in your case, the things that come with salvation. God is not unfair; he will not forget your work and the love you have shown for him by helping his people, as you still do.

On a Tuesday. Look for the fruit in someone else this week, and tell them. The writer encouraged his readers by naming what God was doing in them, and most Christians go years without hearing anyone do that. And look at your own service: are you still doing it, or did it belong to an earlier, keener season? Pick up one act of love you have let drop, a visit, a meal, a regular prayer for a struggling believer, and do it for his name.

For worship. How tender the Lord is with his people. He warns them because he loves them, and he calls them beloved in the same breath. He sees what no one else sees: the unthanked kindness, the hidden prayer, the service given to the least of his brothers, and he counts it as done to Christ himself. He who produced that love in us by his Spirit will not forget his own work. Nothing done for his name is lost, because the God who remembers it is the God who will finish what he began.

verseByVerse.quote: And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness. “Desire” (epithymoumen) is a strong word: we long for it. And “each one” (hekaston) is the individual concern again, as at 3:12 and 4:1. He has just expressed confidence about the congregation as a body; he will not let that confidence become a blanket that covers someone quietly slipping. “Earnestness” (spoudē) is diligence, zeal, eager effort: the same as they have shown in serving the saints. He is not asking them to start something new. He is asking them to apply to their hope the diligence they already apply to their neighbours.

To have the full assurance of hope until the end. The word for full assurance (plērophoria) means full conviction, certainty, being carried to the full like a ship under full sail. The hope is the hope of glory (3:6), and “until the end” (achri telous) is the phrase of 3:14. And notice that assurance is here something to be pursued. It is not merely a feeling that arrives or fails to; it is a state a Christian may grow into, and the writer thinks earnestness is how. Assurance is possible, and it is not presumption but a fruit of faith (10:22; 2 Peter 1:10).

So that you may not be sluggish. The word is nōthroi, the same one used at 5:11, where they had become dull of hearing. He is joining the two: sluggish ears and sluggish lives are the same condition, and the remedy for both is the same earnestness. They had become sluggish in hearing; they must not become sluggish in hope.

But imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises. Against the dullness, examples: real people who waited and received. “Imitators” (mimētai) is the word Paul uses when he says, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). Here the letter turns a corner that will not be completed until chapter 11, where the long line of the faithful passes before us. And “faith and patience” is the pairing that runs to the end of the letter. Patience (makrothymia) is long-temperedness, the endurance that keeps going when the promise is slow. Faith takes God at his word; patience keeps taking him at it for years.

What had run out. That is what these readers were short of. Not information: they had the foundation. Not zeal at the start: they had stood their ground and lost property for it. What had run out was the long, unglamorous willingness to keep believing a promise that had not yet arrived, and the writer knows exactly which patriarch to produce as the answer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean assurance comes by our own efforts. It comes from God’s promise (vv. 17–18), but we are to pursue it diligently, using the means God gives: Scripture, prayer, sacraments, fellowship, obedience.

Can a Christian really be sure he is saved, or is that arrogant? He can, and it is not arrogance, because the confidence rests on God, not on himself. Hebrews wants every believer to have full assurance. It rests first on God’s promises in Christ, which cannot fail (vv. 17–18); it is confirmed by the Spirit’s witness that we are God’s children (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit he produces in us (v. 10). The Westminster Confession says that true believers may be infallibly assured, though they may wait long and struggle for it, and that it may be shaken and then revived (Westminster 18.3–4). Assurance is humble certainty: I am sure, not because I am strong, but because he is faithful.

How do I grow in assurance? Look mostly at Christ and his promises, not mostly at yourself. Read and trust the promises made to all who come to him (John 6:37; 10:28). Use the means of grace: the preached word, the Lord’s Supper, prayer, the fellowship of other believers. Obey in the small things, because disobedience clouds assurance and obedience clears it. Deal quickly with known sin. Serve others, as these readers did. And when you are low, remember that assurance is not the ground of your salvation. A believer with weak assurance is as safe as one with strong assurance, because both are held by the same hand.

In a sentence. We want each of you to show this same eagerness right to the end, so that you have full assurance of what you hope for. We do not want you to become lazy, but to follow the example of those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.

On a Tuesday. Who is a believer from the past or present whose faith and patience you could imitate? Read about them this week: a biography, or a conversation over coffee with the oldest Christian in your church. Ask how they kept believing through the long years. And take the energy you give to one area of your Christian life, perhaps service, and give the same earnestness to your hope: time with God’s promises, thinking about heaven, praying for the return of Christ.

For worship. God has not left us to invent perseverance. He has surrounded us with the faithful who went before, men and women who waited for promises they could not see and were not put to shame. And he is the God of their patience, the God who kept every one of them to the end. The promises they inherited are ours, sealed in Christ, and the hope he sets before us is the same: not a wish, but a certainty carried to the full by the faithfulness of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Two Unchangeable Things, and an Anchor Behind the Curtain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God made his promise to Abraham, he swore by himself, since there was no one greater, and Abraham, after waiting patiently, received what was promised. People swear by something greater, and an oath settles a dispute. So God, wanting to show the heirs of the promise how unchangeable his purpose is, confirmed it with an oath. By these two unchangeable things, in which God cannot lie, we who have fled to him for refuge are strongly encouraged to hold fast to our hope. It is a sure anchor for the soul, entering behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead of us.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Anchor That Goes Upward

God confirmed his promise with an oath so that we might have strong encouragement. Our hope is anchored behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as forerunner.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac, not always steadily, and obtained the promise.

Now: We are those who have fled for refuge. The storm and the anchorage are in different places.

verseByVerse.quote: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.

For when God made a promise to Abraham. Here is the example, and he is the obvious one. Abraham is the great example of one who through faith and patience inherited the promises (v. 12). To Jewish readers he was the father of the nation and the pattern of faith, and the writer is about to make him the pattern of waiting. God promised him descendants, land and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1–3; 15:5; 17:4–8).

Since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself. The occasion is Genesis 22, on the mountain, immediately after Abraham had raised the knife over Isaac: the point at which the promise looked most impossible and the man had proved he would trust God with it anyway. It is the only time in Genesis God swore to Abraham: by myself I have sworn, declares the LORD (Genesis 22:16). The logic of an oath is that you invoke something greater than yourself as surety. God has no such thing available. So he swore (ōmosen) by himself, which means the guarantee of the promise is his own existence: for it to fail he would have to cease to be God.

Surely I will bless you and multiply you. The quotation is from Genesis 22:17, compressed; Genesis says more, and the writer takes the two verbs that matter for his purpose. “Surely” (ei mēn) is a strong oath formula, and behind it lies a doubled Hebrew expression, literally blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you, which underlines the certainty.

And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise. Everything hangs on the middle phrase (makrothymēsas, having been patient). Put the years against it. Abraham was seventy-five when the promise was first made and a hundred when Isaac was born (Genesis 12:4; 21:5). Twenty-five years, most of them with no evidence whatever, and through a stretch in which he twice passed off his wife as his sister to save his own skin, took Hagar to arrange the heir himself, and laughed when God repeated the promise (Genesis 12; 16; 17:17; 20). The waiting was not serene. It was long and it was patchy, and Hebrews still calls it patience.

The comfort in a patchy patience. That should be a comfort to anybody measuring their own faith against the patriarchs. What the New Testament commends in Abraham is not that he never wobbled; it is that he was still there at the end. And he was still there because God was still there. The patience was Abraham’s, but the faithfulness that held him through his failures was God’s.

Obtained, and not yet. “Obtained the promise” (epetychen tēs epangelias) needs a note, because the writer will say something apparently opposite at 11:13: these all died in faith, not having received the things promised. Abraham received Isaac, the first fulfilment; he did not receive the city, the nation or the blessing to all peoples. The promise was kept and it was not yet finished, which is exactly the position of the letter’s readers, and of ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham received everything promised in his lifetime. He saw the beginning; the fulfilment came in Christ and will be completed in the new creation (11:10, 16).

How do I wait when God seems to be doing nothing? Abraham’s story answers in three ways. First, remember what God has said, not what you have assumed he would do; Abraham held a promise, not a timetable. Second, keep obeying in the meantime. Abraham kept building altars, kept moving when told, kept praying, and the waiting years were full of ordinary faithfulness. Third, do not try to force the outcome; Hagar was the fruit of impatience, and it brought grief for generations. Waiting on God is not passivity but steady trust that goes on doing the next right thing while the promise ripens.
