In a sentence. When God made his promise to Abraham, since there was no one greater for him to swear by, he swore by himself, saying, “I will certainly bless you and give you many descendants.” And so, after waiting patiently, Abraham received what was promised.

On a Tuesday. What promise of God are you waiting for? Write it down, with the verse it comes from, so that you are waiting on what he actually said. Then notice where you are tempted to manufacture the answer yourself, as Abraham did with Hagar. Wait patiently, like Abraham. God keeps his word, and he keeps it on his own calendar.

For worship. The God of Abraham swore by himself. There was nothing higher in heaven or earth for him to stake, so he staked his own name, his own being, and on that mountain where a ram was caught in a thicket he pointed forward to another Son who would not be spared. Every promise God made to Abraham finds its yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). The blessing for all nations came through the seed of Abraham, and it has reached us. Our God does not hurry, and he does not fail. He kept his word to a wavering old man, and he will keep it to us.

verseByVerse.quote: For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.

For people swear by something greater than themselves. The writer explains why oaths exist at all. Human beings are not reliably truthful, so societies devise a mechanism for ending argument: you call something greater to witness and guarantee, and the matter is closed.

And in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. “Final” (peras) is end, limit. “Confirmation” (bebaiōsis) is a legal word for a guarantee, a validation. An oath is the point at which a dispute stops.

So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise. Sit with that for a moment, because it is astonishing. God’s bare word is already as reliable as anything in the universe; an oath cannot make him more truthful. He did it because he wanted to convince us. The oath adds nothing to God and everything to our confidence, and he swore it for that reason alone. In kindness he stooped to our weakness and added an oath. And notice the beneficiaries: the heirs of the promise. The oath sworn on a mountain to one old man is described as made for everyone who would ever inherit it, Abraham and all who share his faith (Galatians 3:29). That includes the congregation hearing this letter, and it includes anyone reading it now.

The unchangeable character of his purpose. “Unchangeable” (ametatheton) means immovable, irrevocable; it was a legal term for a will that cannot be altered. “Purpose” (boulē) is counsel, plan, will. God’s saving plan cannot change: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and he works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11).

He guaranteed it with an oath. The verb (emesiteusen) is literally he mediated, he stood in the middle as guarantor. God made himself the guarantor of his own promise, standing between himself and us, as it were, to pledge that he would keep it.

So that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie. The two are the promise and the oath: his word, and his word sworn. Both are unchangeable, because God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2). And “impossible” (adynaton) is the same word that opened verse 4. The letter’s two impossibilities face each other: it is impossible to restore an apostate, and it is impossible for God to lie. The second is the one to build on. It is impossible for apostates to be renewed; it is equally impossible for God to break his word to his own.

We who have fled for refuge. The phrase (hoi kataphygontes) is drawn from the cities of refuge (Numbers 35; Joshua 20), where a man who had killed accidentally ran for his life to a walled town, pursued by the avenger of blood. He was safe inside and dead outside, and the running was undignified and absolutely necessary. That is the writer’s picture of a Christian, and it is not a flattering one. Not a seeker weighing options but a man running for his life to the only place that will hold him. Believers have fled to God in Christ for safety from judgment.

Might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us. And there is the purpose of the whole paragraph. “Strong encouragement” (ischyra paraklēsis) is powerful comfort. “Hold fast” (kratēsai) is to seize, to grasp firmly. And the hope set before us (prokeimenē, lying ahead) is eternal salvation in God’s presence, set before us like the prize at the end of a race (12:1–2). God swore an oath so that frightened people would keep their grip.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God needs an oath to be trustworthy. He added it for our sake, to strengthen weak faith.

What does fleeing for refuge look like for me? It means coming to Christ as your only safety from God’s just judgment against your sin, and it means coming back to him whenever guilt or fear pursues you. The manslayer did not argue with the avenger or try to prove his innocence on the road; he ran. So when your conscience accuses you, do not try to settle the matter by your own record. Go to Christ in prayer, plead his blood, and rest inside the walls. You do not flee once and then live outside. You live in the city.

But what if my grip on the hope is weak? Then look again at what God has done to strengthen it. He gave two unchangeable things for exactly that reason: for people whose grip was failing. Your safety does not depend on the strength of your hold but on the strength of the city. The manslayer was safe because he was inside, not because he was brave. Hold fast as well as you can, and when you cannot, remember that the one who swore the oath holds you (John 10:29).

In a sentence. People swear by someone greater than themselves, and an oath confirms what is said and ends all argument. Because God wanted to make the unchangeable nature of his purpose very clear to the heirs of what was promised, he confirmed it with an oath. He did this so that, by two unchangeable things in which God cannot possibly lie, we who have fled to him for safety may be greatly encouraged to hold on to the hope set before us.

On a Tuesday. Take one promise of God that you find hard to believe for yourself, perhaps that he will never leave you, or that nothing can separate you from his love, and read it each morning this week alongside this verse. Say to yourself: God promised this, and he swore by himself, and it is impossible for him to lie. Then, when fear comes during the day, do what the manslayer did. Do not reason with it. Run to Christ.

For worship. God has given us his word and his oath. He who cannot lie has bound himself twice over, not because his word needed strengthening, but because our faith did. He has stooped to the weakness of his creatures and sworn by his own name to people running for their lives. And the city of refuge is open: it is Christ himself, whose gates are never shut against a sinner who flees to him, and in whom the avenger has no claim, because the blood has already been shed.

verseByVerse.quote: We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul. “This” is the hope of verse 18. The anchor (ankyra) was a common image of security; anchors appear on ancient coins and tombs, and early Christians carved them in the catacombs as a symbol of hope. The two adjectives are precise. Sure (asphalēs) means secure, not slipping: it will not fail in itself. Steadfast (bebaios) means firm, reliable: it will not shift under strain. A bad anchor fails either by breaking or by dragging, and this one does neither. An anchor keeps a ship from drifting (2:1), and our hope holds us steady in the storm.

A hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain. But the writer immediately does something no one else does with the metaphor, and it is the making of the passage. An anchor goes down. This one goes up and in. The curtain is the veil of the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31–33; Leviticus 16:2, 12), the barrier no one crossed but the high priest, once a year, with blood, where God’s presence dwelt. That is where the anchor is lodged. Not in circumstances, not in the believer’s own steadiness, not even in the visible church. The cable runs out of this world altogether and is made fast inside the sanctuary of God, where nothing can move it.

The storm and the anchorage. That means the storm and the anchorage are in different places. A ship in heavy weather is held by ground it cannot see, and the state of the sea has no bearing on the holding. For a congregation whose property had been seized and whose neighbours had turned against them, that is the entire point.

Where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf. And the metaphor changes again, into something more startling still. “Forerunner” (prodromos) is one who runs ahead. The word was used of scouts sent ahead of an army, and it has been explained by the picture of a small boat that carried a ship’s anchor ahead into the harbour when the water was too shallow for the ship to enter, fixing it to a rock so the ship could be pulled in. Either way, a forerunner is not merely someone who has arrived; he is someone who goes first so that others follow. The high priest of old went behind the curtain alone and came out again, and nobody followed him. This one went in and stayed, and the rope is attached to us (10:19–20). And he went “on our behalf” (hyper hēmōn): as our representative, so that where he is, we shall be.

Having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. The words of Psalm 110:4 return for the third time, bringing the author back to the subject he paused at in 5:10. And now the writer has his congregation where he wants them: warned, reassured, anchored and ready. Chapter 7 begins the argument he broke off at 5:11.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our hope depends on how strongly we feel. An anchor holds the ship, not the other way round. Our hope is secure because of where it is fixed: in Christ, in God’s presence.

What if I feel no hope at all? Then this verse is for you more than for anyone. The anchor does not depend on the feeling of the sailor. In the worst storm the deck heaves, the crew is frightened and nobody on board feels secure, and the ship holds, because the anchor is fixed somewhere the storm cannot reach. Your hope is not your feeling of hopefulness; it is Christ, alive in God’s presence for you. On days when you feel nothing, tell yourself where he is and what he is doing: he is there, he is your forerunner, and he always lives to intercede for you (7:25).

In a sentence. This hope is an anchor for our souls, firm and secure. It reaches into the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus, who went ahead of us, has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest for ever, in the order of Melchizedek.

On a Tuesday. Notice what you are anchored to when things go wrong this week. When the bad news comes, what do you reach for: your plans, your savings, your reputation, the approval of the people around you? Every one of those is in the sea. Practise a simple habit: when you feel yourself drifting, pray one sentence that names where your anchor is, Lord Jesus, you are in heaven for me. Say it until it becomes the reflex.

For worship. Our anchor is not in the sea. It is behind the curtain, in the holiest place of all, in the presence of God, and it is held there by the hand of our high priest. He went where no one could follow, and he went so that we could follow. He did not come out again and leave us outside, as every Aaron did; he stayed, a priest forever, and the cable runs from his throne to every one of his people. The storms are real, but they are in a different place from the anchorage. We will not drift away, because he will not let go.
verseByVerse.note: The high priest passed behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place once a year, on the Day of Atonement.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God,<sup>2</sup>and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.<sup>3</sup>And this we will do if God permits.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit,<sup>5</sup>and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,<sup>6</sup>and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.<sup>7</sup>For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God.<sup>8</sup>But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.<sup>9</sup>Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation.<sup>10</sup>For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.<sup>11</sup>And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end,<sup>12</sup>so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.<sup>13</sup>For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself,<sup>14</sup>saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.”<sup>15</sup>And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.<sup>16</sup>For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation.<sup>17</sup>So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath,<sup>18</sup>so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.<sup>19</sup>We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain,<sup>20</sup>where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

7.title: The Order of Melchizedek: A Priest Forever
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the theological centre of Hebrews. From two brief Old Testament references, Genesis 14:17–20 and Psalm 110:4, the writer argues for the supremacy and finality of Jesus’ priesthood over the whole Levitical system.

Melchizedek was king of righteousness and king of peace, priest of God Most High, king and priest in one. Genesis gives him no genealogy, birth or death, and that silence makes him a picture of the eternal Son. Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, so Melchizedek was greater than Abraham and, in Abraham, greater than Levi. If the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, why promise another? Jesus is a priest “by the power of an indestructible life”, guarantor of a better covenant, able to save to the uttermost because he always lives to intercede.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Melchizedek, and What Abraham Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham after the battle, blessed him and received a tenth of the spoils. His name means king of righteousness; Salem means peace. Without recorded father, mother or genealogy, beginning or end, he resembles the Son of God and remains a priest. Abraham the patriarch paid him tithes and was blessed by him, and the lesser is blessed by the greater. Even Levi, still in Abraham’s body, paid tithes through him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading the Silence of Scripture

Genesis gives Melchizedek no genealogy, and the writer reads the silence as a portrait of a priesthood that does not rest on descent. Abraham tithed to him and was blessed by him — the lesser by the greater.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi, still in Abraham's loins, paid tithes to Melchizedek.

Now: Righteousness comes first, then peace; there is no peace with God that bypasses righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.

Meaning first. Hebrews 7 is the heart of the letter’s argument that Jesus is a better priest than the priests of Israel. It begins with Melchizedek, the mysterious priest-king who appears in Genesis 14 (vv. 1–3). His name and title mean king of righteousness and king of peace; Scripture records no genealogy, birth or death for him, so he stands as a picture of a priest who continues forever. He was greater than Abraham, because Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, and so greater than Levi, Abraham’s descendant, who in a sense paid tithes through Abraham (vv. 4–10). Then the argument: if perfection could have come through the Levitical priesthood, why would Psalm 110 speak of another priest in the order of Melchizedek? A change of priesthood means a change of law, and Jesus came from Judah, not Levi (vv. 11–14). He became priest not by physical descent but by the power of an indestructible life (vv. 15–17). The old commandment is set aside because it was weak and could not make anything perfect; a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God (vv. 18–19). Jesus was made priest with God’s oath, making him the guarantor of a better covenant (vv. 20–22). The old priests died and had to be replaced; Jesus lives forever, so he can save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them (vv. 23–25). He is exactly the high priest we need: holy, innocent, separate from sinners, exalted, who does not need to offer daily sacrifices, because he offered himself once for all (vv. 26–28). The chapter is long and closely argued, and every step of it is climbing toward one sentence: he is able to save to the uttermost.

The argument resumes. The argument broken off at 5:11 resumes, and everything now turns on a man who appears in three verses of Genesis (14:18–20) and is never mentioned again in the Old Testament except in one line of one psalm (110:4). The writer has warned his readers, reassured them and anchored them. Now he gives them the solid food.

For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God. The episode is Genesis 14. Salem was probably the early name of Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2), the city where David would one day reign and where the temple would stand. And “priest of the Most High God” (El Elyon in Genesis) is the arresting phrase. This is centuries before Sinai, before Levi is born, before there is any Israelite priesthood at all, and here is a Canaanite king who is already a priest of the true God, the creator of heaven and earth, outside the line of Abraham. Abraham recognises him as such. A priest and king in one person, as Christ is.

Met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him. Abraham had just rescued his nephew Lot by defeating a coalition of four kings in a night raid (Genesis 14:1–17), and on the way home a stranger comes out to meet him. Melchizedek brings bread and wine, blesses Abraham in the name of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, receives a tenth of the spoil, and vanishes from the narrative. One meeting, a meal and a blessing, and he is gone.

And to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. “A tenth” (dekatē) is a tithe. Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils, recognising him as a priest of God. That detail will carry the whole argument of verses 4–10. Abraham, the father of the nation, the man to whom the promises were made, handed over a tithe, and a tithe is what you give to a superior.

He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness. Then the writer works on the names, and the method needs understanding rather than dismissal. He is not inventing meanings; he is reading the text the way its own authors read names, as carrying significance. The Hebrew name Malki-tsedeq divides into melek, king, and tsedeq, righteousness: my king is righteousness, or king of righteousness. Christ is the righteous King of whom the prophets spoke, the branch of David who would be called the LORD is our righteousness (Isaiah 9:7; 32:1; Jeremiah 23:5–6).

And then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace. Salem is shalem, related to shalom, peace. Christ is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who makes peace between God and sinners and himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). And note the order, which the writer does press: first, and then. Righteousness first, then peace. That is not decoration but the shape of the gospel, and the order cannot be reversed. There is no peace with God that does not come by way of righteousness: righteousness and peace kiss each other (Psalm 85:10), and since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1). That is why the cross was necessary, and why a merely merciful God who waived the problem of sin would have given us neither.

Where Christians differ: are believers required to tithe? Some teach that the tithe, a tenth of income, is binding on Christians, since Abraham tithed before the law of Moses, Jacob vowed a tenth (Genesis 28:22), and Jesus told the Pharisees not to neglect the tithe (Matthew 23:23). Others answer that Abraham’s tenth is recorded as a single gift from the spoils, not a rule; that the tithes the law commanded belonged to the Levitical system that this chapter says has changed (v. 12); and that Jesus was speaking to men still under that law. Verdict: Abraham’s tithe was a voluntary act of honour on a single occasion. The New Testament does not command a fixed percentage. It teaches generous, regular, proportional, cheerful giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–15; 9:6–7). A tenth is a good starting guide for many, but Christians under grace should often give more, not less, and never under compulsion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Melchizedek’s name is merely a lucky coincidence. The author sees God’s providence shaping the Old Testament record to point to Christ.

How did Melchizedek know the true God, outside Abraham’s family? Genesis does not tell us, and we should not invent an answer. What we know is that the knowledge of God had not yet died out everywhere after the flood, and that God is free to make himself known where he will. Melchizedek is one of a few such figures, like Jethro the priest of Midian later on. His existence is a quiet sign that the God of Abraham was never a tribal deity. He is God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, and the blessing to all nations was always his intention.

Was the bread and wine a kind of Lord’s Supper? Not in the sense of a sacrifice. Genesis says Melchizedek brought out bread and wine to a tired army returning from battle; it was hospitality and refreshment, and Hebrews, which makes so much of every detail, never mentions the bread and wine at all. Christians have long seen in it a beautiful foreshadowing of the table where Christ, our priest-king, feeds his people. But it gives no support to the idea that the Supper is an offering of Christ’s body by a priest. The writer’s whole point in this chapter is that Christ offered himself once for all (v. 27).

In a sentence. This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham as he was returning from defeating the kings, and blessed him, and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means first “king of righteousness,” and then, since he was king of Salem, it also means “king of peace.”

On a Tuesday. Are you trying to have peace without righteousness: a quiet conscience without dealing with the sin that disturbs it, peace in a relationship without putting right the wrong? God’s order is righteousness first, then peace, and the righteousness has been provided in Christ. Take the thing that is troubling your conscience to him by name today, and receive his peace on the right foundation. And when you give, give as Abraham did: freely, gladly, in honour of the one who has blessed you.

For worship. Christ is our Melchizedek. He is the King of righteousness, who did not set aside the demands of God’s law but fulfilled them, and the King of peace, who made peace by the blood of his cross. He comes out to meet his weary people with bread and wine, and he blesses them in the name of God Most High. Our King is our priest, and our priest is our King, and in him righteousness and peace have kissed each other for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.

He is without father or mother or genealogy. This verse has been read as meaning Melchizedek was a supernatural being, an angel or an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ. What the writer is actually doing is reading the silence of Scripture, and it was a recognised way of arguing that his readers would have followed easily. The three words are apatōr, without father, amētōr, without mother, and agenealogētos, without genealogy. Genesis is a book of genealogies. It tells you who fathered whom, how long they lived and when they died, for chapter after chapter. Melchizedek walks into the narrative with none of it. No father, no mother, no ancestry, no birth, no death.

Why the silence matters. For a priest that absence is extraordinary, because the Levitical priesthood was entirely a matter of documentation. A man’s right to serve depended on proving his descent from Aaron, and after the exile men who could not produce the records were excluded from the priesthood as unclean (Ezra 2:61–63). Melchizedek has no papers whatever, and Scripture presents him as a priest of the Most High God. His priesthood did not depend on descent.

Having neither beginning of days nor end of life. Scripture records neither. The author is arguing from the silence of the text: as Melchizedek appears in Scripture, he has no recorded beginning or end. The silence is not an accident of an incomplete record. The writer takes it as deliberate. Genesis has drawn a portrait with the genealogy left out, in order to sketch a priesthood that does not depend on descent and does not end with a funeral. He is a living picture of an eternal priesthood.

But resembling the Son of God. “Resembling” (aphōmoiōmenos) is made like, made to resemble. And note the direction of the comparison, because it is easy to get backwards. The writer does not say Christ is like Melchizedek. He says Melchizedek was made to resemble the Son of God. The eternal reality came first; the man in Genesis is the sketch. He is the copy; Christ is the original. The Son truly has no beginning or end; Melchizedek only appears that way in the record.

He continues a priest forever. “Continues” (menei) is remains; “forever” here (eis to diēnekes) is perpetually, continually. This is true of Melchizedek only in the sense that the text never records him stopping. It is true of Christ absolutely, and that is the point of the whole chapter. In the record, Melchizedek’s priesthood never ends. In Christ, the reality.

Where Christians differ: was Melchizedek Christ himself? Some believe Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (a Christophany), or an angel. Verdict: Melchizedek was most likely a real, historical human king and priest, whose recorded life God arranged to foreshadow Christ. The text says he was made like the Son of God, which would be odd if he were the Son: a thing does not resemble itself. He is a type, a living prophecy, not the reality itself. His lack of recorded genealogy is the point, not a claim that he literally had no parents.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Melchizedek was literally immortal or divine. It means the way Scripture presents him makes him a picture of Christ’s eternal priesthood.

Is it fair to build an argument on what Scripture does not say? Yes, when the silence is part of the shape God gave the text. The writer is not saying that Melchizedek had no parents; he is saying that God, who inspired Genesis, chose to present him without them, in a book where almost everyone else gets a genealogy, and then named him in a psalm about an eternal priest. Notice also that the writer never rests his case on silence alone. His foundation is the plain statement of Psalm 110:4, sworn by God. The silence of Genesis illustrates what the psalm declares.

In a sentence. No father, mother or family line is recorded for him, nor any beginning or end of his life; in this he is made to resemble the Son of God, and he remains a priest for ever.

On a Tuesday. Your standing with God does not depend on your pedigree either. Some Christians feel second-class because they did not grow up in church, or have a family history they are ashamed of; others quietly rely on their Christian background. Neither counts in the priesthood of Christ. When you pray this week, come as one whose access rests entirely on him, not on where you came from.

For worship. The Son of God has no beginning of days and no end of life. Before Abraham was, he is. God sketched him in Genesis with a few strokes, a priest-king who appears without origin and vanishes without a grave, and left the portrait waiting for the original. Now the original has come. Our high priest will never die, never be replaced, never hand his robes to another, never stop praying for us. He remains, and so we remain in him.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis records no parents, birth or death for Melchizedek. The writer draws out the meaning of that silence, not a claim that Melchizedek had no parents.

verseByVerse.quote: See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.

See how great this man was. “See” (theōreite) is consider, contemplate, look carefully. “How great” (pēlikos) asks for a measurement. The argument now shows Melchizedek’s superiority to Abraham, and therefore to Levi, and it builds on two customs the readers understood perfectly: who pays tithes to whom, and who blesses whom.

To whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! The title is deliberate. Not simply Abraham, but the patriarch (patriarchēs), the founding father, the greatest name a Jewish reader possessed. Whatever is proved about Melchizedek is proved against the highest possible standard. And the spoils (akrothinia) are literally the top of the heap, the best of the plunder, the choicest part that was traditionally offered to a god.

And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people. Then the comparison. Under the law of Moses, the Levites received tithes from the other tribes (Numbers 18:21–26), on the authority of a written command.

That is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. Note the qualification the writer adds. The Levites collected from their own relatives, fellow descendants of Abraham, by a commandment of the law: from people of exactly the same standing as themselves.

But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham. Melchizedek did none of that. He was not a Levite and had no legal warrant to collect, and the man who paid him was not a brother but Abraham himself. He received the tithe on the basis of his own greatness. It was given, not levied.

And blessed him who had the promises. This is the second and stronger argument. Abraham was the man who held the promises of God, the bearer of the blessing for all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:2–3), and he stood there and received a blessing from a stranger.

It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior. “Beyond dispute” is literally without any contradiction (chōris pasēs antilogias). The writer states it as a self-evident social fact, and in that world it was. In a formal blessing, blessing runs downhill: father to son, as Isaac blessed Jacob and Jacob blessed his sons (Genesis 27; 48–49); priest to people, as Aaron blessed Israel (Numbers 6:22–27); king to subject. Nobody blesses upward. So Abraham, who was carrying the promise, the father of the nation, the man in whom all families of the earth would be blessed, put himself in the lower position twice in a single meeting, and Genesis records it without comment. The writer’s readers had been reading that chapter all their lives and had never noticed what it implied.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that an ordinary believer cannot ask God to bless someone greater; this concerns formal, authoritative blessing.

Why does it matter to me who was greater than whom? Because the readers were tempted to go back to the Levitical priests as if they were the real thing. The writer shows from their own Scriptures that before Levi was born, Abraham himself bowed to a greater priest. If Abraham honoured the shadow, how much more should we honour the reality? Every argument in this chapter is designed to make you see that leaving Christ for anything else, however old and venerable, is trading up for something smaller. And it means that the blessing you receive from Christ is a blessing from above, from the greatest, with all of God’s authority behind it.

In a sentence. Just think how great he was: even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the best of the plunder! The law requires the descendants of Levi who become priests to collect a tenth from the people, their own relatives, although they too are descended from Abraham. But this man, who did not trace his descent from Levi, collected a tenth from Abraham and blessed the one who had God’s promises. And without doubt the lesser person is blessed by the greater.

On a Tuesday. Abraham gave the best of the spoils, not the leftovers. Look at what you give to Christ: your money, your time, your best energy of the day. Is it the top of the heap or what remains after everything else? Choose one place this week to give him the first and best, before anything else gets it. And when you receive a blessing in the Lord’s name at the end of a service, receive it as a blessing from above, not a formality.

For worship. Consider how great our high priest is. Abraham, the friend of God, bowed before his shadow. Levi, still unborn, paid his tithe to the picture of him. And the reality of whom Melchizedek was only a sketch has come, not to receive our tithes, but to give himself. He blesses us from above with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places (Ephesians 1:3), and there is no blessing higher, because there is no one greater.

verseByVerse.quote: In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.

In the one case tithes are received by mortal men. The contrast is between men who die and a man whose death is not recorded. “Mortal” (apothnēskontes) is literally dying men. The Levitical priesthood was a relay. Aaron served and died on Mount Hor; Eleazar took the robes; and so on for fourteen centuries, every generation burying its high priest and consecrating another. The system was designed around mortality.

But in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. The writer is careful with his language: not who lives, but of whom it is testified (martyroumenos) that he lives. The claim rests on what Scripture says and does not say, which is exactly the argument of verse 3. The record of Genesis says nothing of his death, and Psalm 110 says of the priest in his order, You are a priest forever. So in the record, he lives. And this points to Christ, who truly lives forever (v. 16).

One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham. The writer knows he is pressing hard. “One might even say” (hōs epos eipein) is so to speak, a way of putting it. He is not claiming this as a knock-down proof; he is offering it as a way of seeing the thing. Levi was Abraham’s great-grandson and was not born for a century and more.

For he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him. The loins (osphys) are the source of descendants. In the Hebrew way of reckoning, a descendant is genuinely present in his ancestor and acts in him. In a real sense, the whole Levitical priesthood bowed to Melchizedek when Abraham did, and so Melchizedek’s priesthood is greater than Levi’s.

Representation is the logic of the Bible. That way of thinking is not a curiosity. It is the logic of the whole Bible. It is why the sin of one man could involve a race, and why the obedience of one man can make many righteous (Romans 5:12–19). A modern reader who finds representative solidarity strange will find most of the doctrine of salvation strange, since it all runs on the same principle. So the conclusion stands: the tribe that would one day collect Israel’s tithes had already, in its ancestor, paid them to somebody else. The Levitical priesthood acknowledged a greater priesthood before it existed, and Genesis 14 has been sitting in the Torah all along saying so.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Levi was personally guilty or responsible for Abraham’s act. It is an argument from representation and headship, which the author marks as a manner of speaking.

Is it fair that I should be counted in someone else? It can feel unfair when the head is Adam, whose sin brought death to all. But the same principle is the only reason anyone is saved. If God did not deal with people through a representative, Christ could not have stood in our place, his death could not count as ours, and his righteousness could not be credited to us. No one complains that it is unfair to be counted righteous in Christ. The question that matters is not whether we are represented, because everyone is, but by whom: Adam or Christ.

In a sentence. In the case of the Levites, the tenth is received by men who die; but in Melchizedek’s case, by someone who, as Scripture testifies, is alive. You might even say that Levi, who collects the tenth, paid the tenth through Abraham, because when Melchizedek met Abraham, Levi was still in the body of his ancestor.

On a Tuesday. Picture what the relay meant for an ordinary Israelite: the man who represented you before God would one day be carried out. Now think about whom you lean on spiritually: a pastor, a parent, a gifted friend. Thank God for them, and remember they are mortal. Let them point you past themselves to the one representative who will never be carried out. And if a beloved Christian leader has died or fallen, your access to God has not been interrupted for a moment.

For worship. Every Levite died, and every priest of Aaron’s line was buried by the next. But the one of whom it is testified that he lives has no successor, because he has no grave. He died once for our sins, and he lives for ever as our priest. We are counted in him as Levi was counted in Abraham, and what he has done stands as done for us. Thanks be to God, we are represented before him not by dying men but by the living Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–28 — A Priest Forever, and the Change That Follows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, why promise another of a different order? A change of priesthood means a change of law. Jesus came from Judah, a tribe with no priests, and he is a priest not by descent but by the power of an indestructible life. The old command is set aside as weak; a better hope lets us draw near to God. God swore an oath to this priesthood, making Jesus guarantor of a better covenant. The old priests were many because they died; he lives forever, so he saves completely those who come to God through him, always interceding. Holy and exalted, he offered himself once for all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Change the Priesthood and the Law Must Follow

The law rested on the Levitical priesthood, and God has replaced that priesthood by oath with a priest who holds office by the power of an indestructible life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The former priests were many, because death stopped each one.

Now: He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.

Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood. Now the argument turns from Genesis to the psalm, and the question is put with real force. “Perfection” (teleiōsis) means completion, the bringing of a thing to its intended goal: the same root as made perfect in 2:10 and 5:9, and a keyword of the letter. Perfection here means bringing people fully into God’s presence, with sins dealt with completely and consciences cleansed (9:9; 10:1, 14). The question is not whether the Levitical priesthood was good, but whether it could finish anything. It could not.

For under it the people received the law. The parenthesis matters. Priesthood and law are not two separate systems that happen to coexist. The law established the priesthood, and the priesthood administered the law; the law was given through a priestly arrangement and depends on it. They stand or fall together. You cannot keep one and discard the other.

What further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek? The logic is simple and unanswerable. Psalm 110 was written by David, centuries into the Levitical system, and in it God announces a priest of a different order. You do not announce a replacement for something that is working. If the Levitical priesthood had been sufficient, why would God promise a new priest of a different kind? The very existence of the promise is evidence that the arrangement it replaces was not final. The promise itself proves the old system was inadequate and temporary.

Rather than one named after the order of Aaron? The new priest is not in Aaron’s line. God did not promise a better Aaron, a reformed Levitical priesthood with holier men in it. He promised a different order altogether.

For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well. This is one of the most consequential sentences in the letter. “Change” (metatithemenēs) is transfer, alteration, the word used of moving something from one place to another. Since the law of Moses was tied to the Levitical priesthood, a new priesthood means the whole Mosaic covenant arrangement changes. This is radical: the old covenant system, with its sacrifices, priesthood and ceremonies, has been replaced.

What it meant for the first readers. Follow what that means for the people receiving this letter. They were being drawn back to the temple, the sacrifices, the food laws, the calendar, and being told, no doubt, that these were God’s own commands and could not simply be dropped. The writer agrees that they were God’s commands. And he says the entire structure was attached to a priesthood, that God himself has changed the priesthood, and that the law therefore cannot stand as it did. This is the moment the letter’s argument becomes irreversible. Not that the law was bad, not merely that it was disobeyed, but that its foundation has been replaced by the God who laid it, and a building does not outlive its foundation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s moral law has changed. The moral standards expressed in the Ten Commandments reflect God’s unchanging character and are confirmed in the New Testament (Romans 13:8–10). What changed is the ceremonial and priestly system, the covenant administration, which pointed forward to Christ.

Does this mean the Ten Commandments are abolished? No. The law that changes is the law bound up with the priesthood: the sacrifices, the temple, the purity rules and the calendar. Reformed Christians have long distinguished the ceremonial law, fulfilled in Christ and set aside; the civil law, given to Israel as a nation; and the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still shows believers how to love God and neighbour (Matthew 5:17–19; Romans 13:8–10). Some Christians prefer to say that the whole law of Moses has given way to the law of Christ; but they agree that its moral demands come to us again in the New Testament, and the new covenant writes God’s law on the heart (8:10). What changes is not God’s standard but the way to him.

Should Christians keep the Old Testament food laws and festivals, then? Not as a duty before God. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Paul calls the festivals, new moons and food rules a shadow of the things to come, whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). A Christian may eat or abstain, and may find it instructive to learn about Passover or the Day of Atonement, because they point so clearly to Christ. What he must not do is treat them as necessary for acceptance with God or as a mark of a superior holiness. That was exactly the pull these readers felt, and the writer says it means going back to a priesthood God has retired.

In a sentence. If perfection could have been reached through the Levitical priesthood, on which the law given to the people was based, why was there still a need for another priest to come, one in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed too.

On a Tuesday. Notice the old-covenant instincts in your own religion: the feeling that you must perform something before you can come to God, that a bad week puts you outside until you have made up for it, that some ritual or routine earns his favour. These are the habits of a priesthood that has been changed. Keep God’s commandments gladly, as his child, and come to him through Christ alone, today, as you are.

For worship. The God who gave the law to Israel through Aaron’s priesthood was never content with what it could do. From the days of David he was promising something better, and he has kept his word. He has not left us under a system that could never make us perfect, but has brought us under Christ, who by a single offering has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14). The God who laid the old foundation has laid a new one, and it is his own Son.

verseByVerse.quote: For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.

For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe. The writer now names the constitutional obstacle. Under the law, priesthood was a matter of tribe (phylē heteras, a different tribe), and the boundary was absolute. Jesus was not from Levi.

From which no one has ever served at the altar. “Served” (proseschēken) is attended to, officiated. Under the law, only Levites served the sanctuary, and only Aaron’s descendants served as priests at the altar. Not a single man from Judah had ever served at the altar in fourteen hundred years. The one king of Judah who tried, Uzziah, went into the temple to burn incense and was struck with leprosy on the spot (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah. Note the word “evident” (prodēlon, clearly known, obvious). It is common knowledge, not a claim requiring proof. The genealogies were public (Matthew 1:1–16; Luke 3:23–33), and the expectation had always been that the deliverer would come from Judah and from David: the sceptre shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and he is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5). And the word for “descended” (anatetalken) is lovely: it is used of the sun rising and of a shoot springing up. The prophets used both pictures of the Messiah, the sunrise from on high (Luke 1:78) and the branch from Jesse’s stump (Isaiah 11:1).

The two requirements collide. So the two requirements collided. The Messiah had to be from Judah, because the promise said so. A priest had to be from Levi, because the law said so. And Psalm 110 says the Messiah will be a priest.

And in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests. Once again the argument runs on a silence, as it did with Melchizedek’s genealogy. The law is not merely quiet about priests from Judah; its quietness is the point. There was no provision, because the priesthood being announced was never going to run through the law at all. Under the law, Jesus could not have been a priest. His priesthood must be of a different order altogether.

The objection conceded. This is the answer to an objection the readers would certainly have heard. Anyone defending the old arrangement could say, quite correctly, that Jesus had no right to priestly office: he was not a Levite, he had never served in the temple, and the law was explicit. The writer concedes every word of it. Jesus has no claim to the Levitical priesthood whatever, and never claimed one. He holds a different office, older than Levi and established by an oath the law knew nothing about, which is precisely why the objection, though true, misses everything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus was unqualified. He was qualified by something far greater than tribal descent (v. 16). Nor does it mean the Levitical priesthood was wrong; it was God-given, but temporary.

Why did God arrange it so that the Messiah would come from the wrong tribe for priesthood? So that no one could mistake Christ’s priesthood for a continuation of the old one. If Jesus had been a Levite, his ministry could have been read as the best chapter of the old system. By bringing him from Judah, God made it plain that something new had come: a king who is also a priest, uniting in one person the two offices that Israel had always kept apart. The kings of Israel could rule but not atone; the priests could atone in shadow but not rule. Christ does both, perfectly and for ever.

In a sentence. The one these things are said about belonged to a different tribe, and no one from that tribe has ever served at the altar. For it is clear that our Lord came from the tribe of Judah, and Moses said nothing about priests coming from that tribe.

On a Tuesday. You need both a king and a priest, and you have both in one person. When you are tempted to treat Jesus as only a priest, a source of forgiveness who makes no claims on your life, remember he is from Judah: he rules. When you are tempted to treat him only as a demanding king, remember he is a priest: he forgives and prays for you. Bring him today both your obedience and your sins.

For worship. Praise Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who is both your King and your Priest. The sun has risen from the tribe of Judah with healing in its wings, and the shoot from Jesse’s stump has become the high priest of heaven. What no king of Israel dared and no priest of Israel could, he has done: he rules his people and atones for them, sits on the throne and stands at the altar, and he does it all for the people he loves.

verseByVerse.quote: This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”

This becomes even more evident. “Even more evident” (perissoteron eti katadēlon) is much more obvious still. The change of law becomes clearer still when we look at the kind of priest the psalm promises.

When another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek. The word for “another” (heteros) means another of a different kind, not merely one more of the same sort. This is not a successor. It is a different species of priest. And “likeness” (homoiotēs) is resemblance, picking up the made like of verse 3.

Who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent. Then the contrast that is the heart of the chapter. The Greek behind “legal requirement concerning bodily descent” is literally a law of a fleshly commandment (nomon entolēs sarkinēs): a rule about physical pedigree. That is what qualified a man under the old system. Not his character, not his devotion, not his gifts, but his birth certificate. A godly Israelite from the wrong tribe could not serve; an indifferent one from the right family could. It was a merely external, earthly qualification.

But by the power of an indestructible life. Against that stands “the power of an indestructible life”, and power (dynamis) is the word for the mighty works of 2:4. The word akatalytos means undissolvable, incapable of being broken up or destroyed; it is related to the word for taking down a tent or pulling down a building (2 Corinthians 5:1). Not merely a life that happens to go on, but one that cannot be ended, and the resurrection is behind the phrase. Death did its worst and could not dissolve it. God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it (Acts 2:24). His priesthood is based not on genealogy but on who he is and on his victory over death.

Two qualifications side by side. Set the two side by side and the difference is the whole argument. One priesthood rests on a document about ancestry; the other on a life that death could not destroy. The first is guaranteed by records that can be lost, as they were after the exile (Ezra 2:61–62). The second is guaranteed by an empty tomb.

For it is witnessed of him, You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek. And Psalm 110:4 is quoted again. The writer keeps returning to it because the whole case rests on those few words, and he wants his hearers to know them by heart. Everything hangs on the word “forever”: only someone with an indestructible life could be a priest forever. A priest forever needs no successor, takes no holiday, and cannot be replaced by a better one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus did not truly die. He died truly and rose truly. His life is indestructible in that death could not keep him and he will never die again (Romans 6:9; Revelation 1:18).

What difference does an indestructible life make to me? It means your priest cannot be taken from you. Every human helper you have can be lost: by death, distance, illness, failure or simply their own limits. Christ cannot. His care for you does not depend on his health, his mood or his circumstances, and it will not be interrupted by any crisis in your life or in the world. It also means his life is the guarantee of yours. Because I live, you also will live, he said (John 14:19). The life that could not be dissolved is the life he shares with everyone united to him.

What should this mean for how churches choose leaders? It is a warning against choosing people for pedigree. The old priesthood ran on bloodline; the new people of God are not to be led on the basis of family, wealth, education or connections, but on character and gifts given by the Spirit (1 Timothy 3:1–7). A pastor’s son is not thereby fit to be a pastor, and a convert from a broken home is not thereby disqualified. The church that follows a priest qualified by an indestructible life should look for leaders marked by his life in them.

In a sentence. And it becomes clearer still when another priest like Melchizedek appears, one who has become a priest not by a rule about human ancestry but by the power of a life that cannot be destroyed. For Scripture testifies about him: “You are a priest for ever, in the order of Melchizedek.”

On a Tuesday. Think of the thing you most fear losing, and the person you most depend on. Bring both to Christ this week and say plainly: you are the one who cannot be lost. Then take the fear of death itself, your own or someone else’s, and set it beside the empty tomb. Your priest has been through death and out the other side, and his life is indestructible.

For worship. Rejoice that your High Priest has an indestructible life. Men tried to destroy it with nails and a spear, and sealed it in a tomb, and on the third day it broke out of every bond they had put on it. Death could not hold him, and death will never touch him again. That life is now poured out in priestly care for us, and nothing can stop it: not our sins, not our weakness, not the grave itself. He lives, and so his people will live.

verseByVerse.quote: For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.

For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside. “Set aside” (athetēsis) is annulment, cancellation; it was a legal term for annulling a decree or a contract. The former commandment, the law establishing the Levitical priesthood, is cancelled. These are strong words about God’s own law, and they must be read exactly or they will be misread badly. The writer is not saying the law was a mistake, or evil, or contemptible. He has just said the people received it under the Levitical priesthood by divine arrangement.

Because of its weakness and uselessness. “Weakness” (asthenes) is powerlessness; “uselessness” (anōpheles) is unprofitableness. These are judgments about capacity for a particular purpose. Not that the law was bad, but that it was weak for this purpose: it could not achieve full cleansing and access to God. The law was perfectly effective at what it was given to do. It exposed sin, regulated a nation and pointed forward. It was useless for making anybody perfect, which it never claimed to do. A thermometer is useless for heating a room, and the fault is not in the thermometer. And the weakness lay in the flesh it worked through: what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3).

For the law made nothing perfect. Hence the parenthesis, which is the plainest statement of it in Scripture. Not nobody: nothing. In fourteen centuries the entire apparatus of priesthood, sacrifice and ceremony never brought one thing to completion. The law pointed to perfection but could not provide it (9:9; 10:1). It was a shadow (10:1), a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24).

But on the other hand, a better hope is introduced. “Better” (kreittōn) is the letter’s signature; it uses the word some thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together: a better priest, better covenant, better promises, better sacrifices, better country. And “introduced” (epeisagōgē) is brought in besides, ushered in, like a new heir brought into a house. The better hope is the new covenant hope in Christ.

Through which we draw near to God. And then the purpose clause, which is where the whole chapter has been going. That is the point of all of it: the genealogies, the tithes, the tribes, the oath. Not to win an argument about priesthood but to get people into the presence of God. The old system existed to manage distance: curtains, courts, and a single man admitted once a year. The new one exists to remove it. Under the law the people stayed at a distance; only the high priest drew near. Through Christ every believer can draw near (4:16; 10:19–22). “Draw near” (engizomen) is the letter’s word for what a Christian actually does, and everything else is scaffolding around it. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you (James 4:8).

What it does not mean. “Uselessness” does not mean the law had no value. It was God’s gift, holy and good (Romans 7:12), and it served its purpose of pointing to Christ. But it could not do what only Christ could do.

If the law made nothing perfect, why did God give it? Because it was never meant to make perfect. It was given to show sin for what it is (Romans 3:20; 7:7), to restrain evil, to set Israel apart, and above all to point forward: every sacrifice, every washing, every feast and every priest was a picture of Christ. Like scaffolding round a building, it was essential until the building stood, and then it came down. The law did not fail; it did its work, which was to lead us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith (Galatians 3:24).

What does drawing near to God actually look like? It is the whole life of faith gathered into a single act: coming to God, through Christ, with nothing in your hands. You draw near when you pray, speaking to God as Father in Jesus’ name; when you confess sin and receive his forgiveness; when you hear his word with faith; when you come to the Lord’s Table; when you worship with his people. And you draw near without the old fear, because the way is open. You do not need a priest, a holy place, a special mood or a good week. You need Christ, and in him you have everything.

In a sentence. The earlier regulation is cancelled because it was weak and could not achieve its goal (for the law brought nothing to perfection), and in its place a better hope is brought in, through which we come near to God.

On a Tuesday. When did you last simply draw near to God, not to get something done, but to be with him? Set aside ten minutes today. Come with no performance, no list of your good deeds, no promise to do better. Come through Christ, and say so: Father, I come in Jesus’ name. Then stay a while. The curtain is open, and you are welcome.

For worship. The law made nothing perfect, and God has done what the law could not. He has introduced a better hope, and its name is Jesus. Where once only one man could approach, once a year, trembling, with blood not his own, now the weakest believer may come at any hour, by the blood of the Son of God. The old system kept us at a distance. The new one brings us home. Blessed be God, who did not leave us outside the curtain, but has drawn near to us in his Son so that we may draw near to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ’You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ‘You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.

And it was not without an oath. The writer returns to the argument he made about Abraham in chapter 6 and applies it now to the priesthood. The oath (horkōmosia, oath-swearing) is another sign of superiority. God’s oath gives absolute certainty (6:16–18).

For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath. That is a striking observation, easily verified by anyone who goes and looks. Aaron and his sons were appointed by command, not by oath (Exodus 28–29). The whole Levitical arrangement was instituted by command; Exodus and Leviticus are full of instructions about the priesthood, and God never once swears to it. He legislated it. He did not guarantee it on oath.

But this one was made a priest with an oath. Psalm 110:4 again, and this time the writer quotes the clause he has previously left out. The psalm does not merely announce the priesthood; it records God swearing to it and declaring that he will not reverse the decision.

The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, You are a priest forever. “Change his mind” (metamelēthēsetai) is regret, repent, have second thoughts. God will never revoke this appointment. An arrangement made by command can be amended by a later command, and the Levitical system was in fact amended repeatedly and finally set aside. An arrangement established by the oath of God, who has already been said to find lying impossible (6:18), cannot be. Christ’s priesthood is permanent and irrevocable.

This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant. The word is engyos, a legal and commercial term used only here in the New Testament: a surety, the person who stands behind an obligation with his own property and his own person. If the debtor fails, the guarantor pays. Judah offered himself to his father in exactly this way for Benjamin: I will be a pledge of his safety; from my hand you shall require him (Genesis 43:9), and when the moment came he offered to become a slave in the boy’s place (Genesis 44:32–33). Jesus personally guarantees that the new covenant will be fulfilled. He stands surety for his people: he pledges that their debts are paid and that God’s promises to them will be kept.

Why a guarantor matters. Consider what that means. A covenant has two parties, and covenants fail because one of them does, which is exactly what happened to the first one: they did not continue in my covenant (8:9). Jesus is not the covenant’s administrator or its witness. He is the surety, and he stands behind it with himself. That means the new covenant cannot fail on our side, because our side has a guarantor who has already paid. The word appears once in the New Testament, and it is the strongest security a first-century reader had a category for. And “better covenant” (kreittonos diathēkēs) is the first mention of covenant in Hebrews; chapter 8 will develop it as the new covenant of Jeremiah 31.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God was uncertain about the old priesthood and certain only about the new. Rather, the old was always meant to be temporary; the new was meant to be permanent, and the oath marks that.

What is a covenant? A covenant is a binding relationship established by God with promises and obligations, sealed in a solemn way. It is more than a contract: it is God committing himself to a people and taking them as his own. The Bible traces a series of covenants, with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai and David, all leading to the new covenant promised by Jeremiah and established in Christ’s blood (Luke 22:20). In the new covenant God promises to forgive sins, to write his law on our hearts and to be our God. Christ is both the one who makes it, by his death, and the one who guarantees it, by his life.

In a sentence. And this was not done without an oath. Others became priests without any oath, but he became a priest with an oath when God said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest for ever.’” Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant.

On a Tuesday. When your failures make you wonder whether God will finally give up on you, remember that the new covenant does not rest on your keeping it but on Christ’s guaranteeing it. Say it to yourself in the words of this verse: Jesus is the guarantor. Then, because you are secure, take up the obedience you have been avoiding. A child who knows his place in the family is safe obeys from love, not from fear of being sent away.

For worship. The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind. Of all the things God might have bound himself to by oath, he chose to swear that his Son would be our priest for ever. And the Son has made himself our surety. Like Judah standing before Joseph, offering himself in Benjamin’s place, he has stood before the Father and said of every one of his people, from my hand you shall require him. He paid the debt with his own life, and he guarantees every promise by the life he now lives. There is no security in the universe stronger than that.

verseByVerse.quote: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.

The former priests were many in number. Josephus counted eighty-three high priests from Aaron to the destruction of the temple in AD 70. Eighty-three men, eighty-three funerals, eighty-three consecrations, one after another.

Because they were prevented by death from continuing in office. The reason there were so many is stated plainly: death kept interrupting. “Prevented” (kōlyesthai) is hindered, stopped. Aaron died on Mount Hor, and his son Eleazar was dressed in his garments before the people (Numbers 20:23–29). Picture what that meant for an ordinary Israelite. The man who represented you before God would one day be carried out, and somebody else would put on the robes. Every priest’s intercession ended at death, and whatever confidence you had in him died with him.

But he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. The word for “permanently” (aparabaton) means unchangeable, non-transferable; it was used of things that cannot pass to another. His office is not on loan and will never be handed on. Christ’s priesthood will never pass to a successor. He has no successor, because he never dies.

Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost. And everything in the chapter now cashes out in one of the great verses of the Bible. “Able” (dynatai) is has power. “To the uttermost” (eis to panteles) can mean completely or forever, and the ambiguity is a gift: both are true. He saves entirely, leaving nothing unfinished, and he saves permanently, without expiry. Nothing in a person is beyond its reach and no stretch of time is outside it. There is no sinner too far gone, no sin too great, no time too long.

Those who draw near to God through him. The letter’s word again (proserchomenous, those who come), and it is the only qualification named. Not those who understand, or who have never failed. Those who come. It is through Christ alone: no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). And it describes believers as those who keep coming to God through Christ, not once but as the habit of their lives.

Since he always lives to make intercession for them. And there is the ground, and the place to rest. What is Christ doing now? Hebrews answers: he is praying for his people, and he never stops. “Always lives” is pantote zōn; “make intercession” (entynchanein) is to plead, intervene, appeal on behalf of. Christ’s intercession is not begging an unwilling Father, but his presence before the Father as the one whose sacrifice has been accepted, continually presenting his finished work on behalf of his people and asking for all they need (Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1). His intercession guarantees their perseverance: he prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and he prays for all his own (John 17:9, 15, 20, 24).

At three in the morning. That is a strange and steadying thing to hold on to. At three in the morning, when a Christian is too tired or too ashamed to pray for himself, there is somebody at the right hand of God who is praying for him and has not paused. The salvation reaches to the uttermost because the interceding does.

What it does not mean. Christ’s intercession does not mean his sacrifice was incomplete. His intercession is based on his finished sacrifice. Nor does it mean he prays for those who do not come through him; he intercedes for “them,” those who draw near (John 17:9).

Do Christians, then, need human priests? No. If Christ holds his priesthood permanently and offered himself once for all (v. 27), no other mediator is needed and no sacrifice is to be repeated. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Every believer draws near to God through him (4:16; 10:19–22), and the whole church is a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). Pastors are shepherds and teachers, not priests. We may and should ask one another to pray for us, but no believer needs anyone except Christ to stand between him and God.

If Jesus is praying for me, do I still need to pray? Yes, and his praying is the reason your prayers count. You pray in his name, which means your prayers rise to the Father carried by his intercession, made acceptable by his blood. His intercession does not make yours unnecessary any more than a father’s love makes a child’s requests unnecessary. And on the days when you cannot find words, both he and the Spirit pray for you (Romans 8:26–27, 34). You are never praying alone.

Can I be beyond his saving? Not if you come to God through him. The verse names no limit except coming. Whatever you have done, however long you have been away, however many times you have fallen in the same place, the word is uttermost. The only person beyond his saving is the one who will not come. If you are coming, or want to come, you are exactly the person this verse is about.

In a sentence. There were many of those earlier priests, because death prevented them from continuing in office; but because Jesus lives for ever, his priesthood is permanent and passes to no one else. That is why he is able to save completely and for ever those who come to God through him, because he is always alive to plead for them.

On a Tuesday. Pick the sin or the weakness that makes you most doubt whether God can keep you to the end. Write the word uttermost beside it. Then, whenever it accuses you this week, answer it with this verse: he is able to save to the uttermost, because he always lives to intercede for me. And pray for someone who is struggling; it is the one way we can share, in a small way, in the work our high priest is doing for them now.

For worship. Right now, Jesus is interceding for us. While we sleep, while we work, while we fail and while we forget him, he is at the right hand of the Father, presenting the sacrifice that was accepted and asking for everything his people need. Aaron died on a mountain and the robes passed to another; our high priest lives for ever, and the robes will never come off him. He saves completely, and he saves for ever. Nothing in us is beyond his reach and no day in our lives is outside his prayers. To him who is able, be glory for ever.
