verseByVerse.quote: For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.

For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest. “Fitting” (eprepen) is suitable, appropriate, the word from 2:10 again. Not merely that we needed one, but that it suited the character of God to provide him. Jesus is exactly the high priest sinners need. Five descriptions follow, and they move outward from his character to his location.

Holy. The word here (hosios) is not the usual one for holiness but a term for devout, pious, wholly given to God; it describes his Godward disposition, pure toward God.

Innocent. Literally without evil (akakos): guileless, harmless, containing no malice toward people.

Unstained. Undefiled (amiantos), untouched by any pollution. The high priest had to avoid ritual defilement, and could not even go near a dead body, not even his own father’s (Leviticus 21:10–15). Jesus was free from all moral defilement. He touched lepers and the dead, and instead of being defiled by them, he made them clean.

Separated from sinners. This requires care, because it can be read to contradict everything the Gospels show. “Separated” (kechōrismenos) is a perfect tense: set apart, and remaining so. The man who was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, who ate with them (Luke 15:2), is not being described as aloof. The separation is moral and, since the ascension, positional. He was among sinners without becoming one, utterly different from them in character, and is now exalted beyond their reach to harm him.

And exalted above the heavens. Raised to the highest place (4:14; Ephesians 4:10). The old high priest went through a curtain; this one has passed through the heavens and sits above them.

He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily. Then verse 27 sets the two priesthoods side by side one last time, and the difference is in a single phrase. Priests offered daily sacrifices, morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42), and the high priest offered yearly on the Day of Atonement. The repetition proved their inadequacy (10:1–4, 11).

First for his own sins and then for those of the people. As in 5:3 and Leviticus 16:6, 15. Two problems: it never stopped, and the priest had to deal with himself first. Jesus had no sins of his own.

Since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. “Once for all” (ephapax) is once, finally, never to be repeated: a single, unrepeatable, completely sufficient act (9:12, 26, 28; 10:10). It is one of the letter’s great words, and it will dominate chapters 9 and 10. And the last words are where the chapter arrives. Every other priest offered something else: a bull, a goat, a lamb. This one had nothing to bring but himself, and brought it. This is the first explicit statement in Hebrews that Christ’s sacrifice was his own self. Priest and sacrifice in the same person, which no religious system had ever imagined.

For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests. The chapter closes on the two contrasts it has been building. “Weakness” (astheneia): sinful, mortal men.

But the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever. Weak men against a Son, and a temporary command against a later oath. Psalm 110 came after Sinai, centuries after the law of Moses, so it supersedes it; and God does not swear to things he means to revise. “Son” is the eternal Son of God. “Made perfect” (teteleiōmenon) is a perfect tense, completed and remaining so, as in 2:10 and 5:9: fully qualified, forever.

Where Christians differ: is Christ’s sacrifice re-presented in the Mass? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the Mass is the same sacrifice of Calvary made present again in an unbloody manner, offered for the living and the dead. Verdict: Hebrews insists that Christ offered himself “once for all,” and that unlike the old priests he has no need to offer repeatedly (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–18). Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin (10:18). The Lord’s Supper is a memorial and a means of grace, in which believers by faith feed spiritually on Christ, who is truly present by his Spirit, but it is not a re-offering of his sacrifice.

What it does not mean. “Separated from sinners” does not mean Jesus is distant from sinners who come to him. He is exalted, yet sympathises (4:15).

Why does a sinless Son need to be made perfect? Because perfect here does not mean morally improved but completed for a task. Jesus was always without sin. But to be our high priest he had to become man, live a life of obedience, suffer, die, rise and ascend. When all of that was done, he was made perfect: fully and finally qualified, having finished everything a priest must do for sinners. A fully trained surgeon who has completed the operation has not become a better man; he has done the work. Christ has done it, and his qualification will never lapse.

If he offered himself once for all, what does that mean when I fail again? It means there is no new sacrifice to be made for you, and none needed. When you confess sin, you are not asking Christ to be offered again; you are resting on the offering already made, which covers your past, present and future sins. Repentance is real and necessary, but it is not payment. The payment was once, and it was enough. Come back to the cross not to add to it but to receive from it again what it has already accomplished.

In a sentence. Such a high priest is exactly what we need: holy, without evil, pure, set apart from sinners and raised higher than the heavens. Unlike the other high priests, he does not need to offer sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for the people’s. He did that once and for all when he offered himself. For the law appoints as high priests men who are weak; but the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect for ever.

On a Tuesday. Notice how often you try to offer something more for your sins: an extra effort at religion, a period of feeling bad, a promise to God that you will make up for it. Every one of those is a small attempt at a daily sacrifice. Stop offering. Confess, thank him that the offering is finished, and then go and serve him out of gratitude rather than debt. The Supper you take on Sunday is a remembrance of a finished work, not a top-up.

For worship. Such a high priest is exactly what we needed, and it was fitting for God to give him. He is holy toward God and harmless toward us, spotless in a world of stains, among sinners and yet never one of them, and now exalted above the heavens. He did not bring a bull or a goat. He brought himself, once for all, priest and sacrifice in one, and the offering was so complete that it will never be repeated and never need to be. The law gave us weak men; the oath has given us the Son, perfect for ever. Our sins are dealt with completely, and our worship will never end.

8.title: A Better Covenant: Written on the Heart
8.overview:
Chapter 8 caps the argument about priesthood: a better Priest ministers in a better sanctuary under a better covenant. The “main point” (v. 1) is that our high priest is seated at God’s right hand in heaven, serving in the true tent. The earthly tabernacle Moses built was a copy and shadow of the heavenly reality (Exodus 25:40).

The better covenant is then proved by the longest Old Testament quotation in the New: Jeremiah 31:31–34. Written while the temple stood, it promised a new covenant unlike Sinai: law written on the heart, everyone knowing God, and “I will remember their sins no more”. By calling it “new”, God made the old obsolete, and “what is growing old is ready to vanish away”. There is nothing to go back to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Minister in the True Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer states his main point: we have a high priest who sits at the right hand of God’s majesty in heaven, ministering in the real sanctuary, the true tent set up by the Lord rather than by human hands. Every high priest exists to offer something, so Christ too must have an offering. If he were on earth he would not be a priest at all, since priests already serve there according to the law; but their sanctuary is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly one, as God warned Moses when he told him to build everything according to the pattern shown on the mountain. Christ’s ministry is as much better than theirs as the covenant he mediates is better, founded on better promises.
verseByVerse.theology:
Copy, Shadow, and the Pattern on the Mountain

The earthly tent was a copy of what Moses was shown. Christ ministers in the true tent, and the covenant he mediates is better because it rests on better promises.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers grieving the loss of the temple had not been shut out of the sanctuary.

Now: They had been let into the one the sanctuary pictured, where their high priest is seated.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.

Meaning first. Hebrews 8 sums up the argument so far and introduces the new covenant. The main point is this: we have a high priest seated at God’s right hand, who serves in the true sanctuary in heaven, set up by the Lord, not by human hands (vv. 1–2). Every high priest offers gifts and sacrifices, so Christ also has something to offer; but if he were on earth he would not be a priest at all, since the Levitical priests serve there in a sanctuary that is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly one, built according to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain (vv. 3–5). Christ’s ministry is far better, as the covenant he mediates is better, founded on better promises (v. 6). The proof is that God himself, through Jeremiah, found fault with the first covenant and promised a new one (vv. 7–12): not like the covenant with the fathers at the exodus, which they broke, but one in which God writes his laws on their hearts, is their God and they his people, in which all of them, from least to greatest, know him personally, and in which he forgives their sins and remembers them no more. By calling it “new,” God has made the first one old, and what is old is about to disappear (v. 13). It is the chapter where the letter shows its readers that they have not lost the temple; they have been given what the temple was always about.

Now the point in what we are saying is this. The word for “point” (kephalaion) means the chief thing, the head of the matter, and it can also mean the sum of an account, the total at the bottom of the column. The writer is stopping to tell his readers what all of it adds up to, which is a kindness in the middle of a long argument. After seven chapters of Scripture and reasoning, here is the bottom line.

We have such a high priest. Not: such a high priest exists. Not: there ought to be one. We have (echomen): possession, present tense, belonging to the frightened congregation hearing this read. It is not a theory but a reality the readers already possess. Why would they return to the old priesthood, when they already have this one?

One who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven. The seated posture (ekathisen) has been in the letter since 1:3, and by now the reader knows what it signifies: his work is finished (10:12). No priest in the tabernacle ever sat down, because there were no chairs and the work never ended. And note where the seat is. Not beside the throne but at the right hand of it, the place of supreme authority, Psalm 110:1 again. This priest is not waiting on the throne’s pleasure; he shares its authority. No Levitical priest ever sat in God’s presence, still less on a throne.

A minister in the holy places. The word for minister is leitourgos, from which we get liturgy: a public servant, someone performing priestly service on behalf of others. The “holy places” (tōn hagiōn) are the sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, the very presence of God. The one who sits on the throne is also the one who serves. He is enthroned and still at work for us.

In the true tent that the Lord set up, not man. And there is the claim that governs the next two chapters. There is a real sanctuary, and it is not in Jerusalem. “True” (alēthinos) here does not mean genuine as against fraudulent; the tabernacle was not a fake. It means original as against derivative, the thing itself rather than the representation of it. Moses built a good copy of something. The “tent” (skēnē) is the tabernacle, and “set up” (epēxen) is the word for pitching a tent. The Lord himself pitched this one, not human hands (9:11, 24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean heaven literally contains a tent made of heavenly materials. The language describes the heavenly reality of God’s presence, which the tabernacle pictured. Nor does “true” mean the earthly tabernacle was false; it was a true copy, but only a copy.

The answer to their grief. For readers grieving the loss of access to the temple, perhaps already shut out by their own families and synagogues for following Jesus, this is the writer’s answer and it is a large one. You have not been shut out of the sanctuary. You have been let into the one the sanctuary was a picture of, and there is a man of your own flesh and blood sitting in it.

If my high priest is in heaven, is he far away from me? No. He is far above, but not far off. Being in heaven means he is in the place of all power and all access, not in a distant room out of earshot. He sympathises with our weaknesses (4:15), he intercedes for us always (7:25), and by his Spirit he is with his people to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). His being in heaven is the guarantee that our prayers reach the throne, because the one who presents them is sitting at the Father’s right hand. A high priest on earth could only get as close as a curtain. Ours is inside.

In a sentence. The main point of what we are saying is this: we do have such a high priest, one who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who serves in the sanctuary, the true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by any human being.

On a Tuesday. When you pray this week, picture where your prayer is going: not into the ceiling, but into the true sanctuary, to the throne where your high priest is seated. Begin a prayer with that thought, and notice the difference it makes. And when you feel shut out, from a group, a family, a place you used to belong, remember the sanctuary that no one can shut you out of.

For worship. Lift your eyes to heaven: our High Priest is there now, enthroned, serving for us in God’s very presence. He has sat down, because the work of atonement is finished; and he still ministers, because his love for his people is never finished. The tent he serves in was pitched by God himself, and nothing in it is a copy or a shadow. Every sanctuary on earth was a sketch of the place where he now sits, and the sum of all the Scriptures is this: we have such a high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”

For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. As in 5:1. Offering is the essence of priesthood.

Thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. The logic is exact, and the writer leaves the full answer hanging for two chapters. A priest without an offering is a contradiction. So what did this one bring? The answer was given in passing at 7:27, he offered up himself, and will be worked out in detail in chapters 9 and 10. The tense of the verb “offer” (ti kai touton ho prosenenkē) points to a single offering, made once: himself (7:27; 9:14).

Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all. A startling admission, and it concedes the objection completely. Under the earthly arrangement Jesus has no standing whatever. On earth the priesthood belonged to Levi’s line, and Jesus was from Judah (7:13–14). His priestly ministry is exercised in heaven. His sacrifice was made on earth, at the cross; but he entered heaven with it and serves there.

Since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. There are already priests, appointed by law, from the right tribe, doing the work. He is not one of them and could not be. And “there are” is a present tense: the temple was still standing and its priests still offering, which suggests the letter was written before AD 70.

They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. Two words, and both are careful. A copy (hypodeigma) is a sketch, an outline, a model of something real. A shadow (skia) is cast by a body: it has the shape and none of the substance, and it proves the body exists (10:1; Colossians 2:17). Neither word means false. A shadow is genuinely there and genuinely tells you something. But nobody mistakes a shadow for the man, and nobody prefers it once the man has walked into the room. The tabernacle and its ritual were God-given sketches of heavenly realities, pointing to Christ.

For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God. Then the proof, from Moses himself. “Instructed” (kechrēmatistai) means warned, divinely directed: it is a word for an oracle.

See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain. It is Exodus 25:40, and the writer’s use of it is telling. The “pattern” is typos, a model, a design, the word from which we get type. God did not simply hand Moses a set of measurements; he showed him something on Mount Sinai and told him to reproduce it. That means the tabernacle was, by its own founding charter, a copy, and the original was not on earth. This is not the writer imposing a Greek idea of shadows and forms on Scripture. It is the plainest reading of what God said when the tent was commissioned. Everything in it had to be exact, because it was a picture of something greater.

They had it backwards. And that reframes the readers’ whole crisis. They thought they were leaving the real thing for something less tangible. They had it exactly backwards. The incense, the lampstand, the altar and the veil were the sketch. Christ is the substance.

Where Christians differ: will the temple and its sacrifices be restored? Some dispensationalists expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem with renewed animal sacrifices during a future millennium, often as memorials. Verdict: Hebrews teaches that the earthly sanctuary and its sacrifices were shadows, now fulfilled and made obsolete in Christ (v. 13; 10:1–18). To return to them would be to go back from the reality to the shadow, the very thing the letter warns against. The true temple now is Christ himself and his people (John 2:19–21; Ephesians 2:19–22), and the future hope is the new creation where God and the Lamb are the temple (Revelation 21:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the tabernacle was unimportant. It was designed by God himself. But its importance lay in what it pointed to.

How far should I look for Christ in the details of the tabernacle? Far enough to follow the New Testament, and carefully beyond it. Hebrews itself shows the main lines: the priest, the sacrifices, the altar, the curtain, the Most Holy Place, the blood, the ark (9:1–14). John sees Jesus as the one who tabernacled among us (John 1:14), and the curtain tore when he died (Matthew 27:51). Those lines are sure. But the writer himself refuses to go into every detail (9:5), and readers who find a hidden meaning in every peg and thread are usually inventing it. Hold the big picture firmly: the whole tent says that God dwells with his people, but only through a priest and a sacrifice, and Christ is both.

Is it wrong to have beautiful church buildings, or to call the worship room a sanctuary? No, provided we know what they are and are not. A church building is not a temple where God is more present than elsewhere, and no place on earth is holy ground in the old covenant sense; the church is the people, not the bricks (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5). A beautiful, well-kept building can serve worship and be an act of care. But if a building, a style of music or a particular ritual starts to feel necessary for meeting God, we have drifted back toward the shadows. The true sanctuary is in heaven, and we enter it by faith wherever we gather.

In a sentence. Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, so this one too had to have something to offer. If he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, because there are already priests who offer the gifts the law prescribes. They serve in a sanctuary that is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. That is why Moses was warned when he was about to build the tabernacle: “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.”

On a Tuesday. Ask what shadows you are clinging to: religious habits, places, feelings or performances that have become a substitute for Christ himself. None of them is bad in its place, but a shadow is only useful when it turns you toward the body that casts it. This week, whenever a religious routine comes round, a Sunday service, a grace before meals, a quiet time, use it to look past itself to him.

For worship. Thank God that we do not live among shadows but in the light of the reality, Christ himself. The God who showed Moses the pattern on the mountain had his Son in mind all along. Every curtain and lampstand and altar of acacia wood was his sketch of the coming one, drawn with loving exactness, and when the Son came, the shadows bowed and gave way. He is the tent where God dwells with men, the priest who enters, and the offering he brings. What the tabernacle drew in outline, the cross and the empty tomb have filled in with flesh and blood.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.

But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old. “But as it is” (nyn de, but now) is the phrase that turns from what would be true on earth to what is actually the case. “Obtained” (tetychen) is a perfect tense: he has attained it, and holds it. “Ministry” (leitourgia) is priestly service. And “more excellent” (diaphorōteras) is the same word used of his name in 1:4. The structure is one the writer has used before: the superiority of the minister is measured by the superiority of the covenant, exactly as at 1:4 the Son’s superiority to angels was measured by the excellence of his name. He does not merely assert greatness; he ties it to something the reader can weigh.

As the covenant he mediates is better. A “covenant” (diathēkē) is a binding arrangement, initiated by God, in which he commits himself to his people and they to him. And “mediates” introduces a word that will matter for the rest of the letter: mesitēs, mediator, go-between (1 Timothy 2:5). A mediator stands between two parties who cannot deal directly. Moses was the mediator of the first covenant (Galatians 3:19), standing on the mountain between a holy God and a terrified people who begged Moses to speak to them instead, lest they die (Exodus 20:19). Christ mediates the new (9:15; 12:24). “Better” (kreittōn) again.

Two mediators. There is a difference between the two mediators that the letter will press. Moses stood between; he did not reconcile. He carried the terms down and carried the people’s answer up, and the arrangement failed anyway. This mediator is also the guarantor (7:22) and the sacrifice (7:27). He does not merely convey the covenant; he pays for it.

Since it is enacted on better promises. “Enacted” (nenomothetētai) is legally established, legislated. And “better promises” is the phrase to hold on to, because it locates the difference precisely. The better promises are the promises of verses 10–12: an inward law, a personal relationship with God, universal knowledge of God among his people, and complete forgiveness. The old covenant had promises too, but they were conditional on Israel’s obedience, which failed. The new covenant promises are unconditionally guaranteed by Christ (7:22).

The verbs have changed hands. That is the heart of the matter, and it is easily missed by people who assume the difference between old and new is a difference in strictness. The new covenant is not better because its rules are easier or its standard lower. It is better because of what God undertakes to do in it, and the next verses will quote him undertaking it. The Sinai covenant said: if you keep my statutes, you shall live (Leviticus 18:5). The new one says: I will put my laws in their minds, I will write them on their hearts, I will be merciful, I will remember their sins no more. The verbs have changed hands.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God changed his mind about his people. The new covenant fulfils what the old covenant always pointed toward, and continues the promises God made to Abraham (Galatians 3:15–18).

Were Old Testament believers saved in a different way from us? No. Everyone who has ever been saved has been saved by grace through faith in the promised Saviour. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3), and David rejoiced in the forgiveness of sins (Romans 4:6–8). The faithful of Israel looked forward through the sacrifices and promises to the Christ who was to come, as we look back to the Christ who has come. What differs is the administration: shadows then, substance now; promise then, fulfilment now (Westminster 7.5–6). Chapter 11 will parade the Old Testament believers as our examples of faith, not as people who were saved by a different route.

In a sentence. But in fact the ministry Jesus has received is far greater than theirs, just as the covenant he mediates is better than the old one, because it is founded on better promises.

On a Tuesday. Notice how much of your Christian life runs on if: if I pray more, if I stop this habit, if I serve better, then God will accept me. Those are the grammar of the old covenant. Take one of the new covenant promises, I will remember their sins no more, and live this week on God’s I will instead of your own if. Obedience will follow, not as the price of acceptance but as its fruit.

For worship. Thank Christ, the mediator of the new covenant, for its better promises, all of which find their yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). Moses stood trembling between God and the people and could not hold the covenant together. Christ stood between God and us and held it together with his own blood. He did not bring down terms that we must keep to live; he kept them, paid for our breaking of them, and now ministers in heaven as the one in whom every promise of God is sure. His ministry is more excellent, because he is more excellent, and the covenant he mediates will never fail.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The New Covenant Promised by Jeremiah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the first covenant had been without fault, there would have been no need for a second. But God found fault with the people and promised through Jeremiah a new covenant, unlike the one at Sinai which they broke. He would write his laws on their hearts, be their God, and all would know him, from the least to the greatest, for he would forgive their sins and remember them no more. By calling it new, he made the first obsolete, and what is obsolete will soon disappear.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Verbs Have Changed Hands

In Jeremiah's promise God says “I will”: the law written on the heart, knowledge of God for all, and sins remembered no more.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God found fault with the people, not with the covenant.

Now: God does not forget; he has resolved never to act toward his people on the basis of their sins.

verseByVerse.quote: For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.

For if that first covenant had been faultless. “Faultless” (amemptos) is blameless, without defect. The argument is the one used of the priesthood at 7:11, and it is equally simple. The existence of a promised replacement is evidence that the first arrangement was not final. God does not announce a new covenant while the old one is doing everything required.

There would have been no occasion to look for a second. “Occasion” (topos) is literally place or room. There would be no room for a second, if the first had done everything.

For he finds fault with them when he says. Then a crucial qualification, and it is easy to read past. “Finds fault” (memphomenos) is blames, and the blame falls on them: not with it, but with the people. The defect was not in the covenant but in those who were party to it. Paul says the same at more length: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12), and what it could not do was because it was weakened by the flesh (Romans 8:3). A perfect law given to imperfect people cannot produce righteousness, and the failure is not the law’s. The old covenant had no power to change hearts.

Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord. Then the quotation begins, and it is the longest citation of the Old Testament anywhere in the New. It runs from here to verse 12: Jeremiah 31:31–34, all four verses, quoted in full. The writer is not making a passing allusion. He wants the whole passage in front of his readers, because his entire case is that the Old Testament itself announced the passing of the old arrangement. And Jeremiah spoke these words around 600 BC, as judgment closed in and exile loomed, when the first covenant was most visibly collapsing because of Judah’s covenant-breaking. It is one of the great instances of hope announced at the point of maximum ruin. God promised a new beginning.

When I will establish a new covenant. “Establish” (syntelesō) is accomplish, bring to completion. “New” (kainē) is new in quality, fresh, not merely recent: not another edition of the old but a different kind. And it is entirely God’s initiative. He will make it.

With the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. The whole of God’s people, reunited; the kingdom had divided after Solomon, and the prophet sees the two halves gathered again under one covenant. In the New Testament the new covenant is fulfilled in Christ for the church, the true Israel, made up of believing Jews and Gentiles. Jesus took the cup and called it the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6; Galatians 6:16).

Not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. The Sinai covenant. And the tenderness of that image is worth noticing. God describes the exodus, with its plagues and parted sea, as leading a child by the hand. When Israel was a child, I loved him, he says through Hosea, and taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by their arms (Hosea 11:1–4).

For they did not continue in my covenant. There is the failure, stated without softening. “Continue” (enemeinan) is remain. They did not keep it. Israel broke the covenant again and again, beginning with the golden calf at the foot of the very mountain where it was given (Exodus 32). And the whole point of what follows is that the new covenant is constructed so that it cannot fail in the same way.

And so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord. “Showed no concern” (ēmelēsa) is disregarded, neglected, following the Greek translation of Jeremiah; the Hebrew reads though I was their husband. Either way, the broken covenant brought judgment, and the hand that had led them out of Egypt let them go into Babylon.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has abandoned ethnic Israel. Paul teaches that God still has a purpose for Israel, and that many Jews will be brought into the new covenant through faith in Christ (Romans 11:25–29). But the new covenant is entered only through Christ.

Who is this covenant for? The promise is made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and dispensational Christians hold that it will be fulfilled to the nation of Israel in the future, while the church shares only in some of its blessings. But Hebrews quotes it to explain what Christ has already done for its readers. He is the mediator of this better covenant now (v. 6; 9:15); the Holy Spirit bears witness to it now (10:15–17); believers have already come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (12:24). The more likely reading is that the new covenant is fulfilled in Christ and his people, Jew and Gentile together. Its promises are already ours, though their fullness, when all shall know the Lord, waits for his return. Christians who agree on all this still differ over how to read Paul’s hope that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:26–27): some expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end, others read all Israel as the whole number of God’s elect, Jew and Gentile. On either view, there is one covenant, one Mediator and one people, and every Jew who comes to Christ comes home to promises first made to his fathers.

In a sentence. If the first covenant had been without fault, no one would have looked for a second. But God found fault with the people and said: “The days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the people of Israel and the people of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their ancestors when I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, because they did not stay faithful to my covenant, and so I turned away from them, says the Lord.

On a Tuesday. If your life feels like a collapsing covenant, a broken marriage, a ruined reputation, a pattern of failure you cannot escape, notice when God spoke these words: at the point of ruin, to people who had brought the ruin on themselves. Do not wait until things improve to look for his promise. Read Jeremiah 31:31–34 this week, slowly, and hear it spoken over the wreckage.

For worship. Thank God that when his people failed, he did not give up but promised something new and better. He took them by the hand out of Egypt, and they let go of his hand at the foot of the mountain; he bore with them for centuries, and they broke his covenant again and again. And at the darkest hour, as the city was about to fall, he did not say, it is finished between us. He said, behold, the days are coming. The God who finds fault with his people is the God who finds a way to make them new, and he found it in his Son.
verseByVerse.note: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament runs from v. 8 to v. 12.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.

For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. Now the content of the new covenant: four great promises. And the thing to watch is the grammar. Count the times God says I will.

I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts. The first promise: inward transformation. Under the old covenant the law was written on tablets of stone (Exodus 31:18) and stood outside the people, telling them what to do. The new one is written inside them. Note carefully that the content does not change. It is the same law; God does not say he will give a different or easier one. What changes is its location. The problem was never the standard; it was that the standard was external to people who did not want it. The remedy is not a lower demand but a new heart that wants what the law commands: I will give you a new heart, and I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezekiel 36:26–27; 2 Corinthians 3:3). This is regeneration. The law is not abolished but taken inside.

A different kind of obedience. That is what makes obedience under the new covenant a different kind of thing. It is not compliance with a rule imposed from outside but the expression of something now written inward, which is why the New Testament can say that his commandments are not burdensome (1 John 5:3) without lowering any of them. A child who loves music does not experience practice the way a child forced to the piano does, though the scales are the same.

And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. The second promise: relationship. This is the covenant formula, and it runs through the whole Bible: to Abraham, at Sinai, through the prophets, and finally in the new creation, where the voice from the throne says exactly this (Genesis 17:7; Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Revelation 21:3). It is the sentence God keeps saying, and everything else is machinery for making it true. God gives himself to his people, and takes them as his own.

And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, Know the Lord. The third promise: universal personal knowledge of God among his people. This needs care, since the New Testament plainly commands teaching, and this letter is itself a sermon complaining that its readers ought to be teachers by now (5:12). The promise is not that instruction ceases. It is that membership of the covenant community will no longer be a matter of birth, requiring people to be told about a God they do not know. Under the old covenant, people were born into the covenant community and then had to be urged to know the Lord; many never did.

For they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. “Know” (eidēsousin) is not just knowledge about God but personal, saving knowledge: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). Under the old arrangement you could be born into the nation and live your whole life inside it without knowing God at all, which is precisely the tragedy of the wilderness generation. Under the new, everyone in it knows him. There are no second-hand members. And from the least to the greatest abolishes the tiers: no inner circle with access and an outer ring who take it on trust, no mediating priestly class; every believer has direct access. This does not mean teaching is unnecessary in the church (Ephesians 4:11); it means every member truly knows God.

Where Christians differ: who belongs to the new covenant? Paedobaptists see the new covenant, like the old, as including believers and their children, and so baptise infants as covenant members. Verdict: One of the key differences between the old and new covenants is that all members of the new covenant know the Lord personally, from the least to the greatest, and have the law written on their hearts. The old covenant community was mixed, including many who did not know God; the new covenant community, properly understood, consists of those who have been regenerated. This is why baptism, the sign of the new covenant, belongs to those who profess faith. This credobaptist conclusion is held charitably toward paedobaptist brothers, who agree that only the regenerate are truly saved but understand the visible covenant community differently.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person who attends church is regenerate; the visible church still contains false professors (6:4–6). But the new covenant itself, in its true membership, consists of those who know the Lord.

Do the Ten Commandments still bind the Christian, then? Yes, as the moral law God writes on the heart, though not as the terms of a covenant by which we earn life. What becomes obsolete (v. 13) is the Mosaic administration: its priesthood, sacrifices and temple, and the civil law of Israel as a nation. Some Christians speak instead of the law of Christ replacing the law of Moses; the practical result is close, since the moral substance of the commandments is repeated in the New Testament. The fourth commandment is where views differ most. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that the Sabbath continues as the Lord’s Day, moved to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection (Westminster 21.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath rest is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), while still gladly gathering on the Lord’s Day. Both agree that God’s people need worship and rest, and that Christ is the true rest.

How do I know God has written his law on my heart? Not by never sinning, but by what you love and what grieves you. Do you want to please God, even when you fail? Do you find that sin which once felt natural now troubles you? Do you love God’s word and want to understand it, even when it rebukes you? Do you know God, not only facts about him, so that you speak to him as your Father? These are the marks of a new heart. A person under the old covenant alone felt the law as a weight outside him; a person with the law written within feels it as a description of what he longs to be. If that longing is in you, God put it there.

In a sentence. This is the covenant I will make with the people of Israel after that time, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their minds and write them on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people. No longer will they teach their neighbours, or say to one another, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.

On a Tuesday. Choose one of God’s commandments that you obey grudgingly, perhaps truthfulness at work, purity in what you look at, or honouring a difficult parent. Instead of gritting your teeth, pray the new covenant promise over it: Lord, you said you would write your law on my heart; write this one there. Then obey, and watch over the weeks for the change from duty to desire. And remember that the least of believers knows God as truly as the greatest. Speak to him yourself today.

For worship. Count the I wills of God. I will put my laws in their minds. I will write them on their hearts. I will be their God. They shall all know me. Every promise of the new covenant is God undertaking to do in us what we could never do for ourselves. He does not lower his law; he changes our hearts until we love it. He does not admit us to a building; he gives us himself. The least of his children knows him as surely as the greatest, and the covenant that God makes, God keeps.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”

For I will be merciful toward their iniquities. The fourth promise, and the foundation of the others: complete forgiveness. The little word at the front carries the weight of everything before it. For: this is the reason the others are possible. Law written on hearts, God as their God, everyone knowing him: none of it can happen while the sin question is open. Forgiveness is not the last of the promises but the foundation of them. And “merciful” (hileōs) means propitious, gracious, and it is related to the word for propitiation (2:17). God will be favourable toward his people because their sins have been atoned for. The “iniquities” (adikiai) are their wrongs, their unrighteous deeds.

And I will remember their sins no more. “Remember no more” (ou mē mnēsthō eti) is a strong double negative: I will certainly never again remember. And it must be said plainly what this does not mean, because sentimental readings weaken it. God is not forgetful. Omniscience does not misplace information, and a God who could genuinely lose track of the past would be a smaller God, not a kinder one.

What remembering means. To remember, in Hebrew usage, is not chiefly a mental act but an act of engagement. When God remembered Noah, he acted for him and the waters subsided (Genesis 8:1); when the thief asked Jesus to remember him, he was asking to be acted for (Luke 23:42). So not to remember sins is not to have mislaid the record. It is a settled determination never to act toward the sinner on the basis of it: never to hold sins against his people, never to bring them up again, never to punish them. He has removed our transgressions as far as the east is from the west, and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea (Psalm 103:12; Isaiah 43:25; Micah 7:19). That is stronger than forgetting, not weaker. A God who had forgotten might be reminded. This is a God who knows exactly what was done and has decided, on grounds outside the sinner altogether, never to bring it up.

The reversal. Notice how this reverses the old arrangement at its most painful point. Under the law, the annual Day of Atonement was a reminder of sins year by year (10:3); every one said, in effect, here we are again. The new covenant’s promise is the exact opposite: sins completely and permanently forgiven (10:17–18). For a congregation being drawn back to that calendar, this verse is the writer’s most personal argument. They were considering returning to a system whose annual centrepiece existed to bring their sins to mind, and leaving a covenant in which God has undertaken never to raise them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never experience the consequences of sin in this life, or that God never disciplines them (12:5–11). It means the guilt and condemnation are gone forever.

If God remembers my sins no more, why can I not stop remembering them? Because memory and conscience are not the same as God’s verdict. You may remember a sin for the rest of your life, and Satan, the accuser, will gladly remind you. But the question is not whether you remember it but whether God holds it against you, and he has said he will not. When an old sin rises, do not argue with the memory or try to make up for it. Answer it with the promise: God has said he will remember it no more, because Christ has paid for it. Let the memory become an occasion for thanks rather than shame (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1).

Does this mean I must forgive and forget when others sin against me? Forgive, yes, freely and from the heart, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32). Forgetting in the sense of losing the memory is not possible, and God does not ask it. What he asks is what he does: that you decide not to hold the wrong against the person, not to keep bringing it up, not to take revenge. That does not mean pretending nothing happened, or trusting someone who has not changed, or staying exposed to abuse; forgiveness and safety are different questions, and a victim of abuse should seek protection and help. But in your heart, release the debt to God, as he has released yours.

In a sentence. For I will show mercy for their wrongdoing, and I will never again remember their sins.”

On a Tuesday. Name the sin from your past that still haunts you. Write it down if it helps, and then write beside it Hebrews 8:12. Thank God aloud that he will remember it no more, and then do something you would not do if you were still carrying it: pray boldly, serve gladly, or tell someone else about the mercy you have received. And if there is someone whose sin against you you keep rehearsing, bring it to God today and begin, in his strength, to stop bringing it up.

For worship. If our past sins haunt us, hear God’s promise: he remembers them no more. The God who knows everything has chosen never to act against us on account of anything we have done, because his Son has already borne it all. The record is not lost; it is nailed to the cross and cancelled (Colossians 2:14). Where once a priest went in every year to remind God and the people of their sins, now a high priest sits at the right hand of the Majesty, and the subject is closed. Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity, who delights in steadfast love? We rest in that forgiveness today, and we will sing of it for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. The argument is drawn from a single adjective. God said new, and the word itself does the work: you cannot call something new without implying that something else is old. “Makes obsolete” (pepalaiōken) is a perfect tense: has made old, declared old and remaining so. The very word “new” in Jeremiah’s prophecy shows that the old covenant was always meant to be temporary. When God spoke of a new one, six centuries before Christ, he already marked the old one as old.

And what is becoming obsolete and growing old. The image is of something wearing out. “Becoming obsolete” (palaioumenon) is being made old, a word used of clothing worn thin. “Growing old” (gēraskon) is ageing, as a person grows old and weak. The old covenant is pictured like a garment fraying at the seams, or a body bending with age.

Is ready to vanish away. “Ready” (engys) is near; “vanish away” (aphanismos) is disappearance, destruction. When this was written the temple was still standing and the sacrifices were still being offered daily; the writer speaks of them throughout in the present tense. Within a few years, in AD 70, the Romans destroyed the temple, and the entire sacrificial system stopped, and has never resumed. God himself brought the shadow to an end once the reality had come.

Arguing from a text. The writer did not know exactly what was coming. He is arguing from a text, not a newspaper. But his readers, if any lived a decade longer, watched the argument confirmed in the most literal way imaginable. And there is real pastoral force in the tense he chooses. He does not say the old covenant has vanished. It is becoming obsolete, growing old, near to disappearing, which is exactly what his readers could see. The temple was busy, the priests were working, the smoke went up every morning, and it looked permanent. He tells them what they are looking at: an institution in its last days, kept going by habit, with the reality it pictured already seated at the right hand of God. Going back to it would not be returning to something solid. It would be stepping onto a floor that was about to give way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament Scriptures are obsolete. They are God’s word, and they testify to Christ. What has become obsolete is the old covenant as a system: its priesthood, sacrifices and ceremonial law.

Does this chapter give any ground for contempt toward Jewish people? None at all. The writer was almost certainly Jewish, writing to Jewish believers. The new covenant was promised in Israel’s own Scriptures, to Israel, by Israel’s God, and its mediator is a son of David from the tribe of Judah. Saying that the old covenant has given way to the new is not saying that Jews are worse than Gentiles; the fault Jeremiah found was in human hearts, and every Gentile heart has the same disease. Paul, who taught the same truth, said he had great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his people (Romans 9:1–3). The right response is not pride but love and prayer, and a glad offer of the Messiah to the people from whom he came.

Are there old-covenant habits that Christians fall into? Yes, often without noticing. Treating the minister as a priest who must stand between us and God. Treating a building as holier than a kitchen table. Measuring ourselves by external rules while our hearts stay cold. Feeling that God keeps a running tally and that each Sunday restarts the account. Believing that our standing depends on our performance this week. Each of these is a kind of going back to the temple. The new covenant answer is the same each time: Christ is our priest, the law is written on our hearts by the Spirit, our sins are remembered no more, and we know God ourselves.

In a sentence. By calling this covenant “new,” God has made the first one old; and whatever is old and ageing will soon disappear.

On a Tuesday. Are you holding onto old ways of approaching God: rituals, merit, a sense that you must earn your place? Let them go. Live in the new covenant. Take one habit this week that has become a performance, and turn it back into a meeting with God: pray because you know him, not to keep your record clean; read because he speaks, not to tick a box; give because you are forgiven, not to be forgiven.

For worship. God has made all things new. The covenant of stone, the priests who died, the sacrifices that reminded, the temple that would fall: he let them grow old and fade, because he had something better ready. In their place stands his Son, mediator of a covenant that will never age, priest of a sanctuary that will never be destroyed, offering of a sacrifice that will never be repeated. The old was glorious and is passing away; the new is more glorious and will last for ever (2 Corinthians 3:11). Blessed be the God who does not leave his people among ruins, but writes his law on their hearts, gives them himself, and remembers their sins no more.

For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”<sup>6</sup>But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.<sup>7</sup>For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second.<sup>8</sup>For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,<sup>9</sup>not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.<sup>10</sup>For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.<sup>11</sup>And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.<sup>12</sup>For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”<sup>13</sup>In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

9.title: The Blood of Christ: Once for All Into the Holy Place
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the heart of Hebrews’ teaching on atonement. The tabernacle’s design was itself a sermon about access to God: restricted, mediated, temporary. Priests entered the outer room daily; only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year, never without blood. By this the Spirit was saying: the way in is not yet open.

When Christ came, he entered not a tent of cloth but heaven itself, not with animals’ blood but with his own, once for all, securing eternal redemption. His blood cleanses not only the body but the conscience, freeing us from dead works to serve the living God. And as we die once and then face judgment, so Christ, offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who eagerly wait for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Closed Door, and the Blood That Opened It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first covenant had a sanctuary: an outer Holy Place with lampstand and bread, and behind a curtain the Most Holy Place with the ark, the manna, Aaron’s staff, the tablets and the mercy seat. Priests went into the outer room daily, but only the high priest went into the inner room, once a year, with blood for his own sins and the people’s. The Spirit was showing that the way in was not yet open; those sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience. But Christ entered the true sanctuary once for all with his own blood. If animals’ blood purified the body, how much more will Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanse our conscience to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Architecture That Preached

By the tabernacle's design the Holy Spirit was saying not yet: one man, one day a year, never without blood. Its sacrifices could not perfect the conscience; the blood of Christ does.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The ark held manna, Aaron's staff and the tablets, with the mercy seat over them.

Now: A cleansed conscience is set free from dead works to serve the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.

Meaning first. Hebrews 9 compares the worship of the old covenant with Christ’s work, showing how the old system pictured and pointed to his once-for-all sacrifice. First, the earthly tabernacle (vv. 1–5): an outer room, the Holy Place, with the lampstand, table and bread; and behind a curtain an inner room, the Most Holy Place, with the ark of the covenant and the mercy seat overshadowed by cherubim. Priests went into the outer room daily, but only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year, with blood for his own sins and the people’s (vv. 6–7). The Holy Spirit was showing by this that the way into God’s presence was not yet open while the old tabernacle stood, and its sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience; they were external rules until the time of reformation (vv. 8–10). But Christ has come as high priest, entering the true sanctuary once for all with his own blood, securing eternal redemption (vv. 11–12). If animal blood could make people outwardly clean, how much more will Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanse our consciences to serve the living God (vv. 13–14). So he is the mediator of a new covenant, whose death redeems from sins and secures the eternal inheritance (v. 15). A covenant, like a will, requires death; even the first covenant was inaugurated with blood, for without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness (vv. 16–22). The heavenly realities needed better sacrifices: Christ entered heaven itself, not repeatedly but once, at the climax of history, to put away sin by sacrificing himself (vv. 23–26). As people die once and then face judgement, so Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those waiting for him (vv. 27–28).

Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. Key words. “Regulations” (dikaiōmata, ordinances, requirements). “Worship” (latreias, service, religious ritual). “Earthly” (kosmikon, belonging to this world). The first covenant had its own God-given system, but it was of this world, as opposed to the heavenly sanctuary.

For a tent was prepared, the first section. Key words. “Tent” (skēnē, tabernacle): the portable sanctuary built in the wilderness (Exodus 25–40), not the later temple. The author always refers to the tabernacle, the original pattern.

In which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. Key words. The lampstand (lychnia, the golden menorah with seven lamps, Exodus 25:31–40), the table (Exodus 25:23–30), and the “bread of the Presence” (twelve loaves set before God each week, representing the twelve tribes, Leviticus 24:5–9). They spoke of light, provision and fellowship in God’s presence, fulfilled in Christ, the light of the world and the bread of life (John 8:12; 6:35).

It is called the Holy Place. Key words. “Holy Place” (Hagia). The outer room, about thirty feet long.

Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place. Key words. “Second curtain”: the thick veil dividing the two rooms (Exodus 26:31–33). The first curtain was at the tabernacle entrance. “Most Holy Place” (Hagia Hagiōn, Holy of Holies): a perfect cube, about fifteen feet each way, where God’s presence dwelt above the ark.

Having the golden altar of incense. Key words. “Golden altar of incense” (chrysoun thymiatērion): either the altar of incense or a golden censer. The altar of incense actually stood in the Holy Place, just in front of the curtain (Exodus 30:1–6). The author says the Most Holy Place “had” it: it belonged to the inner room in function, because the incense from it was taken into the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12–13), and 1 Kings 6:22 says the altar “belonged to the inner sanctuary.” Some take the word as the golden censer used by the high priest. Either way, no contradiction.

And the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold. Key words. “Ark” (kibōton, chest, box): a wooden chest about four feet long, overlaid with gold (Exodus 25:10–22).

In which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Key words. Three reminders: the manna God provided in the wilderness (Exodus 16:32–34); Aaron’s staff, which budded to prove God’s choice of Aaron as priest (Numbers 17:1–11); and the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 25:16; Deuteronomy 10:1–5). By Solomon’s time, only the tablets remained (1 Kings 8:9). Each pointed to Christ: the bread from heaven, the chosen priest who rose to life, and the one who fulfils the law.

Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Key words. “Cherubim” (cheroubin): two golden angelic figures facing each other with wings outspread over the ark. “Of glory”: associated with God’s glory, which dwelt between them (Exodus 25:22; Numbers 7:89). “Mercy seat” (hilastērion, place of propitiation, atonement cover): the golden lid of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15). The same word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25: Christ is our mercy seat, the place where God’s wrath is turned away. Between God’s presence above and the broken law below lay the blood-sprinkled cover.

Of these things we cannot now speak in detail. Key words. The author could say much more about each item, but his focus is the Day of Atonement and its meaning.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every detail of the tabernacle has a hidden allegorical meaning. Interpreters should follow the New Testament’s lead rather than inventing symbolism. But the whole structure did point to Christ.

In a sentence. The first covenant had rules for worship and a sanctuary on earth. A tabernacle was set up. In its first room were the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread; this was called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a room called the Most Holy Place, which had the golden altar of incense and the gold-covered ark of the covenant. The ark contained a gold jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant. Above the ark were the cherubim of the Glory, overshadowing the atonement cover. But we cannot discuss these things in detail now.

For worship. Thank God that Christ is your mercy seat, where his blood covers the law you broke and God meets you in grace.

verseByVerse.quote: These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.

These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section. Key words. “Regularly” (dia pantos, continually). Priests entered the Holy Place every day, morning and evening, to tend the lamps, burn incense, and change the bread weekly (Exodus 27:20–21; 30:7–8). Constant activity, never finished.

Performing their ritual duties. Key words. “Ritual duties” (latreias epitelountes, completing services).

But into the second only the high priest goes. Key words. Only one man in the whole nation.

And he but once a year. Key words. On the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, the tenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29–34; 23:26–32). Even then, he entered more than once that day (incense, then blood for himself, then blood for the people), but only on that one day of the year.

And not without taking blood. Key words. Never without blood. Without a death, no approach to God was possible. The point anticipates verse 22.

Which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people. Key words. First for himself, a bull (Leviticus 16:11); then for the people, a goat (16:15). “Unintentional sins” (agnoēmatōn, sins of ignorance). The sacrifices covered sins of weakness and ignorance (5:2; Numbers 15:22–31), not deliberate, defiant rebellion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only sins of ignorance can be forgiven today. Christ’s sacrifice cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7, 9), including deliberate sins repented of, as David’s were (Psalm 51). What cannot be forgiven is the persistent rejection of the only sacrifice (10:26).

In a sentence. When everything had been arranged like this, the priests went regularly into the outer room to carry out their ministry. But only the high priest entered the inner room, and only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance.

For worship. Imagine standing outside, never allowed in. Then thank God that through Christ you may come into his presence every day.

verseByVerse.quote: By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.

By this the Holy Spirit indicates. Key words. “Indicates” (dēlountos, makes clear, shows). The Holy Spirit, who inspired the design of the tabernacle and its record in Scripture, was teaching something through its very structure.

That the way into the holy places is not yet opened. Key words. “Way” (hodon, road, path). “Holy places”: God’s true presence. As long as the curtain stood and only the high priest could pass once a year, the message was clear: the way to God is not yet open. At Jesus’ death, the temple curtain was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38). The way is now open (10:19–20).

As long as the first section is still standing. Key words. “First section” (prōtēs skēnēs, first tent): the outer room, or perhaps the whole first tabernacle system. As long as that system stood, access was barred.

Which is symbolic for the present age. Key words. “Symbolic” (parabolē, parable, illustration, figure). The tabernacle was a parable for the time then present, the old covenant era.

According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper. Key words. “Perfect” (teleiōsai, complete, bring to the goal). “Conscience” (syneidēsin, the inner moral awareness of guilt). The deepest problem: the old sacrifices could not remove the inner sense of guilt and give a clear conscience before God (10:1–4). They dealt with outward ritual impurity, not the heart.

But deal only with food and drink and various washings. Key words. Food laws (Leviticus 11), drink offerings and regulations (Numbers 6:3), ritual washings (Leviticus 15; Numbers 19). External matters.

Regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation. Key words. “Regulations for the body” (dikaiōmata sarkos, ordinances of the flesh): external rules. “Imposed” (epikeimena, laid on, like a burden, Acts 15:10). “Until the time of reformation” (mechri kairou diorthōseos, until the time of setting things straight, of a new order). The new covenant era in Christ. The old rules were always temporary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the old covenant believers had no forgiveness. They were forgiven through faith in God’s promise, looking forward to what the sacrifices pointed to (11:39–40; Romans 3:25). But the sacrifices themselves could not provide the clear conscience that Christ gives.

In a sentence. The Holy Spirit was showing by this that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been opened as long as the first tabernacle was still standing. This is an illustration for that time, showing that the gifts and sacrifices being offered could not clear the conscience of the worshipper. They dealt only with food and drink and various ceremonial washings, external regulations in force until the time when God would set things right.

For worship. Do you have a guilty conscience? Rituals cannot clean it. Bring it to Christ, whose blood does.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.

But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come. Key words. “Appeared” (paragenomenos, arrived, came on the scene). “Good things that have come” (tōn genomenōn agathōn): the blessings of the new covenant, already present. Some manuscripts read “good things to come” (mellontōn), as in 10:1. Either way: real forgiveness, access to God, a clean conscience.

Then through the greater and more perfect tent. Key words. “Greater” (meizonos) and “more perfect” (teleioteras). The heavenly sanctuary.

Not made with hands, that is, not of this creation. Key words. “Not made with hands” (ou cheiropoiētou), a phrase used to contrast human-made shrines with God’s reality (Acts 7:48; Mark 14:58). “Not of this creation”: heavenly, not earthly.

He entered once for all into the holy places. Key words. “Once for all” (ephapax), as in 7:27. Not once a year, but once in all history, never to be repeated. At his ascension, he entered God’s presence (v. 24).

Not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood. Key words. “His own blood”: his life poured out in death. Not animal blood, which could not cleanse (10:4), but the blood of the sinless God-man. Blood signifies life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11).

Thus securing an eternal redemption. Key words. “Securing” (heuramenos, having obtained, found). Aorist: a finished achievement. “Eternal” (aiōnian): unlike the annual atonement, which lasted only a year, Christ’s redemption lasts forever. “Redemption” (lytrōsin, liberation by payment of a ransom). Not a possible redemption, offered to all and secured for none; an actual redemption, obtained and secured for those for whom he died.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ literally carried a vessel of blood into heaven. “By means of his own blood” means on the basis of his completed sacrifice. Nor does it mean his work in heaven completes an unfinished sacrifice; the sacrifice was completed on the cross (John 19:30).

In a sentence. But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that are now here, he went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by human hands and not part of this created world. He entered the Most Holy Place once for all, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, and so obtained a redemption that lasts for ever.

For worship. Thank Christ that he did not merely offer redemption but secured it, eternally. Nothing can undo what his blood has done for you.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.

For if the blood of goats and bulls. Key words. The Day of Atonement sacrifices (Leviticus 16).

And the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer. Key words. The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone who had become ritually unclean by touching a dead body (Numbers 19). The heifer was burned outside the camp, and its ashes kept for this purpose.

Sanctify for the purification of the flesh. Key words. “Sanctify” (hagiazei, make holy). “Purification of the flesh” (tēn tēs sarkos katharotēta, outward, bodily cleanness). These rites did really restore ritual purity, allowing people to take part in worship again. But only outwardly.
