How much more will the blood of Christ. Key words. “How much more” (posō mallon): the argument from lesser to greater. If the shadow worked outwardly, how much more the reality inwardly.

Who through the eternal Spirit offered himself. Key words. “Through the eternal Spirit” (dia pneumatos aiōniou): most likely the Holy Spirit, who empowered Christ throughout his ministry (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38) and in his self-offering. The whole Trinity is at work: the Son offers himself to the Father through the Spirit. “Eternal”: his sacrifice has eternal value. “Offered himself”: Christ was both priest and sacrifice, offering voluntarily (John 10:17–18).

Without blemish to God. Key words. “Without blemish” (amōmon, spotless, unblemished). Sacrificial animals had to be perfect (Leviticus 22:20–22). Christ was morally perfect, sinless (1 Peter 1:19).

Purify our conscience from dead works. Key words. “Purify” (kathariei, cleanse). “Conscience”: the inner guilt that the old sacrifices could not touch (v. 9). “Dead works” (nekrōn ergōn), as in 6:1: works that lead to death, sins, and perhaps also religious works done to earn favour. Just as touching a dead body defiled a person (Numbers 19), dead works defile the conscience. Christ’s blood cleanses.

To serve the living God. Key words. “Serve” (latreuein, worship, serve as a priest). The purpose of cleansing: to worship and serve. A clean conscience is freed for joyful service. “The living God”: in contrast with dead works.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer will never feel guilt. When we sin, we feel it, and we should; but we bring it to Christ, whose blood keeps cleansing (1 John 1:7–9). Nor does it mean we serve in order to be cleansed; we are cleansed in order to serve.

In a sentence. The blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean make them outwardly clean. How much more, then, will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our consciences from deeds that lead to death, so that we may serve the living God!

For worship. Let Christ’s blood cleanse your conscience today. Then serve the living God with freedom and joy, not with guilt.
verseByVerse.note: The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone defiled by touching a corpse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — A Death That Reaches Backward, and a Return Without Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, and his death redeems people even from the sins committed under the first covenant, so that those God calls can receive the promised eternal inheritance. A will takes effect only when the one who made it dies, and in the same way the first covenant was inaugurated with blood: Moses sprinkled the book, the people, the tent and its vessels, for under the law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. The earthly copies were cleansed with animal sacrifices, but the heavenly realities needed better ones. Christ did not enter a man-made sanctuary but heaven itself, to appear before God for us. He did not offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest entered year after year with blood not his own; he appeared once, at the climax of the ages, to put away sin by sacrificing himself. Just as people die once and then face judgement, Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.theology:
How the Old Testament Saints Were Saved

Christ's death redeems from transgressions committed under the first covenant. There is one way of salvation, looked forward to and looked back on.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: At Sinai the book and the people were sprinkled with the blood of the covenant.

Now: Christ will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.

Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant. Key words. “Therefore” (dia touto): because his blood cleanses the conscience (v. 14). “Mediator” (mesitēs), as in 8:6. “New covenant” (diathēkēs kainēs), as promised in Jeremiah 31.

So that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. Key words. “Those who are called” (hoi keklēmenoi, perfect passive: those who have been called and remain called). God’s effectual call (3:1; Romans 8:28–30). “Receive” (labōsin). “Eternal inheritance” (tēs aiōniou klēronomias): not the land of Canaan, but eternal life, the new creation, God himself (1 Peter 1:4).

Since a death has occurred that redeems them. Key words. “A death” (thanatou genomenou): Christ’s death. “Redeems” (apolytrōsin, release by ransom, redemption).

From the transgressions committed under the first covenant. Key words. Christ’s death reaches back to cover the sins of Old Testament believers, which the animal sacrifices could not truly remove (10:4). Those who trusted God before Christ were forgiven on the basis of what Christ would do (Romans 3:25–26). His death is the ground of all forgiveness, before and after the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ died only for Old Testament sins; it means his death covers them too, along with all the sins of all the called. Nor does “those who are called” mean everyone who hears the gospel invitation; it means those effectually called by God.

In a sentence. That is why Christ is the mediator of a new covenant: so that those God has called may receive the eternal inheritance he promised, now that a death has taken place that sets them free from the sins committed under the first covenant.

For worship. Thank God that you are among the called, and that your eternal inheritance is secured by Christ’s death.

verseByVerse.quote: For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.

For where a will is involved. Key words. The Greek word for “covenant” (diathēkē) can also mean a “will,” and the author makes use of both senses here. In everyday Greek, diathēkē usually meant a last will and testament. The author moves from “covenant” to “will” to make a point: an inheritance (v. 15) comes through a will, and a will requires a death.

The death of the one who made it must be established. Key words. “Established” (pheresthai, be brought forward, be proved). Before an inheritance is distributed, the death must be confirmed.

For a will takes effect only at death. Key words. “Takes effect” (bebaia, valid, binding, in force). A will has no power while the testator lives.

Since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Key words. So the eternal inheritance (v. 15) required Christ’s death. Only when he died did his “will” come into force for his heirs.

Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood. Key words. “Inaugurated” (enkekainistai, dedicated, ratified, put into effect). Returning to the covenant sense: the Sinai covenant was ratified by blood (v. 19; Exodus 24:3–8). In ancient covenant-making, a sacrificial death sealed the agreement (Genesis 15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18–20). Death lies at the heart of both wills and covenants.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s covenant is merely a human legal document. The illustration from wills makes a point: a death was necessary. The divine covenant is far greater, and the testator who died is also the one who rose and administers his own will.

In a sentence. In the case of a will, the death of the person who made it must be proved, because a will comes into force only when someone has died; it never takes effect while the one who made it is still alive. That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood.

For worship. Thank Christ that he died so that his will, with all its rich inheritance, might come into force for you.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek word for “covenant” can also mean a “will,” and the writer uses both senses.

verseByVerse.quote: For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.

For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people. Key words. At Sinai, Moses read the Book of the Covenant to the people, and they promised to obey (Exodus 24:3–7).

He took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop. Key words. Exodus 24 mentions bulls; the author adds details (goats, water, scarlet wool, hyssop) drawn from other sprinkling rituals (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:6, 18), perhaps reflecting Jewish tradition or combining related rites. “Hyssop”: a small bushy plant used as a sprinkler (Exodus 12:22; Psalm 51:7).

And sprinkled both the book itself and all the people. Key words. Exodus 24:6–8 mentions sprinkling the altar and the people. The book also is mentioned here. The blood marked both the covenant document and the covenant people as bound together.

Saying, This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you. Key words. From Exodus 24:8. Jesus echoed these words at the Last Supper: “This is my blood of the covenant” (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28), “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The cup of the Lord’s Supper recalls the ratification of the new covenant by Christ’s blood.

And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Key words. The tabernacle and its furnishings were consecrated with blood and oil (Exodus 40:9–11; Leviticus 8:15, 19).

Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood. Key words. “Almost” (schedon): some things were purified by water, fire or flour (Leviticus 5:11–13; Numbers 31:22–24). But blood was the main means.

And without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins. Key words. “Shedding of blood” (haimatekchysias, a word perhaps coined by the author: blood-pouring). “Forgiveness” (aphesis, release, cancellation). A fundamental principle: forgiveness requires a death, life given for life (Leviticus 17:11). Sin deserves death (Romans 6:23); forgiveness comes only when a substitute dies in the sinner’s place. This is the logic of penal substitution, which Christ fulfilled.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is bloodthirsty. It means sin is so serious that it can be dealt with only by death, and God in love provided the death himself, in his Son (Romans 5:8). Nor does it mean animal blood could truly forgive; it pointed to the blood that does (10:4).

In a sentence. When Moses had told all the people every command of the law, he took the blood of calves and goats, together with water, scarlet wool and branches of hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people. He said, “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.” In the same way, he sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and everything used in its worship. In fact, under the law almost everything is made clean with blood, and without the pouring out of blood there is no forgiveness.

For worship. At the next Lord’s Supper, remember: this cup is the new covenant in his blood, poured out for the forgiveness of your sins.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.

Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites. Key words. “Copies” (hypodeigmata), as in 8:5. The earthly tabernacle needed cleansing with animal blood.

But the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. Key words. Why would heavenly things need cleansing? Not because heaven itself is defiled, but because the approach to God for sinners needed to be opened, and his people (who are his true dwelling) needed cleansing. Some suggest that sinners’ access to heaven had been defiled by sin and needed to be consecrated. “Better sacrifices” (plural, as a general category): Christ’s single sacrifice.

For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things. Key words. “Copies” (antitypa, antitypes, corresponding figures). Earthly shrines are copies of the real.

But into heaven itself. Key words. Not a heavenly building, but heaven itself, God’s very presence.

Now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Key words. “Appear” (emphanisthēnai, be made visible, present himself). “Now”: at this very moment. Christ stands in God’s presence as our representative (7:25; Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1).

Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly. Key words. Unlike the high priest’s annual repetition.

As the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own. Key words. “Not his own”: animal blood.

For then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. Key words. If his sacrifice needed repeating, he would have had to die again and again, throughout history, since sin began. The absurdity proves the point: one death was enough.

But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages. Key words. “Appeared” (pephanerōtai, been manifested, perfect tense). His first coming. “Once for all” (hapax). “End of the ages” (epi synteleia tōn aiōnōn, the consummation, completion of the ages): the climax of history (1:2).

To put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Key words. “Put away” (athetēsin, abolish, annul, cancel, the same word used of setting aside the commandment, 7:18). Christ annulled sin, cancelling its guilt and power. “By the sacrifice of himself”: not of an animal, but of himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean heaven was dirty. The cleansing language is about consecrating the way of access for sinners. Nor does Christ’s appearing for us mean the Father is reluctant; the Father sent him (John 3:16).

In a sentence. So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified by these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves needed better sacrifices. For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by human hands, a mere copy of the true one; he entered heaven itself, now to appear for us in God’s presence. Nor did he enter heaven to offer himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. Otherwise Christ would have had to suffer many times since the creation of the world. But now he has appeared once for all at the climax of history to do away with sin by sacrificing himself.

For worship. Christ is in God’s presence for you right now. Your sin has been put away by his one sacrifice. Worship him.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

And just as it is appointed for man to die once. Key words. “Appointed” (apokeitai, laid up, reserved, destined). “Once” (hapax). Every human being dies once (except those alive at Christ’s return, 1 Corinthians 15:51–52, and Enoch and Elijah). Death is God’s appointment because of sin (Genesis 3:19; Romans 5:12).

And after that comes judgment. Key words. “Judgment” (krisis). After death, every person faces God’s judgement. There is no second chance after death, no reincarnation, no purgatory, no ceasing to exist. At death, the soul goes immediately into conscious existence, the believer to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), the unbeliever to punishment (Luke 16:22–26); at Christ’s return, all will be raised and judged (John 5:28–29; Revelation 20:11–15).

So Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many. Key words. “Offered once” (hapax prosenechtheis). Christ’s death corresponds to the one death of every person; but his death was for others. “To bear the sins” (anenenkein hamartias, carry up sins), echoing Isaiah 53:12 (“he bore the sin of many”). He carried our sins, bearing their penalty (1 Peter 2:24). “Many” (pollōn): Isaiah’s word, also used by Jesus (Mark 10:45). The “many” are those for whom he died, the many sons brought to glory (2:10).

Will appear a second time. Key words. “Appear” (ophthēsetai, will be seen). Christ’s second coming will be visible. On the Day of Atonement, the people waited outside while the high priest was in the Most Holy Place; when he came out, they knew the sacrifice had been accepted. So Christ will come out from heaven, to the joy of his people.

Not to deal with sin. Key words. Literally “without sin” (chōris hamartias): not to bear sin again. His dealing with sin was finished at his first coming.

But to save those who are eagerly waiting for him. Key words. “Save” (eis sōtērian, for salvation): the final, full salvation of his people, including the resurrection of their bodies (Romans 8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). “Eagerly waiting” (apekdechomenois, waiting with eager expectation): a mark of true believers (Titus 2:13; 2 Timothy 4:8).

Where Christians differ: is there a second chance after death, or a purgatory? Some teach that those who never heard the gospel will have an opportunity after death; Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers pass through purgatory to be purified before heaven. Others teach soul sleep (unconsciousness until resurrection) or annihilation. Verdict: This verse is clear: death, then judgement. Our eternal destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26). Believers enter conscious joy with Christ immediately (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23); there is no purgatory, because Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice fully cleanses (10:14). Unbelievers face conscious punishment, eternal and real (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). The time to respond to the gospel is now (3:13; 2 Corinthians 6:2).

What it does not mean. “Appear a second time” does not mean there will be a secret coming before his visible return. Scripture speaks of one future return, visible and glorious, at which he gathers his people and judges the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10).

In a sentence. Just as everyone is destined to die once and after that to face judgement, so Christ was offered once to carry the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.

For worship. Are you eagerly waiting for Christ? Pray today for his return, and live as one ready to meet him.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness.<sup>2</sup>For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place.<sup>3</sup>Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place,<sup>4</sup>having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant.<sup>5</sup>Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.<sup>6</sup>These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties,<sup>7</sup>but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.<sup>8</sup>By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing<sup>9</sup>(which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper,<sup>10</sup>but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.<sup>11</sup>But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation)<sup>12</sup>he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.<sup>13</sup>For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh,<sup>14</sup>how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.<sup>15</sup>Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.<sup>16</sup>For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established.<sup>17</sup>For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive.<sup>18</sup>Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.<sup>19</sup>For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people,<sup>20</sup>saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.”<sup>21</sup>And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship.<sup>22</sup>Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.<sup>23</sup>Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.<sup>24</sup>For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.<sup>25</sup>Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own,<sup>26</sup>for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.<sup>27</sup>And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment,<sup>28</sup>so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

10.title: Once for All: The New and Living Way
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the summit of the letter’s central argument. Priesthood (chapters 5–7), covenant (8) and sacrifice (9) converge here. The law’s yearly animal sacrifices are set against Christ’s single offering, with Psalm 40 as the key: “I have come to do your will, O God.” By that will, through the offering of his body once for all, “we have been sanctified.”

Then the longest application (vv. 19–39): draw near to God, hold fast the confession, and stir one another up to love and good works. The fourth and severest warning follows (vv. 26–31), balanced at once by encouragement: remember how you once joyfully accepted the loss of your property. You need endurance for a little while more. The coming one will come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — One Sacrifice, and a Priest Who Sat Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer explains why the old sacrifices could never deal with sin. The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, not the reality, so its sacrifices, repeated year after year, could not make worshippers complete; their repetition was itself a yearly reminder of sin, since animal blood cannot remove it. Psalm 40 shows what replaces them: Christ came to do God’s will in the body prepared for him, setting aside the old system. By that will we have been made holy through the once-for-all offering of his body. The old priests stood daily, repeating sacrifices; Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down at God’s right hand, waiting for his enemies to be subdued. The Spirit’s promise of the new covenant in Jeremiah confirms it: God will remember sins no more, and where sins are forgiven no further offering is needed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Tenses in One Sentence

By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Where sins are forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins, and their repetition confessed that they had not finished the work.

Now: Standing before God does not wait on our progress; our progress flows from a finished offering.

verseByVerse.quote: For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?

Meaning first. Hebrews 10 completes the great argument about Christ’s sacrifice and then turns it into urgent appeal. First, the old sacrifices could never perfect worshippers; their endless repetition proved it, reminding people of sins every year, since animal blood cannot take sins away (vv. 1–4). Christ came, as Psalm 40 foretold, not to offer more animals but to do God’s will in the body prepared for him, and by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of his body once for all (vv. 5–10). The old priests stood daily offering sacrifices that could never remove sin; Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down, for by that single offering he has perfected forever those being made holy, as the Spirit testifies in Jeremiah’s promise that God will remember sins no more; where there is forgiveness, no more offering is needed (vv. 11–18). Then the appeal (vv. 19–25): since we have confidence to enter God’s presence by Jesus’ blood through the new and living way he opened, let us draw near with sincere hearts, hold fast our hope, and stir one another to love and good works, not giving up meeting together. Then the fourth warning (vv. 26–31): for those who deliberately go on sinning after knowing the truth, trampling the Son of God and insulting the Spirit of grace, no sacrifice remains, only fearful judgement. Finally, encouragement (vv. 32–39): remember how you endured persecution and joyfully accepted the loss of property; do not throw away your confidence; you need endurance; the coming one will come soon; we are not those who shrink back and are destroyed, but those who believe and are saved.

For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come. Key words. “Shadow” (skian), as in 8:5. A shadow shows the outline of something real but is not the thing itself. “Good things to come”: the blessings of the new covenant in Christ (9:11).

Instead of the true form of these realities. Key words. “True form” (eikona, image, actual likeness, the very substance). The law had a shadow, not the reality. Christ is the substance (Colossians 2:17).

It can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Key words. “Never” (oudepote). “Continually” (eis to diēnekes, perpetually). “Every year”: the Day of Atonement. “Make perfect” (teleiōsai), as in 7:19 and 9:9: bring to full cleansing and access.

Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? Key words. The logical argument: if the sacrifices really worked, they would have stopped. A medicine that cures is not taken forever.

Since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins. Key words. “Once been cleansed” (hapax kekatharismenous, cleansed once for all). “Consciousness of sins” (syneidēsin hamartiōn, conscience of sins, sense of guilt). If truly cleansed, they would no longer carry guilt. Not that they would never be aware of sinning, but that they would no longer bear the burden of unremoved guilt before God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the old sacrifices were useless or that God did not command them. They were God’s appointed shadows, pointing to Christ. But they could not achieve what only Christ’s sacrifice could.

In a sentence. The law is only a shadow of the good things that were coming, not the realities themselves. That is why it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who come near to worship. If it could, would the sacrifices not have stopped being offered? The worshippers would have been cleansed once for all and would no longer have felt guilty for their sins.

For worship. If you still carry guilt for forgiven sins, hear this: Christ has cleansed you once for all. Let your conscience rest in him.

verseByVerse.quote: But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. Key words. “Reminder” (anamnēsis, remembrance, recollection). Instead of removing sins, the annual sacrifices reminded people of them. Each Day of Atonement said: your sins are still there. Contrast the new covenant, where God remembers sins no more (8:12; 10:17). Interestingly, Jesus uses the same word, anamnēsis, of the Lord’s Supper (“do this in remembrance of me,” Luke 22:19). The old ritual remembered sins; the new remembers the Saviour who removed them.

For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Key words. “Impossible” (adynaton), the same strong word as 6:4, 18. “Take away” (aphairein, remove, lift off). An animal cannot substitute for a human being; it is not of the same nature, nor can it willingly offer itself, nor is it of infinite worth. The old sacrifices could cleanse ritually, and pointed to Christ, but they could not remove guilt before God. Only the sacrifice of a sinless man who is also God could do that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Old Testament believers were not truly forgiven. They were forgiven through faith in God’s promise, and the sacrifices were the means God appointed for that faith, but the forgiveness was grounded in Christ’s future sacrifice (9:15; Romans 3:25).

In a sentence. Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take sins away.

For worship. At the Lord’s Table, remember not your sins, but your Saviour, who took them away.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”

Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said. Key words. “Came into the world” (eiserchomenos eis ton kosmon): his incarnation. The words of Psalm 40:6–8 are presented as the words of Christ himself, spoken to the Father as he entered the world. David wrote them, but they find their full meaning in the Son.

Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired. Key words. “Sacrifices” (thysian, animal sacrifices) and “offerings” (prosphoran, grain offerings). God did not desire them for their own sake. What he desired was obedience from the heart (1 Samuel 15:22; Psalm 51:16–17; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8).

But a body have you prepared for me. Key words. “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew reads “you have opened my ears” (literally “ears you have dug for me”), meaning God gave the ability to hear and obey. The Greek translators interpreted it as a reference to the whole body, of which the ears are part: God prepared a whole person for obedience. Under the Spirit’s guidance, the author uses the Greek version because it points precisely to the incarnation: the Father prepared a human body for the Son, in which he could obey perfectly and offer himself as the sacrifice (v. 10).

In burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Key words. “Burnt offerings” (holokautōmata, wholly burnt offerings) and “sin offerings” (peri hamartias). The main categories of Levitical sacrifice.

Then I said, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God. Key words. “Behold, I have come” (idou hēkō). The Son’s willing obedience. His whole life was devoted to doing the Father’s will (John 4:34; 6:38), culminating in the cross (Matthew 26:39, 42).

As it is written of me in the scroll of the book. Key words. “Scroll of the book” (kephalidi bibliou, the head of the scroll, the roll of the book): the Scriptures, which testify of Christ (Luke 24:27, 44; John 5:39).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never wanted the Old Testament sacrifices at all; he commanded them. It means he did not desire them as ends in themselves or as substitutes for obedience. He desired what they pointed to: the perfect obedience and self-offering of his Son.

In a sentence. That is why, when Christ came into the world, he said: “You did not want sacrifices and offerings, but you prepared a body for me; you were not pleased with burnt offerings and sin offerings. Then I said, ‘Here I am, I have come to do your will, my God, as it is written about me in the scroll.’”

For worship. Offer yourself to God today as Christ did: “Here I am, I have come to do your will.”
verseByVerse.note: “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew of Ps 40:6 reads “you have given me an open ear.”

verseByVerse.quote: When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

When he said above. Key words. The author now explains the psalm.

You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings. Key words. All four kinds of sacrifice are listed together.

(these are offered according to the law). Key words. The psalm’s rejection of sacrifices applies to the very offerings the law required. Something remarkable: God, through David, signalled that the law’s sacrifices were not his final desire.

Then he added, Behold, I have come to do your will. Key words. The second statement replaces the first.

He does away with the first in order to establish the second. Key words. “Does away with” (anairei, abolishes, takes away, removes). “The first”: the sacrificial system. “Establish” (stēsē, set up, confirm). “The second”: Christ’s obedience to God’s will. The old system is removed; Christ’s self-offering replaces it.

And by that will we have been sanctified. Key words. “By that will” (en hō thelēmati): by God’s will, which Christ came to do. God’s saving purpose, carried out by Christ’s obedience. “Sanctified” (hēgiasmenoi, perfect tense: we have been made holy and remain so). Here sanctification means being set apart, consecrated to God, made fit for his presence: a definitive, once-for-all act (as in 1 Corinthians 6:11), not the ongoing process of growth in holiness.

Through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. Key words. “Offering” (prosphoras). “Body” (sōmatos): the body prepared for him (v. 5). “Once for all” (ephapax). By his death on the cross, he made his people holy, once and for all time.

What it does not mean. “Sanctified” here does not mean believers are already morally perfect. That process continues (12:14; 2 Corinthians 3:18). It means we have been definitively set apart for God through Christ’s sacrifice.

In a sentence. First he said, “You did not want sacrifices, offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings, and you were not pleased with them,” even though the law required them. Then he said, “Here I am, I have come to do your will.” He sets aside the first system to establish the second. And by God’s will, carried out by Christ, we have been made holy through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

For worship. Thank God that you have been made holy, set apart for him, by Christ’s one sacrifice. Live today as one who belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.

And every priest stands daily at his service. Key words. “Stands” (hestēken). Priests stood; there were no chairs in the tabernacle, because their work was never done.

Offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. Key words. “Repeatedly” (pollakis, many times). “The same”: endless repetition of identical sacrifices. “Take away” (perielein, strip off, remove entirely).

But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins. Key words. “For all time” (eis to diēnekes, perpetually). “Single” (mian, one). One sacrifice, effective forever.

He sat down at the right hand of God. Key words. Sitting signals completion. The contrast is total: they stand, he sits; they offer repeatedly, he offered once; theirs never take away sins, his does forever.

Waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. Key words. Psalm 110:1 again (1:13). “Waiting” (ekdechomenos): not idle, but reigning while the Father subdues his enemies, through the gospel’s advance and finally at his return (1 Corinthians 15:24–28).

For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Key words. “Perfected” (teteleiōken, perfect tense: has completed, and it remains complete). “For all time” (eis to diēnekes). “Those who are being sanctified” (tous hagiazomenous, present tense: those being made holy). A wonderful combination: we are perfected (complete, accepted, cleansed before God) once for all, and yet we are being sanctified (growing in holiness). Our standing is perfect; our condition is improving. The one guarantees the other.

Where Christians differ: can a believer lose what Christ’s sacrifice achieved? Some teach that a believer’s perfected standing can be forfeited. Verdict: This verse says Christ has perfected his people “for all time” by a single offering. What is perfect for all time cannot be undone. Christ’s death did not merely make salvation possible; it actually and permanently perfected those for whom it was made, guaranteeing their sanctification and final glory (Romans 8:30). This is the ground of both definite atonement and the perseverance of the saints.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are sinless now. They are perfected in standing, being sanctified in experience.

In a sentence. Every priest stands day after day performing his religious duties, offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this priest had offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, he sat down at the right hand of God, and since then he waits for his enemies to be made his footstool. For by one sacrifice he has made perfect for ever those who are being made holy.

For worship. Christ sat down; his work is done. Rest in it. Your standing before God is perfect, forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.

And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us. Key words. “Bears witness” (martyrei, present tense: testifies now). As in 3:7, the Holy Spirit speaks through Scripture, here Jeremiah 31. What the prophet wrote, the Spirit says, to us, today.

This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds. Key words. Jeremiah 31:33, quoted in 8:10.

Then he adds, I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more. Key words. Jeremiah 31:34, quoted in 8:12. “Lawless deeds” (anomiōn, iniquities, breaches of law). The author singles out the climax of the new covenant: complete, permanent forgiveness.

Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin. Key words. “Forgiveness” (aphesis, release, cancellation). “No longer any offering” (ouketi prosphora). The conclusion of the whole argument from 7:1: since sins are fully forgiven, no further sacrifice is needed or possible. To go back to the old sacrifices, or to offer any other sacrifice for sin, is to deny that Christ’s sacrifice was enough.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers no longer offer anything to God. They offer spiritual sacrifices: praise, good works, generosity, themselves (13:15–16; Romans 12:1). But these are thank offerings, not offerings for sin.

In a sentence. The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First he says: “This is the covenant I will make with them after that time, says the Lord. I will put my laws in their hearts, and I will write them on their minds.” Then he adds: “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” And where these have been forgiven, there is no longer any need for a sacrifice for sin.

For worship. Thank God that no more sacrifice for sin is needed. Your forgiveness is complete. Offer him instead the sacrifice of praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–39 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because Jesus’ blood has opened a new and living way into God’s presence, and he is our great priest, the writer urges three things: come near to God with sincere, cleansed hearts and full assurance; hold firmly to the hope we confess, because God is faithful; and think how to stir one another to love and good works, not abandoning meeting together. Then comes a solemn warning: for anyone who deliberately rejects Christ after knowing the truth, there is no other sacrifice, only judgement, for falling into the hands of the living God is terrifying. But the readers should recall how bravely they once endured persecution and even the seizure of their property, knowing they had a better and lasting possession. They must not throw away their confidence. They need endurance, because the coming one will not delay, and they are not people who shrink back but people who believe and are saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtain Is His Flesh

The way into the holy places has been opened through the curtain, his flesh. So draw near, hold fast because he who promised is faithful, and stir one another up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had once joyfully accepted the plundering of their property.

Now: The warning of verses 26–31 is aimed at deliberate repudiation of Christ, not at a struggling believer; and it ends in assurance: we are not of those who shrink back.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,

Therefore, brothers. Key words. “Therefore” (oun) marks the great turn from teaching to application. Everything from 4:14 to 10:18 now becomes the basis for appeal.

Since we have confidence to enter the holy places. Key words. “Confidence” (parrēsian, boldness, freedom), as in 4:16. “To enter” (eis tēn eisodon, for the entrance). “Holy places”: God’s very presence. What only the high priest could do once a year, every believer may now do at any time.

By the blood of Jesus. Key words. Not by our worthiness, but by his blood, his sacrifice.

By the new and living way that he opened for us. Key words. “New” (prosphaton, freshly made, recently slain; the word originally meant “freshly killed”). “Living” (zōsan): not a dead ritual path but a living way, Christ himself (John 14:6). “Opened” (enekainisen, inaugurated, dedicated, the same root as 9:18). He opened the road and walked it first.

Through the curtain, that is, through his flesh. Key words. “Curtain” (katapetasmatos, veil): the curtain before the Most Holy Place. “His flesh”: his body given in death. When his body was broken on the cross, the temple curtain was torn (Mark 15:38). The way into God’s presence is through the torn body of Christ.

And since we have a great priest over the house of God. Key words. “Great priest” (hierea megan): a Hebrew way of saying high priest. “Over the house of God”: Christ the Son over God’s household, which we are (3:6). We have both a way and a priest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we approach God casually. We come with confidence because of Christ, but still with reverence (12:28).

In a sentence. So, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place through the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his body, and since we have a great priest in charge of God’s household,

For worship. You may enter God’s presence right now, by the blood of Jesus. Come to him in prayer with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.

Let us draw near. Key words. The first of three exhortations (vv. 22, 23, 24): draw near, hold fast, consider one another. Faith, hope and love. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha), as in 4:16: approach God in worship and prayer.

With a true heart. Key words. “True” (alēthinēs, sincere, genuine). Not hypocritical or divided (Isaiah 29:13).

In full assurance of faith. Key words. “Full assurance” (plērophoria, complete confidence, full conviction), as in 6:11. Not doubting whether we are welcome, but confident because of Christ’s finished work.

With our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience. Key words. “Sprinkled” (rerantismenoi, perfect tense: having been sprinkled and remaining so). Priests were sprinkled with blood at their consecration (Exodus 29:21; Leviticus 8:30), and the people at the covenant’s ratification (9:19). Our hearts have been sprinkled with Christ’s blood, cleansing the guilty conscience (9:14). “Evil conscience”: a conscience burdened with guilt.

And our bodies washed with pure water. Key words. “Washed” (lelousmenoi, perfect tense: bathed). Priests washed before entering the tabernacle (Exodus 29:4; 30:19–21). Most interpreters see here a reference to Christian baptism, the outward sign of inward cleansing (Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21). Inward cleansing (hearts sprinkled) and outward sign (bodies washed) go together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism cleanses the conscience by itself. The heart is cleansed by Christ’s blood, received by faith; baptism is the public sign and seal of that cleansing, given to those who believe.

In a sentence. let us come near to God with a sincere heart and with the full confidence that faith gives, since our hearts have been sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies have been washed with pure water.

For worship. Draw near to God today with full assurance. Remember your baptism, the sign that you have been washed in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.

Let us hold fast the confession of our hope. Key words. The second exhortation. “Hold fast” (katechōmen, hold firmly, keep a grip on), as in 3:6, 14; 4:14. “Confession” (homologian): what we publicly profess. “Of our hope”: our confident expectation of glory. The readers were tempted to let go under persecution.

Without wavering. Key words. “Without wavering” (aklinē, unbending, not leaning to one side, steadfast). Hold it straight and firm, not bending under pressure.

For he who promised is faithful. Key words. “Faithful” (pistos). The reason we can hold fast: not our strength, but God’s faithfulness. He will keep every promise (6:13–18; 11:11; 1 Corinthians 1:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:24). Our grip may be weak, but his is not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we hold on by our own power. We hold fast because God is faithful and holds us. But we are truly called to hold fast, and those whom God holds do so.

In a sentence. Let us keep a firm grip on the hope we profess, without wavering, because the one who made the promise can be trusted.

On a Tuesday. Is pressure making you want to soften or hide your hope? Hold it straight. God will keep his promises.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.

And let us consider how to stir up one another. Key words. The third exhortation. “Consider” (katanoōmen, think carefully about, pay attention to), as in 3:1. “Stir up” (paroxysmon, provoke, incite, spur on; usually used negatively of sharp disagreement, Acts 15:39, here positively). Think creatively about how to provoke each other to good.

To love and good works. Key words. The goal of mutual encouragement: love that shows itself in practical deeds.

Not neglecting to meet together. Key words. “Neglecting” (enkataleipontes, forsaking, abandoning, deserting). “Meet together” (episynagōgēn, assembling, gathering). Regular gathering for worship and fellowship is essential. The Christian life is not meant to be lived alone.

As is the habit of some. Key words. “Habit” (ethos, custom). Some were already staying away, perhaps from fear of persecution, or from drifting, or from returning to the synagogue. Absence from the gathered church is often the first step in falling away.

But encouraging one another. Key words. “Encouraging” (parakalountes, exhorting, urging), as in 3:13.

And all the more as you see the Day drawing near. Key words. “The Day”: the day of Christ’s return and judgement (1 Corinthians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 5:2, 4). “Drawing near” (engizousan). Every passing day brings it closer. It may also include the approaching destruction of Jerusalem, a foretaste of the final judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church attendance alone makes a person a Christian. But a professing Christian who habitually neglects gathering with God’s people is in spiritual danger. Nor does it condemn those who cannot attend through illness or other genuine hindrance.

In a sentence. And let us think about how we can spur one another on toward love and good deeds. Let us not give up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

On a Tuesday. Think of one specific way to spur a fellow believer to love and good works this week. And make Sunday worship a non-negotiable priority.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.

For if we go on sinning deliberately. Key words. The fourth warning. “Go on sinning” (hamartanontōn, present tense: continue sinning, persist in sin). “Deliberately” (hekousiōs, willingly, wilfully). Not occasional sins of weakness, which all believers commit (1 John 1:8–10), but a settled, deliberate course of rebellion. In context, the sin is apostasy: abandoning Christ (v. 29), the opposite of holding fast (v. 23). It echoes the Old Testament distinction between unintentional sins and sins “with a high hand” (Numbers 15:27–31).

After receiving the knowledge of the truth. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōsin, full knowledge). They knew the gospel; they were not ignorant. Rejecting known truth is more serious than rejecting what one has never understood.

There no longer remains a sacrifice for sins. Key words. If you reject Christ’s sacrifice, there is no other. The old sacrifices are obsolete (v. 18), and Christ’s is the only one. To turn from Christ is to turn from the only remedy.

But a fearful expectation of judgment. Key words. “Fearful” (phobera, terrifying). “Expectation” (ekdochē, anticipation). Only judgement awaits.

And a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries. Key words. “Fury of fire” (pyros zēlos, zeal of fire, fiery jealousy). Echoing Isaiah 26:11. God’s holy zeal against those who oppose him. “Adversaries” (hypenantious, opponents). Apostates join the enemies of God (Philippians 3:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who falls into serious sin is lost forever. David committed adultery and murder, and was restored (Psalm 51). Peter denied Christ, and was restored. The warning is against a deliberate, persistent rejection of Christ. And “consume” does not mean annihilation; Scripture describes the punishment of the wicked as conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46; Mark 9:48; Revelation 14:11). Fire that consumes describes the destructive, ruinous character of judgement.

In a sentence. If we deliberately keep on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is left, only a terrifying expectation of judgement and of raging fire that will consume God’s enemies.

For worship. Thank God for the sacrifice of Christ, the only one that saves. Hold onto it, and never let it go.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. Key words. “Set aside” (athetēsas, rejected, nullified). Under the law, deliberate rejection of the covenant, such as idolatry, brought the death penalty on the testimony of witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:2–7).

How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved. Key words. Again the argument from lesser to greater (2:2–3).

By the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God. Key words. “Trampled underfoot” (katapatēsas, stomped on, treated with contempt). Instead of honouring the Son whom God exalted, the apostate treats him as dirt.

And has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified. Key words. “Profaned” (koinon hēgēsamenos, considered common, unholy, ordinary). Treating Christ’s blood as if it were the blood of a common criminal. “By which he was sanctified” (en hō hēgiasthē): this is the hardest phrase. Who was sanctified? Three readings: (1) the apostate had been genuinely sanctified and now lost it; (2) the apostate was outwardly set apart as part of the covenant community, sharing its privileges, without inward regeneration, as Israel as a whole was “sanctified” by the covenant blood at Sinai (9:19–20), though many were unbelievers; (3) “he” refers to Christ, who was consecrated by his own blood as high priest (John 17:19). The second reading fits the context and the rest of Scripture best.

And has outraged the Spirit of grace. Key words. “Outraged” (enybrisas, insulted, treated with arrogant contempt). “The Spirit of grace”: the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s grace and had worked among them (6:4). Echoing the unforgivable sin of blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:28–29).

For we know him who said, Vengeance is mine; I will repay. Key words. From Deuteronomy 32:35 (also Romans 12:19). God himself will judge.

And again, The Lord will judge his people. Key words. Deuteronomy 32:36. Even those within the covenant community are subject to his judgement.

It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Key words. “Fearful” (phoberon, terrifying). “Fall into the hands”: to fall under his direct judgement, with no mediator. David once chose to fall into God’s hands because his mercy is great (2 Samuel 24:14); but for those who have rejected his mercy in Christ, God’s hands mean only judgement.

Where Christians differ: does this verse show that the sanctified can be lost? Verdict: “Sanctified” in Hebrews can refer to the outward consecration of covenant membership, as when the whole people of Israel was sprinkled with covenant blood. The apostate had been outwardly identified with the new covenant community, baptised, sharing its life, and so in an outward sense set apart by the covenant blood, without inward renewal. Those whom Christ has perfected for all time by his single offering (v. 14) cannot be lost. Verse 39 makes the distinction: there are those who shrink back and are destroyed, and those who have faith and are saved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is cruel or arbitrary. His judgement is just: the punishment fits the magnitude of the offence, which is the rejection of his greatest gift.

In a sentence. Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much more severely, do you think, will someone be punished who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, who has treated as unholy the covenant blood by which he was set apart, and who has insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know the one who said, “It is mine to avenge; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a terrifying thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

For worship. Thank God that because you are in Christ, you will never fall into his hands as an enemy, but rest in them as his child.

verseByVerse.quote: But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.

But recall the former days. Key words. After the severe warning, encouragement, as in 6:9–12. “Recall” (anamimnēskesthe, remember, keep remembering).

When, after you were enlightened. Key words. “Enlightened” (phōtisthentes), as in 6:4: when they first came to faith.

You endured a hard struggle with sufferings. Key words. “Endured” (hypemeinate). “Hard struggle” (pollēn athlēsin, great contest, athletic struggle). Possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, partly because of disturbances over “Chrestus” (probably Christ), according to the Roman historian Suetonius (Acts 18:2).

Sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction. Key words. “Publicly exposed” (theatrizomenoi, made a spectacle, put on show in a theatre). Mocked and abused in public.

And sometimes being partners with those so treated. Key words. “Partners” (koinōnoi, sharers). Standing with persecuted believers, sharing their shame.

For you had compassion on those in prison. Key words. “Had compassion” (synepathēsate, suffered with, sympathised), the same word used of Christ in 4:15. Prisoners in the Roman world depended on friends for food and care; visiting them meant identifying with them (13:3; Matthew 25:36).

And you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property. Key words. “Plundering” (harpagēn, seizure, robbery). Their goods were confiscated or looted. “Joyfully” (meta charas): not merely enduring loss, but rejoicing (Matthew 5:11–12; Acts 5:41).

Since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one. Key words. “Better possession” (kreittona hyparxin, better property). “Abiding” (menousan, lasting, permanent). They knew their real treasure was in heaven, which no one could take (Matthew 6:19–21; 1 Peter 1:4). Some manuscripts add “in heaven.”

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be careless about possessions or seek their loss. It means that when faithfulness costs us our goods, we can let them go with joy, because our true wealth is secure.

In a sentence. Remember those earlier days after you had first received the light, when you stood your ground through a great struggle with suffering. Sometimes you were publicly exposed to insults and persecution; at other times you stood side by side with those who were treated that way. You felt for those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, because you knew that you had better and lasting possessions.

On a Tuesday. Visit, write to, or pray for a believer in prison for their faith this week. Remember them as if you were with them.
verseByVerse.note: Possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.

Therefore do not throw away your confidence. Key words. “Throw away” (apobalēte, cast off, discard, as a soldier might throw away his shield in flight). “Confidence” (parrēsian, boldness), as in 3:6; 4:16; 10:19. Don’t abandon the bold faith you once had.

Which has a great reward. Key words. “Reward” (misthapodosian, recompense, payment). God rewards persevering faith (11:6, 26).

For you have need of endurance. Key words. “Endurance” (hypomonēs, steadfastness, patient perseverance under pressure). What the readers most needed (12:1–3; James 1:3–4).

So that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised. Key words. “Done the will of God”: persevering in faith and obedience, as Christ did God’s will (v. 7). “Receive what is promised” (komisēsthe tēn epangelian, carry off the promise, obtain it): the eternal inheritance (9:15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the reward is earned by works. The reward is the gracious inheritance promised to those who persevere in faith. Endurance is how faith shows itself over time.

In a sentence. So do not throw away your confidence; it will be richly rewarded. You need to keep going, so that when you have done what God wants, you will receive what he has promised.

On a Tuesday. What tempts you to give up? Ask God for endurance today, and take the next faithful step.

verseByVerse.quote: For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”

For, Yet a little while. Key words. From Isaiah 26:20 (“for a little while”) and Habakkuk 2:3–4, following the Greek translation. “A little while” (mikron hoson hoson, a very, very little while): the time of waiting is short.

And the coming one will come and will not delay. Key words. “The coming one” (ho erchomenos): a title for the Messiah (Matthew 11:3). In Habakkuk, the vision of God’s deliverance will come; the Greek translation reads it as a person, which the author applies to Christ’s return. “Will not delay” (ou chronisei): it may seem slow, but it will come at the right time (2 Peter 3:8–9).

But my righteous one shall live by faith. Key words. Habakkuk 2:4, also quoted by Paul (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Here the emphasis is on faith as persevering trust that keeps living while waiting. The righteous person lives, now and eternally, by trusting God. Faith is not a one-time act but a way of life. This verse introduces chapter 11, the great chapter on faith.

And if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him. Key words. “Shrinks back” (hyposteilētai, draws back, cowers, withdraws, as a soldier retreats or a sailor lowers sail). “No pleasure” (ouk eudokei). God does not delight in those who retreat from faith.

Textual note. The author reverses the order of Habakkuk’s two clauses in the Greek translation, so that “my righteous one” becomes the subject of “if he shrinks back.” This makes clear that the warning is addressed to those who profess to be God’s people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the coming of Christ was expected within a few years only. “A little while” is God’s perspective; from his view, the whole age is brief.

In a sentence. For, “In just a very little while, the one who is coming will come and will not be late. But my righteous one will live by faith; and if he draws back, I will take no pleasure in him.”

For worship. Live by faith today, waiting for the Coming One. He will not be late.

verseByVerse.quote: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

But we are not of those who shrink back. Key words. “We are not” (hēmeis de ouk esmen): the author’s confidence in the readers, including himself. “Shrink back” (hypostolēs, retreat, drawing back), picking up verse 38.

And are destroyed. Key words. “Destroyed” (eis apōleian, unto destruction, perdition). The end of those who shrink back is eternal ruin (Philippians 1:28; 2 Thessalonians 1:9).

But of those who have faith and preserve their souls. Key words. “Have faith” (pisteōs, of faith). “Preserve their souls” (eis peripoiēsin psychēs, unto the gaining, preserving, possessing of the soul). Those with true faith keep going and are saved. There are only two categories: those who shrink back and perish, and those who believe and are saved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the author is uncertain about his readers. He expresses confidence that they belong to those who believe, which is why he warns them: the warning is one of the means God uses to keep his own.

In a sentence. But we are not the kind of people who draw back and are lost; we are those who believe and are saved.

For worship. Thank God that he has given you faith and that he will keep you to the end. Pray for anyone you know who is drawing back.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near.<sup>2</sup>Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?<sup>3</sup>But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.<sup>5</sup>Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me;<sup>6</sup>in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure.<sup>7</sup>Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”<sup>8</sup>When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law),<sup>9</sup>then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.<sup>10</sup>And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.<sup>11</sup>And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.<sup>12</sup>But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God,<sup>13</sup>waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet.<sup>14</sup>For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.<sup>15</sup>And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying,<sup>16</sup>“This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,”<sup>17</sup>then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.”<sup>18</sup>Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.<sup>19</sup>Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus,<sup>20</sup>by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh,<sup>21</sup>and since we have a great priest over the house of God,<sup>22</sup>let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.<sup>23</sup>Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.<sup>24</sup>And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works,<sup>25</sup>not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.<sup>26</sup>For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,<sup>27</sup>but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.<sup>28</sup>Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>29</sup>How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?<sup>30</sup>For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.”<sup>31</sup>It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.<sup>32</sup>But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,<sup>33</sup>sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated.<sup>34</sup>For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.<sup>35</sup>Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.<sup>36</sup>For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.<sup>37</sup>For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay;<sup>38</sup>but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”<sup>39</sup>But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

11.title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
11.overview:
