Ten chapters have argued that Jesus is better. Chapter 11 shows what it looks like to live on that: a gallery of people who took God at his word about things they could not see, and acted on it. Faith here is never an opinion held; it is always something done that makes no sense without a promise from God.

The gallery is honest. Its members are often inconsistent (Sarah laughed, Jacob deceived, Samson was a disgrace), and its outcomes are opposite: some shut lions’ mouths, some were sawn in two. All are commended, and none received what was promised. The chapter ends by saying why: God was keeping something better, so that they and we would be made perfect together. The readers were tempted to go back to the age these saints longed to see the end of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — By Faith: Title Deeds and Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer defines faith as a firm grip on what is hoped for and conviction about what cannot be seen, and shows it at work in the people of old. By faith we understand that God made the universe by his word. Abel, Enoch and Noah trusted God and were approved; without faith no one can please him. Abraham left home not knowing where he was going, lived in tents in the promised land as a foreigner, and looked for a city built by God; Sarah, past age, received power to conceive. They all died without receiving what was promised, seeing it from far off and admitting they were strangers seeking a better, heavenly homeland, and God is not ashamed to be called their God. Abraham offered Isaac, reasoning that God could raise the dead; Isaac, Jacob and Joseph spoke in faith about a future they would not see.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as a Title Deed

Faith gives the things hoped for a footing in the present, because it rests on the reliability of the one who promised. Everyone in this gallery is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in tents in the land of promise and died without receiving it.

Now: God is not ashamed to be called the God of people who are visibly waiting for a better country.

verseByVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.

Meaning first. Hebrews 11 is the great chapter on faith, answering the call of 10:38–39 to live by faith and not shrink back. It opens by describing faith as confident assurance about what we hope for and conviction about what we cannot see (vv. 1–3). Then it walks through the Old Testament, showing faith at work in a long line of people. Abel offered a better sacrifice; Enoch pleased God and was taken; and without faith it is impossible to please God (vv. 4–6). Noah built the ark; Abraham left home not knowing where he was going, lived as a stranger in the promised land, and looked for God’s city; Sarah received power to conceive (vv. 7–12). All of them died without receiving the promises in full, confessing that they were strangers seeking a heavenly country, and God is not ashamed to be their God (vv. 13–16). Abraham offered Isaac, believing God could raise the dead; Isaac, Jacob and Joseph blessed their children and looked ahead to the future (vv. 17–22). Moses’ parents hid him; Moses chose suffering with God’s people over Egypt’s treasures, considering reproach for Christ greater wealth; he kept the Passover; Israel crossed the Red Sea; Jericho fell; Rahab was spared (vv. 23–31). And many more, judges, kings and prophets, conquered by faith, while others were tortured, mocked, imprisoned, stoned and killed, people of whom the world was not worthy (vv. 32–38). Yet none of them received the fulfilment in their lifetime, because God planned something better, so that they would be made perfect together with us (vv. 39–40). The chapter shows that faith trusts God’s word about the unseen and the future, and acts on it, whatever the cost.

Now faith is. Key words. “Faith” (pistis, trust, confidence, reliance). Not a full definition of saving faith, but a description of what faith does and how it works, particularly in relation to the future and the unseen.

The assurance of things hoped for. Key words. “Assurance” (hypostasis). The word has a range of meanings: substance, reality, foundation, confidence, title deed. In 1:3, it meant God’s essence (“nature”); in 3:14, confidence. Here, faith gives substance and reality to things hoped for: it treats God’s promises as already real. In ancient papyri, hypostasis was used of a title deed, proof of ownership. Faith is the title deed to what God has promised. “Things hoped for”: the promised future: the city, the inheritance, resurrection, Christ’s return.

The conviction of things not seen. Key words. “Conviction” (elenchos, proof, evidence, being convinced, as in a court case where something is proved). Faith is persuaded of realities that cannot be seen: God himself, heaven, Christ at God’s right hand, and future events (2 Corinthians 4:18; 5:7). It is not believing without reason, but trusting God’s word about what our eyes cannot yet see.

For by it the people of old received their commendation. Key words. “People of old” (hoi presbyteroi, the elders, the ancients): the Old Testament believers. “Received their commendation” (emartyrēthēsan, were testified to, received God’s approval). God bore witness in Scripture that they pleased him. This sets the theme for the chapter: faith brings God’s approval.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is wishful thinking or a leap in the dark. Faith rests on God’s word and character, which are utterly reliable (6:18; 10:23). Nor does faith create reality; it trusts the reality God has promised.

In a sentence. Faith is confidence that what we hope for is real, and certainty about what we cannot see. It was for their faith that the people of long ago received God’s approval.

For worship. Ask God for faith that treats his promises as real and the unseen as certain, so that you live today in their light.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.

By faith we understand. Key words. “By faith” (pistei): the phrase that will open each example in the chapter, repeated eighteen times. “Understand” (nooumen, perceive with the mind, comprehend). Faith is not opposed to understanding; it leads to it. We know creation came from God because God has told us (Genesis 1).

That the universe was created by the word of God. Key words. “Universe” (tous aiōnas, the ages, the worlds, all of space and time), as in 1:2. “Created” (katērtisthai, framed, fitted together, put in order). “By the word of God” (rhēmati theou, by God’s spoken word). God said, “Let there be,” and it was (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6, 9).

So that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible. Key words. The visible universe did not come from pre-existing visible materials. God created from nothing (ex nihilo), by his word alone (Romans 4:17; Colossians 1:16). This was a radical claim against Greek philosophy, which generally held that matter was eternal. The first lesson of faith is that the God who made everything from nothing can be trusted to keep every promise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith rejects evidence or reason. Creation itself bears witness to its Creator (Romans 1:20; Psalm 19:1). But the fact that it was made by God’s word out of nothing is known with certainty only by trusting God’s revelation.

In a sentence. It is by faith that we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what can be seen was not made from anything visible.

For worship. Look at the sky or a tree today and praise the God who spoke it into being from nothing. That God can keep his promises to you.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.

By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain. Key words. “More acceptable” (pleiona, greater, better, fuller). Genesis 4:3–5 records that God had regard for Abel’s offering but not Cain’s. Why? Not merely because Abel’s was an animal and Cain’s was grain (both kinds were later commanded in the law), but because Abel offered by faith, from a heart right with God, and offered the firstborn and best (Genesis 4:4). Cain’s heart was wrong, as his murder of Abel showed (1 John 3:12).

Through which he was commended as righteous. Key words. “Commended” (emartyrēthē, testified to). “Righteous” (dikaios): Jesus called him “righteous Abel” (Matthew 23:35). His righteousness came by faith.

God commending him by accepting his gifts. Key words. God himself bore witness to Abel’s faith by accepting his offering.

And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. Key words. Abel was the first person to die, murdered by his brother. But his blood cried out from the ground (Genesis 4:10), and through Scripture he still speaks, testifying to the power of faith. Christ’s blood speaks a better word than Abel’s (12:24): Abel’s blood cried for justice; Christ’s cries for mercy.

By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death. Key words. “Taken up” (metetethē, transferred, translated, removed). Genesis 5:24: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. Enoch did not die; God took him directly to himself, like Elijah (2 Kings 2:11).

And he was not found, because God had taken him. Key words. From the Greek translation of Genesis 5:24.

Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God. Key words. “Pleased God” (euarestēkenai tō theō): the Greek translation’s rendering of “walked with God.” To walk with God is to please him, and to please him requires faith (v. 6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abel earned acceptance by the quality of his offering. His faith made the offering acceptable. Nor does Enoch’s being taken mean we should expect the same; it was a unique sign of God’s pleasure and of life beyond death.

In a sentence. By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. Because of his faith he was declared righteous, when God showed his approval of his gifts. And by faith Abel still speaks, even though he is dead. By faith Enoch was taken from this life, so that he did not experience death; he could not be found, because God had taken him away. For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God.

For worship. Walk with God today as Enoch did: in his presence, by faith, seeking to please him.

verseByVerse.quote: And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

And without faith it is impossible to please him. Key words. “Impossible” (adynaton), as in 6:4, 18; 10:4. Not difficult, but impossible. No amount of religious activity, morality or sacrifice pleases God without faith (Romans 14:23). Faith is not one virtue among many; it is the root of all that pleases God.

For whoever would draw near to God. Key words. “Draw near” (proserchomenon), the key verb of the letter for approaching God in worship (4:16; 7:25; 10:22).

Must believe that he exists. Key words. “Exists” (estin, is). The most basic element of faith: believing God is real, the living God, not an idea or a force. But even demons believe that (James 2:19); saving faith goes further.

And that he rewards those who seek him. Key words. “Rewards” (misthapodotēs, one who pays wages, rewarder). God is not indifferent, distant or stingy; he responds to those who seek him and gives them himself and his blessings (Jeremiah 29:13; Matthew 7:7–8). “Seek” (ekzētousin, search diligently, seek out). True faith trusts both God’s existence and his goodness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith earns God’s favour, or that we seek him for what he gives rather than for himself. The great reward is God himself (Genesis 15:1). Nor does it mean that seeking originates in us; God draws us to seek him (John 6:44; Romans 3:11).

In a sentence. Without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who comes to him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him.

For worship. Come to God today trusting not only that he exists but that he is good, and that he delights to reward those who seek him.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.

By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen. Key words. “Warned” (chrēmatistheis, divinely instructed). “Events as yet unseen”: a worldwide flood, which had never happened (Genesis 6:13–17). Faith trusts God’s warnings about the future, even when nothing in present experience supports them (v. 1).

In reverent fear. Key words. “Reverent fear” (eulabētheis, moved with godly fear, taking care), as of Jesus in 5:7. Faith takes God’s word seriously.

Constructed an ark for the saving of his household. Key words. “Constructed” (kateskeuasen, prepared, built). A massive project, perhaps over many decades, in obedience to God’s word. Faith obeys. “For the saving of his household”: his faith led to the rescue of his family (Genesis 7:1; 1 Peter 3:20).

By this he condemned the world. Key words. “Condemned” (katekrinen, judged against). His faith and obedience exposed the world’s unbelief. His actions said that judgement was coming; their scoffing showed they did not believe (2 Peter 2:5, where Noah is called a herald of righteousness).

And became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith. Key words. “Heir” (klēronomos). “Righteousness that comes by faith” (tēs kata pistin dikaiosynēs): the same righteousness by faith that Paul teaches (Romans 4; Philippians 3:9). Noah was declared righteous by God (Genesis 6:9; 7:1) on the basis of faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Noah was saved by building the ark. He was saved by faith in God’s word, which showed itself in building the ark. Faith and obedience are inseparable but distinct.

In a sentence. By faith Noah, when he was warned by God about things not yet seen, reverently built an ark to save his family. Through his faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.

On a Tuesday. Is God calling you to obey him in something that looks foolish to others? Do it by faith, as Noah did.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.

By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called. Key words. Abraham receives more attention than anyone else in the chapter (vv. 8–19). “Obeyed” (hypēkousen, listened and obeyed). “Called” (kaloumenos, present participle: while he was being called): he obeyed immediately (Genesis 12:1–4).

To go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. Key words. Canaan, promised to him and his descendants (Genesis 12:7; 15:18–21).

And he went out, not knowing where he was going. Key words. He left his home in Ur and Haran, his family, security and culture, without a map. Faith trusts God’s leading without needing to see the whole route.

By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land. Key words. “Went to live” (parōkēsen, lived as a resident alien, sojourned). In the very land God promised him, Abraham lived as a foreigner. He owned only a burial plot (Genesis 23).

Living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. Key words. Three generations lived in tents, temporary dwellings, never settling (Genesis 12:8; 26:25; 33:18–19).

For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations. Key words. “Looking forward” (exedecheto, waiting eagerly, expecting). “City that has foundations”: a permanent city, in contrast with tents. This is the heavenly Jerusalem (12:22; 13:14; Revelation 21:2, 10–14, where the city has twelve foundations). Abraham looked beyond Canaan to a heavenly inheritance.

Whose designer and builder is God. Key words. “Designer” (technitēs, craftsman, architect). “Builder” (dēmiourgos, maker, constructor). God himself designed and built it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham had no interest in the land; it was truly promised. But he understood the land as a pointer to something greater, as the New Testament makes clear (Romans 4:13, where the promise is that he would inherit the world).

In a sentence. By faith Abraham obeyed when God called him to leave for a place he would later receive as his inheritance; he set out even though he did not know where he was going. By faith he made his home in the promised land like a foreigner in a strange country; he lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. For he was waiting for the city with lasting foundations, whose architect and builder is God.

On a Tuesday. Hold your earthly home and plans loosely. You are travelling to a better city. Let that shape one decision this week.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.

By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive. Key words. “Sarah herself” (autē Sarra): even Sarah, who had laughed in disbelief (Genesis 18:12). Her faith was not perfect, but it grew. “Power to conceive” (dynamin eis katabolēn spermatos, literally power for the laying down of seed). Some take this phrase as applying to Abraham (with Sarah as a secondary subject, “together with Sarah”), since the expression usually refers to the father’s role. Either way, both shared in the miracle by faith.

Even when she was past the age. Key words. Sarah was ninety and had always been barren (Genesis 11:30; 17:17).

Since she considered him faithful who had promised. Key words. “Faithful” (piston): the heart of faith is trusting God’s faithfulness (10:23). Not trusting her own ability, but God’s reliability.

Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead. Key words. “As good as dead” (nenekrōmenou, deadened): Abraham was a hundred, his body past fathering children (Romans 4:19).

Were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore. Key words. God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:5; 22:17; 32:12). From one man, as good as dead, came a nation, and through Christ, Abraham’s spiritual children from every nation (Galatians 3:7, 29).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Sarah never doubted. She laughed. Faith is not the absence of struggle but trusting God despite it.

In a sentence. By faith even Sarah, who was past childbearing age, was enabled to have a child, because she considered God faithful to his promise. So from this one man, who was as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.

For worship. What seems dead or impossible in your life? Bring it to the God who brought life from Abraham and Sarah, and trust his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.

These all died in faith. Key words. “Died in faith” (kata pistin apethanon, died according to faith). They lived by faith and died still trusting. Faith carried them to the end.

Not having received the things promised. Key words. They did not see the full fulfilment: the land, the nation, the Messiah, the heavenly city.

But having seen them and greeted them from afar. Key words. “Greeted” (aspasamenoi, welcomed, saluted). Like travellers who glimpse their destination on the horizon and wave to it. Jesus said Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56).

And having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. Key words. “Strangers” (xenoi, foreigners) and “exiles” (parepidēmoi, temporary residents, sojourners). Abraham said, “I am a sojourner and foreigner among you” (Genesis 23:4); Jacob spoke of his pilgrimage (Genesis 47:9). Believers are pilgrims in this world (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11).

For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. Key words. “Homeland” (patrida, fatherland, native country). Pilgrims are going somewhere.

If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. Key words. They could have gone back to Mesopotamia. They did not, because their hearts were set on something else.

But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Key words. “Desire” (oregontai, stretch out for, long for). “Better” (kreittonos). “Heavenly” (epouraniou). They longed for heaven, God’s country, the new creation (Philippians 3:20).

Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God. Key words. “Not ashamed” (ouk epaischynetai), as Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers (2:11). God calls himself “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6), a title Jesus used to prove the resurrection (Matthew 22:32).

For he has prepared for them a city. Key words. “Prepared” (hētoimasen). God has already made it ready (John 14:2–3; Revelation 21:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should despise this world or withdraw from it. It means our deepest loyalty and hope are elsewhere, which frees us to serve here without clinging.

In a sentence. All these people were still living by faith when they died. They did not receive the things promised; they only saw them and welcomed them from a distance, admitting that they were foreigners and strangers on earth. People who say such things show that they are looking for a country of their own. If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they could have gone back. Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. That is why God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

For worship. Thank God that he is not ashamed to be your God, and that he has prepared a city for you. Live today as a pilgrim heading home.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.

By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. Key words. “Tested” (peirazomenos, tried, proved). God tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1), not to tempt him to sin but to prove and strengthen his faith. “Offered up” (prosenēnochen, perfect tense: as good as offered). In intention and obedience, the sacrifice was complete, though God stopped his hand.

And he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son. Key words. “Only son” (monogenē, unique, one and only). Abraham had Ishmael too, but Isaac was the unique son of promise (Genesis 22:2, “your only son Isaac, whom you love”). The test was agonising: God seemed to be contradicting his own promise.

Of whom it was said, Through Isaac shall your offspring be named. Key words. From Genesis 21:12. The promised line ran through Isaac. If Isaac died childless, the promise would fail.

He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead. Key words. “Considered” (logisamenos, reasoned, calculated). Abraham reasoned it through: God promised descendants through Isaac; God commanded Isaac’s death; therefore God must raise Isaac from the dead. He told his servants, “I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you” (Genesis 22:5). Faith reasons from God’s promises.

From which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back. Key words. “Figuratively speaking” (en parabolē, in a parable, as a figure). Isaac was as good as dead, and was given back alive: a picture of resurrection. And a picture pointing to the greater Father who did not spare his only Son, and received him back from the dead in reality (Romans 8:32; John 3:16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God approves of human sacrifice; he stopped it and provided a ram instead, and the law forbade child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31). The test revealed faith and pointed to God’s own provision of his Son.

In a sentence. By faith Abraham, when God tested him, offered Isaac as a sacrifice. He who had received the promises was ready to offer his one and only son, even though God had said to him, “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be counted.” Abraham reasoned that God could even raise the dead, and in a manner of speaking he did receive Isaac back from death.

For worship. Thank the Father who did not spare his only Son, but gave him up for you. If you face a test that seems to contradict God’s promises, trust that he can raise the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.

By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. Key words. “Future” (peri mellontōn, concerning things to come). Isaac blessed his sons with blessings about the future (Genesis 27:27–40). Though deceived by Jacob, Isaac recognised that God’s purpose stood and confirmed the blessing (Genesis 27:33). His blessings expressed faith that God’s promises would be fulfilled in their descendants.

By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph. Key words. Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, crossing his hands to give the younger the greater blessing (Genesis 48). God’s choice, not human order.

Bowing in worship over the head of his staff. Key words. “Staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 47:31; the Hebrew, with different vowels, reads “bed.” The Hebrew consonants for “bed” (mittah) and “staff” (matteh) are the same; the Greek translators read it as staff. The staff was the symbol of Jacob’s pilgrim life (Genesis 32:10). Dying, he worshipped.

By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites. Key words. “Made mention” (emnēmoneusen, remembered, spoke of). Joseph, though powerful in Egypt, knew Egypt was not home. He spoke of God bringing Israel out (Genesis 50:24).

And gave directions concerning his bones. Key words. He made Israel swear to carry his bones to Canaan (Genesis 50:25). They did, over four hundred years later (Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32). His bones in their coffin were a constant reminder that Egypt was not their home and that God would keep his word.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these men were perfect. Isaac favoured Esau, Jacob was a deceiver, and the family was full of rivalry. Faith, not perfection, is what is commended.

In a sentence. By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau with regard to their future. By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, and worshipped as he leaned on the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt and gave instructions about burying his bones.

For worship. When you face death, may you die as these did: worshipping, blessing, and trusting God’s promises for the future.
verseByVerse.note: “Staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Gen 47:31; the Hebrew text as later pointed reads “bed”; the consonants are the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–40 — The Turn: Some Were Tortured
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The examples continue. Moses’ parents hid him, unafraid of the king. Moses himself refused the privileges of Egypt’s court, choosing to suffer with God’s people, counting reproach for Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. He left Egypt, kept the Passover, and led Israel through the sea. Jericho’s walls fell and Rahab was spared. Then the writer piles up names, Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets, who by faith won victories and escaped death. But faith did not always mean rescue. Others were tortured, mocked, flogged, imprisoned, stoned, sawn in two, killed by the sword, and wandered destitute in deserts and caves; the world was not worthy of them. None of them received the promise in full, because God had planned something better that includes us, so that they would not be made complete without us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Chapter Turns Over Mid-Verse

In verse 35 faith that raised the dead becomes faith that was tortured to death — the same faith, opposite outcomes, both commended. Of such people the world was not worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel were far from consistent, and they are in the roll.

Now: All these died waiting for what the church now has; apart from us they are not made perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.

By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents. Key words. Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20). Pharaoh had ordered all Hebrew baby boys thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22). They hid Moses at great risk (Exodus 2:1–3).

Because they saw that the child was beautiful. Key words. “Beautiful” (asteion, fine, well-formed, pleasing; used of Moses in Exodus 2:2 and Acts 7:20, “beautiful in God’s sight”). Perhaps they sensed God had a special purpose for him.

And they were not afraid of the king’s edict. Key words. “Edict” (diatagma, decree). Faith overcame fear of the most powerful ruler on earth. Civil disobedience when the state commands sin (Acts 5:29).

By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. Key words. “Grown up” (megas genomenos, having become great): at about forty (Acts 7:23). “Refused” (ērnēsato, denied, renounced). Moses had been raised as Egyptian royalty, educated in all the wisdom of Egypt (Acts 7:22). He renounced it all to identify with his people (Exodus 2:11–12).

Choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God. Key words. “Choosing” (helomenos, preferring, deliberately selecting). “Mistreated with” (synkakoucheisthai, suffer hardship together with). He chose solidarity with despised slaves over the palace.

Than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. Key words. “Fleeting” (proskairon, temporary, for a season). “Pleasures of sin”: sin does offer real pleasures, but they are short-lived. For Moses, staying in the palace would have been sin, because it meant denying God’s people and God’s call.

He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt. Key words. “Reproach of Christ” (ton oneidismon tou Christou, the disgrace associated with the Messiah). How could Moses suffer reproach for Christ, centuries before Jesus? Several meanings: Moses suffered the kind of reproach that belongs to God’s anointed people, the reproach Christ would later bear in fullness (Psalm 89:50–51); and he identified with the people through whom the Messiah would come, looking ahead to him by faith (John 5:46). The readers were facing reproach for Christ (10:33; 13:13). Moses shows it is worth more than all the wealth of Egypt, the richest empire of its day.

For he was looking to the reward. Key words. “Looking” (apeblepen, looked away to, fixed his eyes on). “Reward” (misthapodosian), as in 10:35. He weighed the eternal against the temporary and chose wisely (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean wealth or high position is sinful in itself. Joseph and Daniel served in pagan courts faithfully. For Moses, remaining meant disobeying God’s call. The question is always: what does faithfulness require of me here?

In a sentence. By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after he was born, because they saw he was no ordinary child, and they were not afraid of the king’s order. By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose to be ill-treated along with the people of God rather than to enjoy the short-lived pleasures of sin. He regarded disgrace for the sake of Christ as of greater value than the treasures of Egypt, because he was looking ahead to his reward.

On a Tuesday. What fleeting pleasure or advantage might you have to give up to be faithful to Christ this week? Look to the reward.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.

By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king. Key words. Either his flight to Midian after killing the Egyptian (Exodus 2:14–15), where Exodus says he was afraid, or the exodus itself (Exodus 12:31–42), when he led Israel out in defiance of Pharaoh. The second fits “not being afraid” better, and the following reference to the Passover. Or the first, interpreted as a decision of faith rather than mere panic.

For he endured as seeing him who is invisible. Key words. “Endured” (ekarterēsen, persevered, held out, was steadfast). “Seeing him who is invisible” (ton aoraton hōs horōn): a paradox. God is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17), yet Moses lived as though he saw him. Faith sees the unseen (v. 1; 2 Corinthians 4:18). Moses feared God more than Pharaoh, so he did not fear Pharaoh.

By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood. Key words. “Kept” (pepoiēken, instituted, perfect tense: established it for all time). The Passover (Exodus 12) was a new ritual, never done before. Moses obeyed God’s instructions exactly, trusting that the blood of a lamb on the doorposts would protect Israel.

So that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them. Key words. “Destroyer” (ho olothreuōn, the one who destroys): the angel of death, or the Lord himself acting in judgement (Exodus 12:23). Where the blood was, judgement passed over. The Passover lamb pointed to Christ, our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7; John 1:29), whose blood protects us from judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses never felt fear. It means fear did not govern his decisions; faith in God did.

In a sentence. By faith he left Egypt, not afraid of the king’s anger; he kept going because he saw the one who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch the firstborn of Israel.

For worship. Thank Christ, your Passover Lamb, whose blood covers you so that judgement passes over.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.

By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land. Key words. “The people”: Israel collectively. Hemmed in between the sea and Pharaoh’s army, they went forward at God’s command (Exodus 14:13–22). Their faith was weak (they complained, Exodus 14:10–12), yet they obeyed.

But the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. Key words. “Attempted” (peiran labontes, having made trial). The same action without faith brought destruction. What saved Israel was not the act of walking but God, received by faith (Exodus 14:23–28).

By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. Key words. Joshua 6. No siege engines or battering rams; only marching, trumpets and a shout, as God commanded. A strategy that made sense only to faith.

By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient. Key words. “Rahab the prostitute”: her past is not hidden. A Gentile, a Canaanite, a prostitute, yet included in the list of faith alongside Abraham and Moses. She became part of Israel and an ancestor of David and of Christ (Matthew 1:5). “Disobedient” (apeithēsasin): the people of Jericho, who knew of God’s works but did not believe (Joshua 2:9–11).

Because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies. Key words. “Friendly welcome” (met’ eirēnēs, with peace). She hid the spies and confessed faith in Israel’s God: “The LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). James also commends her faith shown in action (James 2:25).

Where Christians differ: did God approve Rahab’s lie? Rahab lied to the king’s men to protect the spies (Joshua 2:4–6). Some argue that lying is permissible to save lives; others that Rahab sinned in lying but was commended for her faith. Verdict: Scripture commends Rahab’s faith and her protection of God’s people, not her lie. Hebrews and James praise her welcome and her action, not her deception. God used her despite her imperfect understanding, as he uses all his people. Believers today should seek to protect the innocent without sinning, while recognising the extraordinary pressures some face.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Rahab’s past did not matter. It means grace reaches the most unlikely people, and faith transforms them.

In a sentence. By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as though it were dry land; but when the Egyptians tried to do the same, they were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell after the army had marched around them for seven days. By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies, was not killed along with those who were disobedient.

For worship. Thank God that his grace reaches people like Rahab, and people like you. No past is too dark for faith in him.

verseByVerse.quote: And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.

And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of. Key words. A common rhetorical device in ancient speeches: there is too much to tell. The author speeds up.

Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah. Key words. Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges (Judges 4–16). Gideon defeated the Midianites with three hundred men (Judges 7). Barak, urged by Deborah, defeated Sisera (Judges 4). Samson, despite his moral failures, called on God at the end and destroyed the Philistine temple (Judges 16:28–30). Jephthah defeated the Ammonites (Judges 11). All were deeply flawed. Gideon was fearful and later made an idol; Barak hesitated; Samson was lustful and reckless; Jephthah made a rash vow. Yet God commends their faith. Faith, not perfection.

Of David and Samuel and the prophets. Key words. David, the king after God’s heart, who also sinned grievously. Samuel, the last judge and first great prophet. The prophets: Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and others.

Who through faith conquered kingdoms. Key words. Joshua, the judges, David (2 Samuel 8).

Enforced justice. Key words. “Enforced justice” (eirgasanto dikaiosynēn, worked righteousness): judges and kings like Samuel and David who ruled justly (1 Samuel 12:3–5; 2 Samuel 8:15).

Obtained promises. Key words. Received specific promises and fulfilments from God (Joshua 21:45).

Stopped the mouths of lions. Key words. Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6:22); also Samson and David killed lions (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 17:34–37).

Quenched the power of fire. Key words. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the furnace (Daniel 3:23–27).

Escaped the edge of the sword. Key words. David from Saul (1 Samuel 19–27); Elijah from Jezebel (1 Kings 19); Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24).

Were made strong out of weakness. Key words. Gideon (Judges 6:15), Samson at the end (Judges 16:28), Hezekiah in sickness (Isaiah 38).

Became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight. Key words. Jonathan (1 Samuel 14), David, Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith always brings visible victory. The next verses describe those who suffered and died in faith. Nor does including Samson and Jephthah mean their sins were acceptable; Scripture records them honestly as warnings. Jephthah’s rash vow, however it was fulfilled, is not held up as a model.

In a sentence. What more should I say? I do not have time to tell about Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah, about David and Samuel and the prophets. Through faith they conquered kingdoms, ruled with justice and gained what was promised; they shut the mouths of lions, put out the fury of flames and escaped the edge of the sword; their weakness was turned to strength; they became powerful in battle and routed foreign armies.

On a Tuesday. Feeling too weak or flawed to be used by God? Look at this list. God uses weak people who trust him.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges; the lions’ mouths recall Daniel, and the fire recalls his three friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.

Women received back their dead by resurrection. Key words. The widow of Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised (1 Kings 17:17–24), and the Shunammite woman, whose son Elisha raised (2 Kings 4:18–37).

Some were tortured, refusing to accept release. Key words. Now the tone changes. Faith does not always bring deliverance. “Tortured” (etympanisthēsan, beaten to death, stretched on a rack or wheel, a torture instrument shaped like a drum). “Refusing to accept release”: they could have been freed by renouncing their faith, but refused. This probably refers to the martyrs under the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes around 167 BC, during the Maccabean period, recorded in 2 Maccabees 6–7, including a mother and seven sons who were tortured to death rather than eat pork.

So that they might rise again to a better life. Key words. “Better resurrection” (kreittonos anastaseōs). Better than being restored to mortal life like the sons of the widows; they looked to the final resurrection to eternal life.

Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. Key words. Jeremiah was beaten, put in stocks and imprisoned (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15); Micaiah was imprisoned (1 Kings 22:27).

They were stoned. Key words. Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Matthew 23:35).

They were sawn in two. Key words. Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh, a tradition recorded in a later writing called the Ascension of Isaiah.

They were killed with the sword. Key words. Prophets killed by Jezebel and Ahab (1 Kings 19:10); Uriah the prophet (Jeremiah 26:23).

They went about in skins of sheep and goats. Key words. Elijah wore a garment of hair (2 Kings 1:8), a prophetic mark. Fugitives with nothing else to wear.

Destitute, afflicted, mistreated. Key words. “Destitute” (hysteroumenoi, lacking, in need). “Afflicted” (thlibomenoi, oppressed). “Mistreated” (kakouchoumenoi, ill-treated), the same word as verse 25 of Moses.

Of whom the world was not worthy. Key words. A startling reversal: the world thought them unworthy to live; in God’s eyes, the world was unworthy of them.

Wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth. Key words. Elijah in the wilderness (1 Kings 19); prophets hidden in caves by Obadiah (1 Kings 18:4, 13); the Maccabean faithful hiding in caves (1 Maccabees 2:29–38; 2 Maccabees 6:11).

Where Christians differ: does this make the Maccabean books Scripture? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches include 1 and 2 Maccabees in their Old Testament. Verdict: The author refers to events of the Maccabean period, as he refers to the tradition about Isaiah, as true history, without quoting those books as Scripture. Referring to historical events recorded in a book does not make that book inspired. The Old Testament canon received by Jesus and the apostles is the Hebrew Scriptures (Luke 24:44), which do not include the Apocrypha. The canon is closed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that suffering is a sign of God’s disfavour, or that those who suffered had less faith than those delivered. Both groups lived by faith; God simply chose different outcomes for them.

In a sentence. Women received their loved ones back, raised from the dead. Others were tortured, refusing to be released, so that they might gain a better resurrection. Some faced jeers and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were put to death by stoning; they were sawn in two; they were killed by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, persecuted and ill-treated. The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, living in caves and in holes in the ground.

For worship. Pray today for persecuted believers around the world, of whom the world is not worthy. Ask God for courage if your faith costs you.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

And all these, though commended through their faith. Key words. “Commended” (martyrēthentes), as in verse 2, forming a frame for the chapter. All received God’s approval.

Did not receive what was promised. Key words. “What was promised” (tēn epangelian): the great promise, the coming of the Messiah, the new covenant, and its fulfilment in the eternal inheritance. They received many smaller promises (v. 33), but not the ultimate one.

Since God had provided something better for us. Key words. “Provided” (problepsamenou, foreseen, planned in advance). “Something better” (kreitton ti): the new covenant, the coming of Christ, the full revelation and accomplishment of salvation. We live in the age of fulfilment.

That apart from us they should not be made perfect. Key words. “Made perfect” (teleiōthōsin, brought to completion). Their final perfection, resurrection and glory awaited Christ’s work and will be completed together with us, at his return. God’s plan is to bring all his people, Old and New Testament, to glory together, as one family (12:23; Revelation 7:9). They are now with Christ, “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” (12:23), but their bodies await resurrection with ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Old Testament believers were not saved. They were saved by faith in the promise, on the basis of Christ’s future work (9:15). It means they did not live to see that work accomplished, and their final glory awaits the completion of God’s plan.

In a sentence. All these people were commended for their faith, yet none of them received what had been promised, because God had planned something better for us, so that only together with us would they be made perfect.

For worship. Thank God that you live in the age of fulfilment, and that you will share in glory with Abraham, Moses, Rahab and all the faithful.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.<sup>2</sup>For by it the people of old received their commendation.<sup>3</sup>By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.<sup>4</sup>By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks.<sup>5</sup>By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.<sup>6</sup>And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.<sup>7</sup>By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.<sup>8</sup>By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going.<sup>9</sup>By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise.<sup>10</sup>For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.<sup>11</sup>By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised.<sup>12</sup>Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.<sup>13</sup>These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.<sup>14</sup>For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.<sup>15</sup>If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return.<sup>16</sup>But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.<sup>17</sup>By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son,<sup>18</sup>of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>19</sup>He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.<sup>20</sup>By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau.<sup>21</sup>By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff.<sup>22</sup>By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.<sup>23</sup>By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.<sup>24</sup>By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter,<sup>25</sup>choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin.<sup>26</sup>He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.<sup>27</sup>By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible.<sup>28</sup>By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.<sup>29</sup>By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned.<sup>30</sup>By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.<sup>31</sup>By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.<sup>32</sup>And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets—<sup>33</sup>who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,<sup>34</sup>quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.<sup>35</sup>Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life.<sup>36</sup>Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment.<sup>37</sup>They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated—<sup>38</sup>of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.<sup>39</sup>And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised,<sup>40</sup>since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

12.title: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus: The Discipline of the Father
12.overview:
Chapter 11 filled the stadium; chapter 12 says: run. Strip off what slows you, keep going, and look at Jesus, who ran the hardest course and sat down at the finish. Then the writer reads the readers’ hardships for them: not a sign that God has left them, but the training a Father gives his children, painful now and fruitful later.

The chapter ends with two mountains. Sinai was fire, darkness and a voice the people begged to stop. The church has come to Mount Zion: the city of God, angels in festival, the assembly of the firstborn, the righteous dead made perfect, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s. So do not refuse the one speaking, and worship with reverence, because the God of Zion is still a consuming fire.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Run the Race, and Read the Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Surrounded by so many witnesses to faith, believers should throw off every hindrance and the sin that trips them, and run their race with endurance, keeping their eyes on Jesus, who began and completes our faith. For the joy ahead he endured the cross, scorning its shame, and now reigns at God’s right hand. Considering what he endured from sinners will keep them from losing heart; they have not yet resisted to the point of bloodshed. Their hardships should be understood as a father’s discipline. As Proverbs says, the Lord disciplines those he loves; that is proof that they are his children. Human fathers discipline for a short time as they think best; God disciplines for our good, that we may share his holiness. It is painful at the time, but it produces a peaceful harvest of righteousness in those trained by it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Timescales

Run looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him. The Father's discipline is painful for the moment, but later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Suffering believers wondered whether God had abandoned them.

Now: Hardship received from God's hand is a mark of sonship, not of rejection. Do not make light of it, and do not faint under it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,

Meaning first. Hebrews 12 turns the faith of chapter 11 into a call to run. Surrounded by that great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every hindrance and sin and run the race with endurance, fixing their eyes on Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him and now sits enthroned (vv. 1–3). Their hardships are the Father’s loving discipline: the Lord disciplines those he loves, as fathers discipline their sons; it is painful for the moment, but it produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness and a share in his holiness (vv. 4–11). So they must strengthen weak hands and knees, pursue peace with all and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord, and watch that no one falls short of God’s grace, lets bitterness grow, or becomes like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal and later could not get the blessing back (vv. 12–17). Then a magnificent contrast (vv. 18–24): believers have not come to the terrifying mountain of Sinai, with fire, darkness and a voice that made the people beg to hear no more, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to angels in joyful assembly, to the church of the firstborn, to God the judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to his sprinkled blood that speaks better than Abel’s. Then the final warning (vv. 25–29): do not refuse the one who speaks from heaven; God will shake heaven and earth once more, removing what is created so that what cannot be shaken remains; so let us be grateful for an unshakeable kingdom and worship God with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses. Key words. “Therefore” (toigaroun, for that very reason): because of the faith of chapter 11. “Cloud” (nephos, a great mass, a crowd), a classical image for a vast multitude. “Witnesses” (martyrōn): primarily those who bear witness by their lives to the power of faith, testifying to us through Scripture. They are witnesses in the sense of testifiers, not merely spectators.

Let us also lay aside every weight. Key words. “Lay aside” (apothemenoi, put off, strip off, as clothes). Greek runners stripped for races. “Weight” (onkon, bulk, burden, encumbrance). Not necessarily sinful in itself, but anything that slows us down in the race: distractions, entanglements, good things that crowd out the best.

And sin which clings so closely. Key words. “Clings so closely” (euperistaton, easily surrounding, readily entangling, like a long robe that wraps around the legs and trips a runner). A rare word. Sin entangles and trips us. In context, perhaps especially the sin of unbelief and turning back (3:12–13).

And let us run with endurance the race that is set before us. Key words. “Run” (trechōmen, keep running), present tense. “Endurance” (hypomonēs, steady perseverance), as in 10:36. The Christian life is not a sprint but a long-distance race. “Race” (agōna, contest, struggle, from which comes “agony”). “Set before us” (prokeimenon, lying ahead): God has set the course; we must run it.

Where Christians differ: are the departed saints watching us? Some read “surrounded by witnesses” as teaching that departed believers watch and cheer us from heaven, and some traditions draw from this the practice of praying to the saints. Verdict: The main sense of “witnesses” is those who testify by their faith, as chapter 11 has just shown (11:2, 4, 5, 39 use the related verb, “commended”). Whether the departed are aware of events on earth is not clearly taught, and Scripture gives no warrant for praying to them; there is one mediator, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). The departed saints are consciously with the Lord (Philippians 1:23; 12:23), but our eyes are to be fixed on Jesus, not on them (v. 2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we run to earn salvation. We run because we have been saved, toward the prize of final glory.

In a sentence. Since, then, we are surrounded by such a vast crowd of witnesses, let us throw off everything that slows us down and the sin that so easily trips us up, and let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us,

On a Tuesday. What weight is slowing you down in the Christian race? Name it, and lay it aside this week.

verseByVerse.quote: looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.

Looking to Jesus. Key words. “Looking” (aphorōntes, looking away from everything else to, fixing the eyes on). A runner keeps his eyes on the goal, not on the crowd, the other runners, or the obstacles. We look away from the witnesses, away from our circumstances, to Jesus.

The founder and perfecter of our faith. Key words. “Founder” (archēgon, pioneer, leader, originator, champion), as in 2:10. He started the faith; he blazed the trail. “Perfecter” (teleiōtēn, completer, finisher, one who brings to the goal). He finished the course perfectly himself, and he brings our faith to completion (Philippians 1:6). “Our” is not in the Greek; it reads literally “of the faith.” Jesus is the supreme example of faith (the one who trusted God perfectly to the end) and the author and finisher of faith in us.

Who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross. Key words. “For” (anti): either “because of” (for the sake of the joy ahead) or “instead of” (in place of the joy he could have had). Most likely the first: he looked ahead to the joy of completing the Father’s will, redeeming his people, and being exalted (Isaiah 53:11; John 17:5; Philippians 2:9). “Endured” (hypemeinen, persevered under). “The cross”: the most painful and shameful death known in the Roman world.

Despising the shame. Key words. “Despising” (kataphronēsas, thinking little of, disregarding). Crucifixion was designed to shame: naked, publicly exposed, mocked, cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). Jesus counted the shame as nothing compared with the joy. The readers were facing shame (10:33; 13:13); Jesus shows how to bear it.

And is seated at the right hand of the throne of God. Key words. “Is seated” (kekathiken, perfect tense: has sat down and remains seated). The end of his race: enthroned (1:3; 8:1; 10:12). Our race too will end in glory with him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus did not feel the shame or pain. He felt them fully. But he counted them worth bearing for the joy ahead. Nor does it mean his only motive was his own joy; his joy was bound up with his love for the Father and for us.

In a sentence. keeping our eyes fixed on Jesus, the pioneer who leads us in faith and brings it to completion. Because of the joy that lay ahead of him he endured the cross, thinking nothing of its shame, and he has taken his seat at the right hand of God’s throne.

For worship. Look to Jesus today. Whatever you face, he faced worse, for you, and he is now enthroned. Fix your eyes on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.

Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself. Key words. “Consider” (analogisasthe, think it over, compare, reckon up). Compare your sufferings with his. “Hostility” (antilogian, contradiction, opposition, hostile speech). He endured mockery, slander, betrayal, rejection, beatings and crucifixion from sinners. Some manuscripts read “against themselves” (sinners who opposed him were really harming themselves), but “against himself” is better supported.

So that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. Key words. “Grow weary” (kamēte, become tired, exhausted). “Fainthearted” (eklyomenoi, lose heart, give out, collapse like a runner whose strength fails). Remembering Jesus restores strength.

In your struggle against sin. Key words. “Struggle” (antagōnizomenoi, contending against, fighting an opponent). “Sin”: both the persecution of sinners against them and the temptation to sin by giving up. The fight against sin is a fight against the pressure to abandon Christ.

You have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. Key words. “Resisted” (antikatestēte, stood firm against). “Shedding your blood”: martyrdom. They had suffered insults, imprisonment and loss of property (10:32–34), but none of them had yet been killed. Jesus resisted to the point of death. Their suffering, though real, was not yet as great.

What it does not mean. It does not minimise their suffering. It puts it in perspective. Nor does it mean they will certainly be martyred; it means they should not give up when things are less severe than what Jesus endured.

In a sentence. Think about him who endured such opposition from sinners, so that you will not grow tired and lose heart. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood.

On a Tuesday. When you are weary in the Christian life, stop and consider Jesus: what he endured, and why. Let that renew your strength.

verseByVerse.quote: And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”

And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? Key words. “Forgotten” (eklelēsthe, completely forgotten). “Exhortation” (paraklēseōs, encouragement, appeal). “Addresses you” (dialegetai, speaks with you, reasons with you): Scripture speaks to us personally, now. “As sons” (hōs huiois): the words of Proverbs are God’s fatherly words to his children.

My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord. Key words. From Proverbs 3:11–12. “Regard lightly” (oligōrei, think little of, make light of). “Discipline” (paideias, training, education, correction, child-rearing). Not merely punishment, but the whole process of training a child to maturity, including correction. Do not shrug off hardship as meaningless.

Nor be weary when reproved by him. Key words. “Be weary” (eklyou, lose heart, faint), as in verse 3. “Reproved” (elenchomenos, rebuked, corrected, convicted). The two dangers: making too little of discipline, or being crushed by it.

For the Lord disciplines the one he loves. Key words. “Loves” (agapa). Discipline is evidence of love, not rejection. God disciplines because he loves (Revelation 3:19; Deuteronomy 8:5).

And chastises every son whom he receives. Key words. “Chastises” (mastigoi, scourges, whips): a strong word for severe correction. “Receives” (paradechetai, accepts, welcomes as his own). Every true son experiences it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every hardship is punishment for a specific sin. Discipline here includes training through suffering, including persecution. The readers’ suffering came from faithfulness, not from sin, yet God used it to train them. Nor does it mean God is harsh; his discipline flows from love.

In a sentence. And have you completely forgotten this word of encouragement that speaks to you as children? “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, and do not lose heart when he corrects you, because the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he corrects everyone he accepts as his child.”

For worship. Thank God for the hard things he is using to train you. They are evidence that he loves you as his child.

verseByVerse.quote: It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.

It is for discipline that you have to endure. Key words. “For discipline” (eis paideian): the purpose of their suffering is training. “Endure” (hypomenete). Their hardships were not random or meaningless, but God’s fatherly training.

God is treating you as sons. Key words. “Treating” (prospheretai, dealing with, bringing himself to you). Discipline is a mark of sonship.

For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? Key words. In the ancient world, a father who loved his son trained him, often strictly (Proverbs 13:24; 19:18). A father who did not discipline did not care.

If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated. Key words. “All have participated” (metochoi gegonasi pantes, all have become sharers). Every true child of God experiences it, including Jesus himself (5:8), who learned obedience through suffering.

Then you are illegitimate children and not sons. Key words. “Illegitimate” (nothoi, born out of wedlock, bastards). In the Roman world, a father often took no interest in the upbringing of illegitimate children, since they would not inherit. If God never disciplined you, it would show you were not truly his. Discipline proves sonship.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the more we suffer, the more God loves us, or that those who suffer less are less loved. It means that every true believer will experience God’s training, in various forms, and that hardship is not a sign of God’s absence.

In a sentence. Endure hardship as discipline; God is treating you as his children. For what child is not disciplined by their father? If you are not disciplined, as every child is, then you are not true sons and daughters at all.

For worship. If life is hard right now, receive it as from your Father’s hand. You are his child.

parallels.desc: as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Key words. “Earthly fathers” (tēs sarkos hēmōn pateras, fathers of our flesh). “Respected” (enetrepometha, showed reverence). We submitted to imperfect human fathers.

Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? Key words. “Father of spirits” (tō patri tōn pneumatōn): God, the creator of our spirits (Numbers 16:22; 27:16; Zechariah 12:1), in contrast with “fathers of our flesh.” “And live”: submission to God’s discipline leads to life. Rebellion against it leads to death (Deuteronomy 21:18–21).

For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them. Key words. “Short time” (pros oligas hēmeras, for a few days): only during childhood. “As it seemed best to them” (kata to dokoun autois): according to their own judgement, which was imperfect, sometimes wrong, sometimes selfish.
