But he disciplines us for our good. Key words. “For our good” (epi to sympheron, for what is profitable). God’s discipline is never mistaken, never excessive, never selfish (Romans 8:28).

That we may share his holiness. Key words. “Share” (metalabein, partake of). “His holiness” (tēs hagiotētos autou). The goal is that we become like God, holy as he is holy (1 Peter 1:15–16). Suffering refines character as fire refines gold (1 Peter 1:6–7).

For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant. Key words. “Painful” (lypēs, grievous, sorrowful). Honest: discipline hurts. God does not ask us to pretend otherwise.

But later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness. Key words. “Later” (hysteron, afterwards). “Peaceful fruit of righteousness”: a harvest of righteous character and peace with God (James 3:18). The pain is temporary; the fruit lasts.

To those who have been trained by it. Key words. “Trained” (gegymnasmenois, exercised, as in a gymnasium), as in 5:14. Discipline produces fruit in those who submit to it and learn from it, not in those who resist or resent it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all human fathers are good models; some are abusive, and God’s discipline is never abuse. The comparison is from lesser to greater: if even imperfect human discipline is respected, how much more God’s perfect discipline.

In a sentence. Moreover, we all had human fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them for it. How much more should we submit to the Father of our spirits and live! They disciplined us for a little while as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in his holiness. No discipline seems pleasant at the time; it is painful. But later it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it.

On a Tuesday. In your current hardship, ask God: what are you teaching me? How do you want me to grow in holiness through this?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they should strengthen weak hands and shaky knees and make straight paths, so that the lame are healed rather than disabled. They must pursue peace with everyone and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord, making sure no one falls short of God’s grace, that no bitter root springs up to poison many, and that no one is immoral or careless of holy things like Esau, who sold his birthright for a meal and later found no way back. The writer contrasts two mountains. They have not come to Sinai, with its fire, darkness, storm and a voice so terrifying even Moses trembled. They have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to countless angels, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge of all, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus, mediator of the new covenant, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s. So they must not refuse the one who speaks from heaven. God will shake earth and heaven once more, and only what cannot be shaken will remain. Receiving an unshakable kingdom, they should be thankful and worship God with reverence and awe, for he is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Mountains

Believers have not come to the terrors of Sinai but to Mount Zion, to Jesus and his sprinkled blood. And our God is still a consuming fire: what has changed is our access, not his nature.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Esau sold his birthright for a single meal.

Now: Watch for anyone falling short of grace, and ask what you could not bear to lose — that shows what your life rests on.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.

Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees. Key words. “Therefore”: since hardship is God’s loving training. “Drooping” (pareimenas, hanging down, slack, paralysed). “Weak” (paralelymena, enfeebled, paralysed). From Isaiah 35:3, a promise of restoration for exhausted exiles. The picture of a runner whose arms hang and knees buckle near the end of the race. Get up and keep going.

And make straight paths for your feet. Key words. From Proverbs 4:26 (Greek). “Straight” (orthas, level, upright). Remove obstacles from the path, and walk in the right way. Live in a straightforward, obedient way, without crooked compromises.

So that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed. Key words. “Lame” (chōlon, limping, crippled). “Put out of joint” (ektrapē, dislocated, turned aside). In a community, some are spiritually limping, weak in faith. If the path is rough, they will be further injured or turn aside altogether. If the stronger members make the path straight, the weak can be healed. Our faithfulness helps others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can make ourselves strong by willpower. The strength comes from God (Isaiah 40:29–31). But we are called to respond actively.

In a sentence. So lift up your tired arms and strengthen your weak knees. Make level paths for your feet, so that those who are lame will not be disabled further, but healed.

On a Tuesday. Who in your church is limping spiritually? How could your example or practical help make the path straighter for them?

verseByVerse.quote: Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.

Strive for peace with everyone. Key words. “Strive” (diōkete, pursue, chase, run after). Peace does not happen by accident; it must be pursued (Psalm 34:14; Romans 12:18; 14:19). “With everyone” (meta pantōn): within the church and outside it, as far as it depends on us.

And for the holiness. Key words. “Holiness” (hagiasmon, sanctification, the process of being made holy). Also to be pursued. Holiness is God’s gift and work in us (v. 10; 10:10, 14), but we must actively seek it.

Without which no one will see the Lord. Key words. “See the Lord”: to enter his presence, to enjoy him forever (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2–3; Revelation 22:4). Practical holiness is not optional for believers. It is the evidence of genuine faith and the path to glory. Those who show no desire for holiness show that they do not know God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean holiness earns salvation, or that we must be perfect to enter heaven by our own efforts. We are accepted in Christ’s righteousness alone (Philippians 3:9). But those whom Christ saves, he also sanctifies (1 Corinthians 6:11; Romans 8:29–30). Holiness is the necessary fruit, not the root, of salvation. At death, believers are made perfect in holiness (12:23).

In a sentence. Make every effort to live in peace with everyone and to be holy; without holiness no one will see the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you need to make peace with? Is there a sin you are tolerating? Pursue peace and holiness this week, actively.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;
verseByVerse.commentary:
See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;

See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God. Key words. “See to it” (episkopountes, overseeing, watching over, taking care; the root of “overseer” or “bishop”). The whole church is to watch over one another. “Fails to obtain” (hysterōn, falls short, comes too late, lags behind), as in 4:1. Not that God’s grace is insufficient, but that someone might not receive it, falling back before reaching it.

That no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble. Key words. “Root of bitterness” (rhiza pikrias), from Deuteronomy 29:18, where Moses warned against anyone in Israel whose heart turns from God to idols, a “root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit.” Here it means a person, or an attitude, that begins small, hidden underground, then sprouts and spreads poison. “Causes trouble” (enochlē, disturbs, harasses).

And by it many become defiled. Key words. “Defiled” (mianthōsin, stained, polluted). One bitter person, or one root of unbelief, can poison many. Apostasy and bitterness are contagious.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every negative feeling is a root of bitterness. It refers to a settled turning from God that grows and spreads. Nor does it mean the church should be suspicious and harsh; it should watch over each other in love.

In a sentence. Watch over one another, so that no one falls short of the grace of God, and so that no bitter root grows up to cause trouble and poison many.

For worship. Ask God to uproot any bitterness in your heart before it grows. Forgive, as you have been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.

That no one is sexually immoral. Key words. “Sexually immoral” (pornos, one who commits sexual sin). Genesis does not record sexual sin by Esau, though he married two Hittite women who grieved his parents (Genesis 26:34–35), and Jewish tradition portrayed him as immoral. The word may apply to the general warning rather than specifically to Esau.

Or unholy like Esau. Key words. “Unholy” (bebēlos, profane, godless, treating sacred things as common). Esau’s sin was contempt for spiritual things.

Who sold his birthright for a single meal. Key words. “Birthright” (prōtotokia, the rights of the firstborn): a double inheritance, family leadership, and above all the covenant promise of Abraham (Genesis 25:29–34). Esau traded it for a bowl of stew. Genesis says Esau “despised his birthright” (Genesis 25:34). He chose immediate gratification over eternal blessing. The readers, tempted to give up their heavenly inheritance to escape present suffering, were in danger of doing the same.

For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. Key words. Later, when Isaac blessed Jacob instead, Esau wanted the blessing back but could not have it (Genesis 27:30–40). “Rejected” (apedokimasthē, disqualified, failed the test).

For he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears. Key words. “No chance to repent” (metanoias topon ouch heuren, he found no place for repentance). This is debated. Two main readings: (1) Esau could not change his father Isaac’s mind; the blessing, once given, was irrevocable (Genesis 27:33); (2) Esau himself could not find genuine repentance; his tears were for the lost blessing, not for his sin. “It” (autēn) most naturally refers to the blessing, which he sought with tears (Genesis 27:34, 38). Either way, the lesson: there comes a point when consequences of despising God’s gifts cannot be undone. Esau regretted the loss, but his heart did not change toward God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God refuses those who truly repent. Anyone who genuinely turns to God in Christ will be received (John 6:37). Esau’s tears were tears of regret over lost advantage, not repentance toward God. Nor does it mean that every believer who sins has lost their inheritance.

In a sentence. See that no one is sexually immoral, or godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his rights as the eldest son. Afterwards, as you know, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no way to reverse what he had done, even though he sought the blessing with tears.

On a Tuesday. What “single meal” tempts you to trade away spiritual blessing: a pleasure, comfort, approval? Refuse the trade.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”

For you have not come to what may be touched. Key words. “Come” (proselēlythate, perfect tense: you have come and are there). The same verb used for drawing near to God (4:16; 7:25; 10:22). “What may be touched” (psēlaphōmenō, a physical, tangible mountain): Mount Sinai. The old covenant was earthly and physical.

A blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest. Key words. Describing Sinai when God gave the law (Exodus 19:16–19; 20:18–21; Deuteronomy 4:11–12; 5:22–26). Seven terrifying features: fire, darkness, gloom, storm, trumpet, voice, and the command not to touch.

And the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. Key words. The people were so terrified by God’s voice that they asked Moses to speak to them instead (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:25–27).

For they could not endure the order that was given, If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned. Key words. From Exodus 19:12–13. The mountain was so holy that even an animal touching it had to die. God’s holiness at Sinai kept sinners at a distance.

Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, I tremble with fear. Key words. Moses’ words recall Deuteronomy 9:19, where he feared God’s anger after the golden calf. Even the mediator himself was terrified.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the God of Sinai is different from the God of the gospel. He is the same holy God (v. 29). The difference is the covenant: at Sinai, sinful people met God’s holiness without a perfect mediator; in Christ, they meet the same God through the blood that brings peace.

In a sentence. You have not come to a mountain that can be touched, to a mountain burning with fire, to darkness, gloom and storm, to a trumpet blast and a voice that made those who heard it beg that no more words be spoken to them. They could not bear the command, “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned to death.” The sight was so terrifying that Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.”

For worship. Remember the terror of Sinai, and then thank God that you come to him through Christ, not as a terrified sinner but as a welcomed child.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

But you have come to Mount Zion. Key words. “You have come” (proselēlythate, perfect tense): already, now, by faith. Not only in the future but in present reality, believers have been brought into this heavenly assembly, especially in worship. Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where God dwelt in the temple, symbol of his presence and kingship (Psalm 2:6; 48:1–2).

And to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. Key words. The city Abraham looked for (11:10, 16), the Jerusalem above (Galatians 4:26; Revelation 21:2).

And to innumerable angels in festal gathering. Key words. “Innumerable” (myriasin, myriads, tens of thousands). “Festal gathering” (panēgyrei, festal assembly, joyful celebration). Angels in joyful worship (Revelation 5:11–12). At Sinai, angels were present in terror (Deuteronomy 33:2); at Zion, in celebration.

And to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. Key words. “Assembly” (ekklēsia, church). “Firstborn” (prōtotokōn, plural): all believers, who share the privileges of the firstborn Son (Romans 8:29) as heirs. Unlike Esau, who sold his birthright. “Enrolled” (apogegrammenōn, registered, written down): their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 21:27). The whole church, on earth and in heaven.

And to God, the judge of all. Key words. We come to God himself, who is still judge. But we come to him through Jesus (v. 24).

And to the spirits of the righteous made perfect. Key words. “Spirits” (pneumasi): believers who have died, existing consciously in God’s presence before the resurrection of their bodies. “Made perfect” (teteleiōmenōn): their salvation is complete in that they are free from sin and in God’s presence, though they await the resurrection (11:40). This verse is strong evidence for the conscious intermediate state.

And to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. Key words. The climax: Jesus himself. “New” (neas, young, fresh). He is the one who makes our access possible.

And to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. Key words. “Sprinkled blood”: Christ’s blood, which cleanses (9:13–14, 19–22; 10:22). Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks of pardon and peace (Genesis 4:10; Hebrews 11:4). Abel’s blood called for vengeance against the murderer; Christ’s blood pleads mercy even for those who shed it.

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some teach that the soul sleeps or ceases to exist between death and resurrection. Verdict: This verse speaks of “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” as already present in the heavenly assembly. Jesus promised the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and Paul longed to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). Believers who die go immediately and consciously into Christ’s presence, made perfect in holiness, awaiting the resurrection of their bodies.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are already in heaven physically, or that we should pray to the departed saints. It means we already belong to that heavenly assembly, and in worship we join with it.

In a sentence. But you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to thousands upon thousands of angels in joyful assembly, to the church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven. You have come to God, the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better message than the blood of Abel.

For worship. Next time you gather for worship, remember where you really are: in Zion, with angels and saints, before God, through Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks of pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”

See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. Key words. The fifth and final warning. “Refuse” (paraitēsēsthe, beg off, decline, turn away from), the same word as “beg” in verse 19. Israel begged not to hear; do not refuse to hear. “Him who is speaking” (ton lalounta, present tense): God, who speaks now through his Son (1:1–2) and through his sprinkled blood (v. 24).

For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth. Key words. At Sinai, God warned them on earth, through Moses. Those who rejected him perished in the wilderness (3:16–19).

Much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. Key words. “Reject” (apostrephomenoi, turn away from). The same argument as 2:2–3 and 10:28–29. God now speaks from heaven, through his exalted Son; the responsibility is greater.

At that time his voice shook the earth. Key words. At Sinai, the mountain trembled (Exodus 19:18; Judges 5:4–5; Psalm 68:8).

But now he has promised, Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens. Key words. From Haggai 2:6. In Haggai, God promised to shake the nations and fill his house with glory. The author sees its final fulfilment in the last great shaking at Christ’s return, when the whole created order will be transformed (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 6:12–14). “Promised”: for God’s people, it is a promise, not a threat.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God speaks new revelation from heaven today. He speaks through his Son, whose word is recorded in Scripture. To refuse Scripture is to refuse him.

In a sentence. See to it that you do not refuse the one who speaks. If those who refused him when he warned them on earth did not escape, how much less will we escape if we turn away from him who warns us from heaven? At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”

On a Tuesday. When you read Scripture this week, listen as to God speaking from heaven. Do not refuse what he says.

verseByVerse.quote: This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.

This phrase, Yet once more. Key words. The author draws out the significance of “once more” (eti hapax, yet once for all). The word hapax (once for all) has been used of Christ’s sacrifice (9:26–28). It points to a final, decisive shaking.

Indicates the removal of things that are shaken. Key words. “Removal” (metathesin, change, transformation, transfer), the same word used of the change of priesthood (7:12). The present created order will be removed or transformed.

That is, things that have been made. Key words. Created things, the present heavens and earth (1:10–12). Everything temporary, everything belonging to this passing age.

In order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain. Key words. “Cannot be shaken” (ta mē saleuomena). “Remain” (meinē, abide, last). What belongs to God’s eternal kingdom will remain: God himself, Christ, his people, his word (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:23–25), and the new creation.

What it does not mean. It does not necessarily mean creation will be annihilated and replaced from nothing. Scripture speaks of renewal and transformation (Romans 8:19–21). What is shaken and removed is the old order of sin, decay and death; what remains is renewed creation.

In a sentence. The words “once more” show that what can be shaken, that is, created things, will be removed, so that what cannot be shaken may remain.

For worship. When everything you know is shaken, hold onto what cannot be shaken: God, his Son, his word, his kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Key words. “Grateful” (echōmen charin, have grace, give thanks). “Receiving” (paralambanontes, present tense: we are receiving). We are already receiving this kingdom now, by faith, though it will be fully revealed at Christ’s return. “Kingdom that cannot be shaken” (basileian asaleuton): God’s eternal kingdom, promised in Daniel 7:14, 18, 27, where the saints receive a kingdom that will never be destroyed. Christ reigns now, and his kingdom grows through the gospel, until it is revealed in fullness at his single, visible return.

And thus let us offer to God acceptable worship. Key words. “Offer worship” (latreuōmen, serve, worship as priests). “Acceptable” (euarestōs, well-pleasing). Gratitude leads to worship. The right response to grace is a whole life of worship (Romans 12:1), expressed especially in praise and good works (13:15–16).

With reverence and awe. Key words. “Reverence” (eulabeias, godly fear, devout respect), as of Jesus in 5:7. “Awe” (deous, fear, dread). Grace does not make worship casual. We come with confidence (4:16) but also with awe.

For our God is a consuming fire. Key words. From Deuteronomy 4:24. “Our God”: the God of the new covenant is the same God who appeared in fire at Sinai. His holiness has not changed. For those outside Christ, he is a consuming fire of judgement (10:27). For those in Christ, his fire purifies (1 Corinthians 3:13–15; Malachi 3:2–3), and his holiness evokes worship. Grace and holiness are not opposites.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should live in terror of God. We have peace with him through Christ (Romans 5:1). But we must never treat him lightly. Reverent awe and childlike confidence belong together.

In a sentence. Since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful, and so worship God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

For worship. Come to worship this Sunday with both gratitude and awe: you are receiving an unshakeable kingdom from a holy God.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,<sup>2</sup>looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.<sup>3</sup>Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted.<sup>4</sup>In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.<sup>5</sup>And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him.<sup>6</sup>For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”<sup>7</sup>It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline?<sup>8</sup>If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.<sup>9</sup>Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?<sup>10</sup>For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.<sup>11</sup>For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.<sup>12</sup>Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees,<sup>13</sup>and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.<sup>14</sup>Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.<sup>15</sup>See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;<sup>16</sup>that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.<sup>17</sup>For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.<sup>18</sup>For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest<sup>19</sup>and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them.<sup>20</sup>For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”<sup>21</sup>Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”<sup>22</sup>But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering,<sup>23</sup>and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,<sup>24</sup>and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.<sup>25</sup>See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven.<sup>26</sup>At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”<sup>27</sup>This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.<sup>28</sup>Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe,<sup>29</sup>for our God is a consuming fire.

13.title: Outside the Camp: The Unchanging Christ
13.overview:
The sermon lands in ordinary life: keep loving each other, welcome strangers, visit prisoners, honour marriage, be content with what you have. This is not a change of subject. People who have come to Mount Zion live this way in their own streets.

At the centre stands verse 8: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The founding leaders have died; Christ has not changed, so there is nothing newer to chase. Then the letter’s last appeal: Jesus suffered outside the gate, so go out to him, bearing his disgrace, for here we have no lasting city. The Christian’s sacrifices now are praise and practical kindness. The letter closes with a great benediction: the God who raised the great Shepherd works in us what pleases him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter turns to practical life. Brotherly love must continue. Believers should show hospitality to strangers, for some have entertained angels without knowing it, and remember prisoners and the mistreated as if sharing their suffering. Marriage is to be honoured by all and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. Their lives should be free from the love of money, content with what they have, because God has promised never to leave or forsake them, so they can say with confidence that the Lord is their helper and they need not fear what people can do.
verseByVerse.theology:
Where the Argument Lands

The letter's theology ends in hospitality, prison visiting, marriage and money. Contentment rests on a promise: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Visiting prisoners marked a believer out publicly, and these readers had done it before.

Now: Keep loving, keep welcoming, keep remembering those in prison as though in prison with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.

Meaning first. Hebrews 13 shows what life in the unshakeable kingdom looks like day to day, and closes the letter. It begins with practical love (vv. 1–6): keep loving one another as family, welcome strangers, remember prisoners and the mistreated, honour marriage and keep it pure, stay free from the love of money and be content, because God has promised never to leave or forsake his people. Then it turns to leaders and teaching (vv. 7–19): remember your former leaders and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever; do not be carried away by strange teachings about foods, for the heart is strengthened by grace. We have an altar, Christ’s sacrifice, from which those who cling to the old system have no right to eat; as the sin offering was burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make his people holy by his blood. So let us go to him outside the camp, bearing his disgrace, because here we have no lasting city but seek the one to come; let us offer the sacrifice of praise and of doing good and sharing; obey and submit to your present leaders, who watch over your souls; and pray for the author. The letter closes with a magnificent benediction (vv. 20–21): may the God of peace, who brought back the great Shepherd from the dead by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you to do his will. Then a final appeal and greetings (vv. 22–25).

Let brotherly love continue. Key words. “Brotherly love” (philadelphia, love of brothers and sisters, family affection). The church is a family (2:11). “Continue” (menetō, remain, abide). They had shown it (6:10; 10:33–34); they must keep it up, especially under pressure, when relationships can fray.

Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers. Key words. “Hospitality” (philoxenias, love of strangers). In the ancient world, inns were often dangerous, dirty and immoral. Travelling Christians, missionaries and refugees depended on believers’ homes (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9; 3 John 5–8). Persecution may also have made strangers suspicious; hospitality could be risky.

For thereby some have entertained angels unawares. Key words. “Unawares” (elathon, without knowing it). Abraham, Lot and others welcomed angels without first knowing who they were (Genesis 18:1–8; 19:1–3; Judges 6:11–24; 13:15–21). We never know whom we are serving. Jesus said that welcoming the least of his brothers is welcoming him (Matthew 25:35, 40).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should show hospitality hoping to meet angels. It means that ordinary acts of welcome can have extraordinary significance in God’s eyes. Nor does it require naivety; wisdom in protecting one’s household is still needed.

In a sentence. Keep on loving one another as brothers and sisters. Do not forget to welcome strangers into your homes, because by doing so some people have shown hospitality to angels without realising it.

On a Tuesday. Invite someone into your home this month: a newcomer to church, a lonely neighbour, an international student, a visiting missionary.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham, Lot and others welcomed angels without first knowing who they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.

Remember those who are in prison. Key words. “Remember” (mimnēskesthe, keep in mind, care for). Not just think about, but act on behalf of. Prisoners in the Roman world depended on outside help for food and clothing. Many Christians were imprisoned for their faith (10:34).

As though in prison with them. Key words. “As though in prison with them” (hōs syndedemenoi, as fellow prisoners, bound together with them). Identify with them so closely that you feel their chains.

And those who are mistreated. Key words. “Mistreated” (kakouchoumenōn, ill-treated, tortured), as in 11:25, 37.

Since you also are in the body. Key words. Either “since you also are in the body of Christ” (the same body suffers together, 1 Corinthians 12:26) or “since you too are still in a physical body” and can suffer the same. Probably the second: you too are vulnerable, so feel for them as you would want them to feel for you.

What it does not mean. It does not limit care to Christian prisoners only, though they are the focus. Compassion for all who suffer reflects Christ’s heart.

In a sentence. Remember those in prison as if you were in prison with them, and those who are ill-treated as if you yourselves were suffering, because you too live in a body.

On a Tuesday. Learn the name of one Christian imprisoned for their faith today. Pray for them, and write to them or support an organisation that helps them.

verseByVerse.quote: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.

Let marriage be held in honor among all. Key words. “Honor” (timios, precious, valued, held in high esteem). “Among all” (en pasin): by everyone, or in every respect. Marriage is God’s good gift from creation (Genesis 2:18–25). Some, perhaps influenced by ascetic teachers (1 Timothy 4:3), disparaged it; others, influenced by pagan culture, treated it lightly. Both are wrong.

And let the marriage bed be undefiled. Key words. “Marriage bed” (koitē, bed, a euphemism for sexual union). “Undefiled” (amiantos, pure, unstained), the word used of Christ in 7:26. Sexual union within marriage is good and pure. Outside marriage, it is defiled.

For God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous. Key words. “Sexually immoral” (pornous, those who engage in sexual relations outside marriage). “Adulterous” (moichous, those who violate their own or another’s marriage). God himself will judge (1 Corinthians 6:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21; Revelation 21:8). Sexual sin is not a private matter; God sees and will judge.

Where Christians differ: what counts as marriage, and how should the church respond to sexual sin? Some Christians today accept sexual relationships outside of marriage between a man and a woman. Verdict: Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union is reserved for the lifelong covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). All sexual activity outside it is sin. This is held with compassion: many struggle in this area, and the gospel offers full forgiveness and cleansing to all who repent (1 Corinthians 6:11). The church must uphold the standard and extend grace together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single people are less honourable. Singleness is also a good gift (1 Corinthians 7:7–8). Nor does it mean that past sexual sin cannot be forgiven; judgement falls on those who persist unrepentant.

In a sentence. Marriage should be honoured by everyone, and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge those who commit sexual sin and adultery.

On a Tuesday. If married, do one thing this week to honour your spouse and your marriage. If single, honour marriage in how you speak about it and how you guard your own purity.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”

Keep your life free from love of money. Key words. “Free from love of money” (aphilargyros), as required of elders (1 Timothy 3:3). Money is not evil, but loving it is (1 Timothy 6:10). The readers had lost property (10:34); they might be tempted to cling to what they had left, or to compromise to regain it.

And be content with what you have. Key words. “Content” (arkoumenoi, satisfied, having enough), as in Philippians 4:11 and 1 Timothy 6:8.

For he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you. Key words. “He” is God himself (autos, emphatic). The promise echoes Deuteronomy 31:6, 8 (to Israel and Joshua), Joshua 1:5, and 1 Chronicles 28:20. In Greek, five negatives pile up: “I will never, no never, leave you; never, no never, forsake you.” The reason for contentment is not having enough money but having God. If we have him, we have everything.

So we can confidently say. Key words. “Confidently” (tharrountas, being of good courage).

The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me? Key words. From Psalm 118:6. “Helper” (boēthos, one who runs to help at a cry), as in 2:18. If God is for us, human enemies, persecutors and losses cannot finally harm us (Romans 8:31; Matthew 10:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never work to provide or save. Diligence and provision are biblical (1 Timothy 5:8). It means our security and contentment rest in God, not in money.

In a sentence. Do not let love of money rule your lives; be satisfied with what you have, because God himself has said, “I will never leave you; I will never abandon you.” So we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can mere people do to me?”

For worship. Repeat God’s promise to yourself today: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” Let it cure your anxiety about money.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They should remember the leaders who taught them God’s word, consider the outcome of their lives and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever. They must not be carried away by strange teachings, especially about ritual foods; the heart is strengthened by grace. Christians have an altar from which the old priesthood has no right to eat. Just as the bodies of sacrificial animals were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make his people holy by his blood. So believers should go out to him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace he bore, because here they have no lasting city but seek the one to come. Through him they are to offer God a continual sacrifice of praise and not neglect to do good and share, which pleases God. They should obey and submit to their leaders, who keep watch over their souls and must give account, so that their work is a joy and not a burden. And they should pray for the writer, who has a clear conscience and hopes to be restored to them soon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Outside the Camp

Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp. Go to him there, bearing his reproach, and offer the sacrifices that please God: praise, doing good and sharing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For these readers the camp was home — temple, synagogue, festivals and family table.

Now: Leaving what is not lasting is not homelessness; it is going to where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Key words. “Leaders” (hēgoumenōn, those who lead, guide). Probably the founding leaders of the church, perhaps including apostles, who first preached the gospel to them (2:3) and had since died. “Spoke the word of God”: their authority was the word they preached.

Consider the outcome of their way of life. Key words. “Consider” (anatheōrountes, look carefully at, observe closely). “Outcome” (ekbasin, end, result, exit): how their lives ended. Perhaps some died as martyrs, others in faith. They finished well.

And imitate their faith. Key words. “Imitate” (mimeisthe), as in 6:12. Not their personalities or methods, but their faith.

Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Key words. “The same” (ho autos), echoing 1:12. Leaders come and go, but Jesus remains. The same Christ who sustained their former leaders will sustain them. Yesterday: in his earthly life and ministry, and in the faith of their leaders. Today: interceding for them now (7:25). Forever: unchanging in his person, promises and power. This also prepares for verse 9: since Christ does not change, there is no need for new, strange teachings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is static or inactive. He acts in every generation. It means his character, promises and saving work do not change.

In a sentence. Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Think about how their lives turned out, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever.

For worship. Thank God for those who first taught you the gospel. And rest in the unchanging Christ, who was faithful to them and will be faithful to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.

Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings. Key words. “Led away” (parapheresthe, carried aside, swept off course), like a ship drifting (2:1). “Diverse” (poikilais, varied, many-coloured). “Strange” (xenais, foreign, alien to the gospel). Since Christ does not change (v. 8), new teachings that depart from him should be rejected.

For it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace. Key words. “Strengthened” (bebaiousthai, made firm, established). “By grace” (chariti): by God’s free favour in Christ. The heart is established by grace, received through the gospel, not by rituals.

Not by foods. Key words. “Foods” (brōmasin): probably Jewish food laws, sacrificial meals, or special ritual meals that some taught were necessary for spiritual strength. The old covenant sacrificial meals (where worshippers ate part of the offerings) may be in view, given verse 10.

Which have not benefited those devoted to them. Key words. “Devoted to them” (hoi peripatountes, those who walk in them, live by them). Such practices never truly strengthened anyone spiritually (9:9–10; Colossians 2:16–23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be indifferent to what they eat for health. It means food rules do not make us right with God or spiritually strong (Romans 14:17; 1 Corinthians 8:8).

In a sentence. Do not be carried off course by all kinds of strange teachings. It is good for our hearts to be strengthened by grace, not by rules about food, which are of no value to those who observe them.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of teachings that offer spiritual strength through rules and rituals rather than through grace. Feed your heart on the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.

We have an altar. Key words. “Altar” (thysiastērion, place of sacrifice). The Christian altar is the cross, or Christ’s sacrifice itself. We “eat” from it by faith, feeding spiritually on Christ crucified (John 6:53–58).

From which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. Key words. “Those who serve the tent”: those who cling to the old tabernacle worship. “No right” (ouk echousin exousian, no authority). Under the old covenant, priests ate portions of many sacrifices, but never of the Day of Atonement sin offering, which was wholly burned (Leviticus 6:30; 16:27). Christ is the true sin offering; those who stay with the old system cannot share in him.

For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. Key words. On the Day of Atonement, the blood of the bull and goat was brought into the Most Holy Place, and their bodies were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27).

So Jesus also suffered outside the gate. Key words. “Outside the gate”: Jesus was crucified outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:17, 20; Matthew 27:32). Like the sin offering, he was put outside, rejected, treated as unclean. Outside the camp was the place of the unclean, the leper, the outcast (Leviticus 13:46; Numbers 15:35–36).

In order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Key words. “Sanctify” (hagiasē, make holy), as in 10:10, 14. “The people” (ton laon): his people. Through his rejection and death, he made his people holy.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s Table an altar? Roman Catholic and some Anglo-Catholic traditions identify this altar with the communion table, on which the sacrifice of the Mass is offered. Verdict: The New Testament never calls the Lord’s Table an altar. The altar here is Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice on the cross (7:27; 10:10–14). We “eat” from it by faith in his finished work, especially as we receive the Lord’s Supper, where Christ is spiritually present and we feed on him by faith; but there is no new sacrifice offered.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should despise Jewish people. The point is that the old covenant system cannot give access to Christ’s benefits; only faith in him can.

In a sentence. We have an altar from which those who minister at the tabernacle have no right to eat. The high priest carries the blood of animals into the Most Holy Place as a sin offering, but their bodies are burned outside the camp. In the same way, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make the people holy through his own blood.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he went outside the gate, rejected and shamed, to make you holy. Feed on him by faith today.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.

Therefore let us go to him outside the camp. Key words. “Go” (exerchōmetha, go out, keep going out). “Outside the camp”: for the readers, this meant leaving behind the security and respectability of Judaism, its temple, its rituals and its community, to identify fully with the rejected Christ. Following Jesus means going where he went.

And bear the reproach he endured. Key words. “Reproach” (oneidismon, disgrace, insult), as of Moses in 11:26. Identifying with Christ brings shame from those who reject him. The readers were tempted to avoid it by returning to Judaism. They must embrace it.

For here we have no lasting city. Key words. “Lasting” (menousan, abiding, permanent). Jerusalem itself, the holy city, was not permanent; it would be destroyed in AD 70. No earthly city, nation or institution is our permanent home.

But we seek the city that is to come. Key words. “Seek” (epizētoumen, search for, long for). The heavenly Jerusalem (11:10, 16; 12:22). Like Abraham, we are pilgrims.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should withdraw from society or not care about their earthly cities. We are to seek the welfare of the city where we live (Jeremiah 29:7). But we do not put our ultimate hope there.

In a sentence. So let us go out to him outside the camp, carrying the disgrace he bore. For here we do not have a permanent city; we are looking for the city that is coming.

On a Tuesday. Where does following Jesus mean going “outside the camp” for you: risking reputation, comfort or acceptance? Go to him there.

verseByVerse.quote: Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.

Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God. Key words. “Through him” (di’ autou): through Christ, our High Priest. Our offerings are acceptable only through him (1 Peter 2:5). “Continually” (dia pantos), as the old priests offered continually (9:6); our praise never stops. “Sacrifice of praise” (thysian aineseōs): the Old Testament thank offering (Leviticus 7:12; Psalm 50:14, 23; 116:17). No more sacrifices for sin are needed (10:18), but thank offerings continue.

That is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Key words. “Fruit of lips” (karpon cheileōn), from Hosea 14:2 (Greek). “Acknowledge” (homologountōn, confess, profess). Praising God and confessing Christ openly, the very thing the readers were tempted to stop doing.

Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have. Key words. “Do good” (eupoiias, doing good, kindness). “Share” (koinōnias, fellowship, generosity, sharing possessions). Practical generosity.

For such sacrifices are pleasing to God. Key words. “Pleasing” (euaresteitai), as in 11:5–6. Two kinds of Christian sacrifice: praise (Godward) and good works (manward). Both are worship (Romans 12:1; Philippians 4:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean these sacrifices atone for sin. They are responses of gratitude to Christ’s completed atonement.

In a sentence. Through Jesus, therefore, let us keep offering God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that openly confess his name. And do not forget to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

For worship. Offer God two sacrifices today: praise from your lips and a generous act for someone in need.

verseByVerse.quote: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.

Obey your leaders and submit to them. Key words. “Leaders” (hēgoumenois): their present leaders, in contrast with the former ones (v. 7). “Obey” (peithesthe, be persuaded by, follow). “Submit” (hypeikete, yield, defer). In a time of temptation and false teaching, the church must follow its faithful leaders, the elders who teach God’s word.

For they are keeping watch over your souls. Key words. “Keeping watch” (agrypnousin, staying awake, losing sleep, being vigilant), like a shepherd watching the flock at night (Luke 2:8) or a sentry on guard. Faithful elders lose sleep over their people.

As those who will have to give an account. Key words. “Give an account” (logon apodōsontes). Leaders will answer to God for how they cared for their people (James 3:1; Ezekiel 34; 1 Peter 5:1–4). This makes their task serious and their authority accountable.

Let them do this with joy and not with groaning. Key words. “Groaning” (stenazontes, sighing, grieving). Leaders can serve joyfully or with grief, depending partly on how the people respond.

For that would be of no advantage to you. Key words. “Of no advantage” (alysiteles, unprofitable, harmful). A church that makes its leaders groan harms itself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean blind obedience to leaders who teach error or command sin (Acts 5:29; Galatians 1:8–9). It means willing, respectful following of leaders who faithfully teach God’s word and care for the flock. Nor does it support a single ruling bishop; “leaders” is plural, consistent with a plurality of elders.

In a sentence. Have confidence in your leaders and follow their guidance, because they keep watch over you as people who must give an account. Let them do this with joy, not with sighs of grief, for that would do you no good.

On a Tuesday. How can you make your elders’ work a joy this week? Encourage them, pray for them, and follow their faithful guidance.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.

Pray for us. Key words. “Pray” (proseuchesthe, keep praying). “Us”: the author and his companions. Every leader needs the prayers of God’s people.

For we are sure that we have a clear conscience. Key words. “Sure” (peithometha, are persuaded). “Clear conscience” (kalēn syneidēsin, good conscience). Perhaps the author had been criticised. He is confident that his motives and conduct are right.

Desiring to act honorably in all things. Key words. “Honorably” (kalōs, well, rightly, nobly). His goal is integrity in everything.

I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner. Key words. “Restored” (apokatastathō, given back). The author had been with them before and was now separated, perhaps by imprisonment or other circumstances. He believes their prayers will make a real difference.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the author claimed sinlessness. A clear conscience means not knowingly living in hypocrisy or unconfessed sin.

In a sentence. Pray for us. We are sure that our conscience is clear, and we want to live honourably in every way. I especially urge you to pray so that I may be returned to you soon.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for your pastor and for a missionary you know. Your prayers matter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter closes with a prayer of blessing. The writer asks that the God of peace, who raised our Lord Jesus from the dead, the great shepherd of his flock, through the blood that seals the everlasting covenant, will supply them with every good thing they need to do his will, and will himself produce in them what pleases him, through Jesus Christ, to whom glory belongs for ever. He asks them to take his short message of encouragement patiently, tells them Timothy has been set free and may travel with him, sends greetings to their leaders and to all God’s people, including from believers from Italy, and ends with grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Works in Us

The God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, equips his people and works in them what pleases him. What he requires, he supplies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The writer calls his letter a “word of exhortation”, a sermon sent to people he knows and misses.

Now: After its hardest warnings, the letter ends with grace for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Now may the God of peace. Key words. “God of peace” (ho theos tēs eirēnēs): the God who has made peace with sinners through Christ’s blood, and who gives peace (Romans 15:33; 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:23). Fitting for a church troubled by persecution and tempted toward division.

Who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus. Key words. “Brought again” (anagagōn, led up, brought back). The only explicit mention of the resurrection in Hebrews, though it is assumed throughout (his indestructible life, 7:16; his entry into heaven).

The great shepherd of the sheep. Key words. “Great shepherd” (ton poimena tōn probatōn ton megan). Echoing Isaiah 63:11, where God brought up from the sea the shepherd of his flock (Moses). Jesus is the greater shepherd (John 10:11, 14; 1 Peter 2:25; 5:4), who laid down his life for the sheep and was brought back from death.

By the blood of the eternal covenant. Key words. “Eternal covenant” (diathēkēs aiōniou): the new covenant, which will never be replaced (Isaiah 55:3; Jeremiah 32:40; Ezekiel 37:26). Christ’s blood ratified it; God raised him because his sacrifice was accepted. The resurrection is the Father’s seal on the covenant.

Equip you with everything good that you may do his will. Key words. “Equip” (katartisai, make complete, fit out, mend, restore, as nets are mended). “Do his will”: as Christ came to do God’s will (10:7, 9), so his people do it by his equipping.

Working in us that which is pleasing in his sight. Key words. “Working” (poiōn, doing, producing). God himself works in us what pleases him (Philippians 2:13). Our obedience is real, but it is God’s work in us.

Through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. Key words. “To whom”: probably Christ, though possibly God the Father. Either way, glory is given to God through Christ. The letter that exalts Christ above angels, Moses and Aaron ends by giving him eternal glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are passive. God equips us so that we do his will. Divine work and human obedience go together.

In a sentence. Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with everything good for doing his will, and may he work in us what is pleasing to him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

For worship. Pray this benediction over yourself and your church today. Ask the God of peace to equip you for his will.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.

I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation. Key words. “Bear with” (anechesthe, put up with, listen patiently). The warnings have been severe; the author asks them to receive them in good spirit. “Word of exhortation” (tou logou tēs paraklēseōs): a phrase used of a synagogue sermon (Acts 13:15). Hebrews is essentially a written sermon.

For I have written to you briefly. Key words. “Briefly” (dia bracheōn). Hebrews takes under an hour to read aloud; given the vastness of its subject, it is brief (9:5; 11:32).

You should know that our brother Timothy has been released. Key words. Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Released” (apolelymenon, set free). This is the only mention of Timothy’s imprisonment in the New Testament, perhaps after Paul’s death in Rome.

With whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Key words. The author planned to travel with Timothy to visit the readers.

Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Key words. “All your leaders”: plural, the elders (v. 17). “All the saints”: every believer, holy in Christ.

Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Key words. “Those who come from Italy” (hoi apo tēs Italias) can mean Italians living abroad, sending greetings home to Rome, or people in Italy sending greetings elsewhere. The first reading suggests the letter was sent to Rome, which fits other evidence: the earliest known use of Hebrews was by Clement of Rome, around AD 95.

Grace be with all of you. Key words. The last word of the letter: grace. The letter has warned, exhorted and taught, but all rests on grace (4:16; 12:15; 13:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the letter’s warnings were overstated. The author asks them to bear with his exhortation precisely because it was serious, and loving.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, I urge you to listen patiently to my message of encouragement, for I have written to you only briefly. I want you to know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. Greet all your leaders and all God’s people. Those from Italy send you their greetings. Grace be with you all.

For worship. Thank God for the whole letter to the Hebrews: Christ is better, and his grace is with you all.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Those who come from Italy” may be Italians abroad sending greetings home, or believers in Italy itself.
